data.title: Preprint: Cost Analysis of Vasopressin Use in Septic Shock and Predictive Performance of GOSSIS in ICU Mortality
data.authors: Suh, K.; Wang, S.; Donadee, C.; Boeltz, A.; Barbash, I. J.; Guo, X.; Alam, S.; Horvat, C.; Collier, V.; Rivosecchi, R.
data.category: intensive care and critical care medicine
data.abstract: Background: Vasopressin is a commonly used adjunctive therapy in the management of septic shock. While vasopressin may provide clinical benefits, at times its acquisition cost has risen to being substantially more expensive than other second-line vasopressors such as epinephrine, phenylephrine, or dopamine. Additionally, mortality prediction tools such as the Global Open-Source Severity of Illness Score (GOSSIS) have emerged as a valuable resource to guide resource allocation in critical care. This study aimed to evaluate the healthcare costs associated with vasopressin use and assess the predictive performance of GOSSIS in patients with septic shock. Methods: We conducted a multi-center retrospective cohort study of adult ICU patients with septic shock treated throughout the UPMC Health System from January 2021 to January 2022. Patients who received norepinephrine as a first-line vasopressor followed by either vasopressin or an alternative vasopressor were included. Generalized linear models with a log link and gamma distribution were used to compare adjusted total healthcare costs. Recycled predictions were used to estimate marginal cost differences. GOSSIS performance was evaluated by comparing predicted versus observed ICU mortality across risk groups. Results: Among 3,898 eligible patients, 1,060 received vasopressin and 2,838 received alternative second-line vasopressors. Vasopressin use was associated with significantly higher adjusted hospital costs (cost ratio = 1.14, 95% CI: 1.08, 1.20). The estimated marginal cost difference was $5,887 per patient. Drug costs accounted for a greater proportion of total hospitalization costs among vasopressin users (20% vs. 12%). GOSSIS demonstrated strong calibration, with predicted ICU mortality closely aligning with observed rates across all severity strata. Conclusions: Vasopressin use in septic shock was associated with a 14% increase in hospitalization costs compared to alternative second-line vasopressors. The GOSSIS demonstrated strong predictive validity for ICU mortality, supporting its potential use in guiding resource allocation decisions in critically ill populations.

data.title: Preprint: Uncovering Distinct Phenotypes of Early Onset Heart Failure in Women
data.authors: Khorsandi, J.; Yu, Y.; Tinnium, D.; Ganesh, S.; Alahapphan, R.; Oyinloye, P.; Mueller, K.; Ardekani, S.; Taylor, C. O.; Greenstein, J. L.; Ndumele, C. E.; Michos, E. D.; Bairey Merz, C. N.; Barrett, R. B.; Minhas, A. S.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine
data.abstract: Background: Heart failure in younger women is understudied and may reflect heterogeneous pathways and risk not adequately captured by conventional classifications. We aimed to identify clinically distinct phenotypes of early-onset heart failure in women, assess their prognostic significance, and evaluate their transportability in an independent national cohort. Methods: We identified women aged 18-55 years with heart failure using electronic health record data from a large multi-hospital system. A variational deep embedding model incorporating 283 clinical features was used for unsupervised phenotyping. Associations with subsequent inpatient hospitalization, emergency department utilization, and mortality were evaluated using age-stratified Cox models. Phenotype transportability was assessed by both applying the institutionally trained model and by independent de novo clustering as a replication analysis in the All of Us cohort. Results: Among 1,407 young women with heart failure (median age, 45 years), four phenotypes were identified: hypertensive pregnancy (n=494), cardiorenal (n=276), autoimmune (n=394), and cardiometabolic-ischemic (n=243), with a bootstrap adjusted Rand index of 0.65 and silhouette score of 0.45. Compared with the hypertensive pregnancy phenotype, risks of inpatient hospitalization were highest for the cardiorenal (HR 2.86 [95% CI, 2.35?3.49]) and autoimmune (HR 2.25 [95% CI, 1.87?2.70]) phenotypes; mortality risks were similarly elevated (HR 4.65 [95% CI, 3.17?6.82] and HR 4.38 [95% CI, 3.03?6.31], respectively) in these two groups. In All of Us participants (n=682), transferred phenotypes retained their principal clinical characteristics and continued to stratify hospitalization risk. Independent clustering most strongly reproduced the cardiorenal phenotype (Jaccard index, 0.744). Conclusions: Early-onset heart failure in women comprises distinct cardio-obstetric, cardiorenal, autoimmune, and cardiometabolic-ischemic phenotypes with divergent clinical outcomes. These findings support a life-course approach to heart failure classification in women that complements conventional frameworks and incorporates pregnancy history and female-predominant systemic conditions.

data.title: Preprint: Risk-benefit assessment of oral anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation using virtual clinical trials
data.authors: Cai, M.; Farahani, F.; Rienstra, M.; Severi, S.; Crijns, H. J. G. M.; Schotten, U.; Heijman, J.
data.abstract: Abstract Background: Oral anticoagulation (OAC) reduces stroke risk in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF), and screening can enable earlier AF detection and OAC initiation. However, the population-level trade-off between stroke prevention and OAC-related major bleeding for different types of AF and OAC therapy remains uncertain, and large randomized trials to resolve this are costly and time-consuming. Methods: A state-transition Markov-like model was developed to: 1) simulate the lifetime course of AF, stroke, major bleeding, and death in different virtual populations; 2) quantify benefits (stroke reduction) and harms (major bleeding) of systematic AF screening with screening-triggered OAC across CHA2DS2-VA scores; and 3) compare rhythm-guided, time-delimited ("pill-in-pocket") OAC with continuous OAC. Results: The model synthesized information from multiple clinical sources and reproduced stroke and bleeding incidence across clinical scenarios. At CHA?DS?-VA=2, long-term continuous rhythm monitoring (LT-CRM) with OAC lowered stroke risk (HR, 0.92 [95%CI, 0.88-0.96]) but raised bleeding risk (HR, 1.17 [95%CI, 1.07-1.27]) versus no screening. Time-to-benefit was shorter than time-to-harm for CHA?DS?-VA?4, but longer for CHA?DS?-VA=0. Pill-in-pocket OAC vs continuous OAC showed no difference in stroke/mortality (HR, 1.03, 95%CI [0.91-1.16]) but lower bleeding risk (HR, 0.81, 95%CI: 0.68-0.96]) in patients with elevated bleeding risk, but not at baseline. Sensitivity analyses revealed that the risk-benefit profiles of screening or pill-in-pocket OAC strategy further depend on OAC adherence and bleeding risks. Conclusions: Our model highlights a trade-off between stroke reduction and bleeding for systematic screening-initiated OAC, with net benefit for CHA?DS?-VA?4. We provide the first virtual implementation of an ongoing rhythm-guided OAC trial, showing that pill-in-pocket OAC may lower bleeding risk compared to continuous OAC, highlighting the potential of virtual clinical trials to guide clinical trial design.

data.title: Preprint: Associations of Pathogenic Sequence Variants and Copy Number Variants with Cardiovascular and Major Clinical Outcomes in Adults with Congenital Heart Disease
data.authors: Youssef, P.; Broussous, F.; Alhussain, H.; Rana, K.; Al-Najjar, M.; Islam, M. M.; Kashipovich, A. X.; Dasi, H. C.; Aman, M. H.; Kabul, M. A. K.; Chauhan, P.
data.author_corresponding_institution: University of Toronto Temerty Faculty of Medicine
data.abstract: Background: Genetic abnormalities contribute to the phenotypic heterogeneity of congenital heart disease, yet their prognostic significance in adults with congenital heart disease remains incompletely understood. We examined the associations of pathogenic sequence variants and copy number variants (CNVs) with cardiovascular and major clinical outcomes in ACHD. Methods: In this prospective observational cohort study, 1,000 adults with structurally confirmed CHD were recruited from a tertiary care center in Noida, India, between January 2022 and January 2026 and followed through August 2026. Participants underwent exome sequencing and chromosomal microarray analysis and were classified into four mutually exclusive groups: reference, sequence-variant-only, CNV-only, and dual-positive. The primary outcome was time to first occurrence of a composite of cardiovascular death, unplanned heart failure hospitalization, resuscitated cardiac arrest, sustained ventricular tachyarrhythmia, heart transplantation, or durable mechanical circulatory support. Associations were evaluated using multivariable Cox regression. Results: Of 1,000 participants, 800 comprised the reference group, 120 had sequence variants only, 60 had CNVs only, and 20 had both sequence variants and CNVs. Over a median follow-up of 4.2 years, the primary outcome occurred in 12.0%, 20.0%, 25.0%, and 30.0% of participants, respectively. In fully adjusted analyses, the sequence-variant-only group had a higher risk of the primary outcome versus the reference group (hazard ratio [HR], 1.65; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.01?2.69; p=0.0455). The CNV-only group had an HR of 1.92 (95% CI, 1.04?3.52; p=0.0360). Neither association remained significant after Holm adjustment (adjusted p=0.072 for both). The dual-positive group had an HR of 2.12 (95% CI, 0.83?5.42; p=0.1182). Extracardiac congenital anomalies and neurological disorders were more prevalent among individuals with genetic variants, while secondary outcomes showed no significant associations. Conclusions: Pathogenic sequence variants and CNVs were associated with numerically higher risks of adverse cardiovascular outcomes in ACHD, but independent prognostic significance was not established after adjustment for multiple testing.

data.title: Preprint: Early Valve Replacement vs Surveillance in Moderate Aortic Stenosis: Meta-Analysis of Randomized and Observational Evidence
data.authors: Majed, A.; Kmeid, P.; Safa, A.; Kahwaji, H.; Safieddine, H.; Ghanem, G.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Lebanese American University Gilbert and Rose-Marie Chagoury School of Medicine
data.abstract: BACKGROUND: Moderate aortic stenosis (AS) is associated with excess mortality, and 2 randomized trials have tested early transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR). OBJECTIVES: The authors sought to estimate the effects of early TAVR vs clinical surveillance and to compare randomized with observational estimates. METHODS: Six databases and registries were searched through November 3, 2026. Adjusted observational studies were synthesized separately from trials. Certainty was rated with GRADE. RESULTS: Two trials (922 patients; TAVR UNLOAD, n = 178, HF with reduced ejection fraction; PROGRESS, n = 744, 96.4% symptomatic) and 7 cohorts were included. Early TAVR did not detectably change death over approximately 2 years (HR: 1.05; 95% CI: 0.74-1.49; low certainty), with one-fifth of the deaths needed to detect a 20% reduction. Heart failure (HF) hospitalization was lower (RR: 0.53; 95% CI: 0.36-0.77; low certainty), or 70 fewer patients per 1,000 at 2 years. New pacemakers were more frequent (PROGRESS: 17.3% vs 9.3%; moderate certainty). About half of surveillance patients underwent valve replacement within 2 years. Observational cohorts estimated a 48% mortality reduction (HR: 0.52; 95% CI: 0.43-0.64; very low certainty), which differed from the randomized estimate (ratio of HRs: 2.01; 95% CI: 1.37-2.95). CONCLUSIONS: In older, predominantly symptomatic patients with moderate AS, early TAVR may make little or no difference to 2-year mortality and may reduce HF hospitalization, at the cost of more pacemakers. Because about half of patients under surveillance receive a valve within 2 years, the decision largely concerns timing. Observational survival estimates should not guide practice.

data.title: Preprint: Quantifying the contribution of policy measures to COVID-19 dynamics across 126 countries
data.authors: Trauer, J. M.; Shipman, D. S.; Ryan, M.; Henderson, A. S.; McBryde, E. S.; Meehan, M. T.; Ragonnet, R.
data.abstract: COVID-19 provides an unprecedented opportunity to evaluate the contribution of public health and social measures (PHSMs) to controlling transmission and inform responses to future emerging respiratory pathogens. We analysed SARS-CoV-2 transmission across 126 countries spanning multiple epidemic waves and diverse policy environments during periods when PHSMs were the primary interventions available to influence the epidemic. By explicitly representing key epidemiological drivers of transmission and measuring reductions in residual transmission scaling after incorporating OxCGRT policy time-series data, we isolated the effect of PHSMs on transmission. PHSMs frequently explained a substantial proportion of the observed variation in transmission intensity, with particularly strong effects seen in many high-income countries. In countries with strong evidence for policy effects, reductions in transmission reached 60-80% or above, although the individual policies responsible for these effects varied considerably. Harmonised analyses considering the effect of community mobility showed comparably strong effects in a similar subset of countries.

data.title: Preprint: Community health workers experiences with a digital clinical decision support system for longitudinal hypertension and diabetes care in rural Lesotho: a mixed-methods study
data.authors: Gerber, F.; Raeber, F.; Moruthoane, M.; Khaemba, A.; Bhandari, N.; Kunwar, L.; Sanchez-Samaniego, G.; Gupta, R.; Williams, A.; Tahirsylaj, T.; Mathulise, M.; Kabi, T.; Mokaeane, M.; Maphenchane, M.; Molulela, M.; Khomolishoele, M.; Sematle, M. P.; Sao, L.; Tlahali, M.; Shankar, U.; Basler, D. B.; Kindler, K.; Grimm, P.; Labhardt, N. D.; Amstutz, A.
data.abstract: Community health workers (CHWs) are increasingly delivering chronic care in resource-constrained settings but require support to manage complex longitudinal clinical workflows. In the Community-Based chronic Care Lesotho (ComBaCaL) project in rural Lesotho, CHWs provide longitudinal hypertension and diabetes care, supported by the ComBaCaL Community Health Toolkit (CHT) application. The application combines longitudinal participant management and task coordination with clinical decision support for screening, diagnosis, treatment initiation and adjustment, cardiovascular risk management, referral, and follow-up for hypertension and diabetes care. This model of care has demonstrated improved or maintained clinical outcomes compared to facility-based care only. We conducted a mixed-methods study among all 103 participating CHWs to evaluate their experiences with the application. All CHWs completed a 38-item questionnaire, and 22 participated in qualitative interviews or focus group discussions. Overall usability was high, with a mean System Usability Scale score of 75.6 (SD 13.0), and 98 (95%) CHWs were satisfied or very satisfied with the application. General application functions and diagnosis and treatment tasks were rated easy or very easy by 98% of participants. The most frequently reported benefits were task reminders (92%), structured clinical guidance (87%), overview of allocated participants (81%), and retention of participant information (81%). Main challenges were lengthy questionnaires, difficulties charging tablets, and limited internet connectivity. Qualitative findings showed that ease of use increased with experience, supported by training and supervision. Participants described how algorithmic guidance and task reminders supported care delivery, while also identifying tensions between standardized workflows and flexibility in day-to-day care. The ComBaCaL CHT application was highly usable and valued by CHWs. High perceived usability extended from general application functions to complex clinical workflows. CHT demonstrated suitability as a configurable framework for implementing such context-specific workflows for hypertension and diabetes care when accompanied by appropriate workflow design, training, and supervision.

data.title: Preprint: Epidemiology of acute respiratory infections in adult patients in Hospices Civils de Lyon, France, between October 2016 and April 2025
data.authors: Chauvel, C.; Dananche, C.; Shirreff, G.; Abou Chakra, C. N.; Gaymard, A.; Vanhems, P.; Morfin, F.; Josset, L.; Bal, A.; Casalegno, J.-S.; Nunes, M. C.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Hospices Civils de Lyon, Université Claude Bernard Lyon 1
data.abstract: Background Multiple viruses can cause acute respiratory infections (ARI), impacting morbidity, mortality and hospital resources. The objective of this study was to describe viral circulation among patients with ARI, patients characteristics and severity outcomes. Methods A retrospective cohort was assembled using electronic health records from the Hospices Civils de Lyon, France. Adult patients ([≥]18 years) hospitalised or presenting to the emergency department from October 2016 to April 2025 with either an ICD-10 diagnostic code for ARI or a laboratory-confirmed viral detection were included. Administrative variables and laboratory results collected during the stay were extracted. Results 103,011 hospital visits involving 82,077 patients were included. The number of eligible stays increased substantially since the COVID-19 pandemic, along with year-round laboratory testing. Following disruption during the pandemic, winter peaks of ARI incidence, influenza and RSV detections re-emerged after 2022. Influenza, rhinovirus and SARS-CoV-2 positivity rates peaked in younger adults (<65 years), whereas RSV and hMPV positivity rates were highest in patients aged [≥]80 years. Patients aged [≥]65 years had longer hospitalisations (median 10 vs 8 days, p<0.001), twice in-hospital mortality rate (14% vs 7%, p<0.001), less frequent ICU admission (21% vs 33%, p<0.001) and use of respiratory support than younger adults. Influenza was the virus associated with the shortest length of stays, hMPV was associated with the longest in younger adults. Conclusions Real-world hospital data are valuable for surveillance of viral circulation, early identification of patients at risk of deterioration, and may be used to evaluate the impact of preventive intervention in community.

data.title: Preprint: Wastewater pathogen composition in Atlanta, GA prior to and during the 2026 FIFA World Cup
data.authors: Raymo, N.; Kraft, C. S.; Gulick, D.; Ingersoll, J.; Stoffle, M.; Sablon, O.; Logan, J.; Haslett, E.; Moe, C. L.; Wolfe, M. K.; Freeman, L. D.; Bourne, T.; Lawson, V.; Harton, P. E.
data.abstract: Mass gatherings can have many impacts on public health, including facilitating the spread of infectious diseases. Alternative surveillance modalities, such as wastewater-based surveillance (WBS), can complement traditional clinical surveillance. We utilized WBS to examine the influence of the 2026 FIFA World Cup (FWC'26) on the range of infectious pathogens in Atlanta, GA surrounding matches held in the city. Samples (n = 102) were collected from three water reclamation facilities between April and July of 2026 (34 collection days) and tested using the BIOFIRE(R) WATCHFIRE Respiratory (19 targets) and Gastrointestinal (22 targets) PCR Pathogen Panels. Primary data analysis included a temporal comparison of wastewater pathogen profiles before (April 1 to June 10; n = 60) and during (June 15 to July 15; n = 30) the FWC'26 across the three facilities using a modified Poisson model with Bonferroni correction. There were no statistically significant differences in target detection between the two periods. Samples collected after the FWC'26 (July 20 to 29; n = 12) were included in a sensitivity analysis which showed a statistically significant increase in SARS-CoV-2 (RR = 3.21, 95% CI = 1.40-7.39; p = 0.01, p-adjusted = 0.048) during and after the tournament compared to before. However, this coincided with regional and national increases in SARS-CoV-2 detection in wastewater, suggesting ongoing community burden. Wide confidence intervals, lack of quantitative data, and limited data collection after the matches limit our conclusions. This study demonstrates the use of qualitative, multiplexed PCR assays for WBS during a mass gathering sporting event.

data.title: Preprint: The life course shaping of quality of life in older age: does childhood poverty associate with control, autonomy, self-realisation and pleasure? A retrospective and prospective study of HRS, ELSA, SHARE and TILDA cohorts
data.authors: Tampubolon, G.
data.abstract: Later-life quality of life is increasingly recognised as a life-course achievement, yet ageing research has focused more on dysfunction and decline than on positive wellbeing. This study examines whether childhood poverty shapes later-life quality of life, measured by CASP: control, autonomy, self-realisation and pleasure. METHODS: I analysed harmonised data from 59,569 adults aged over 50 in 29 countries, drawn from HRS, ELSA, SHARE and TILDA (U.S. Health and Retirement Study, English Longitudinal Study of Ageing, Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe, The Irish Longitudinal Study on Ageing). Childhood poverty was modelled as a latent class from retrospectively reported childhood material circumstances, acknowledging recall error in such reports. Country fixed-effects linear models estimated associations with CASP, first adjusting for age, sex and country, then adding education, marital status and later-life wealth. RESULTS: One in five participants grew up in poverty (22.9%). Mean CASP was 38 out of 48. Initially childhood poverty was associated with a 1.2-point lower CASP score; after complete adjustment the penalty attenuated but remained durable at 0.7 points. Education, partnership and wealth were independently associated with higher wellbeing but did not erase the penalty. Predicted age profiles showed poverty penalty in every country. They also revealed striking national differences: Nordic countries achieved markedly higher CASP levels than several Eastern European countries; Finns aged 90 had similar levels of positive wellbeing to Latvians two decades younger. CONCLUSION: Childhood poverty leaves a durable mark on later-life positive wellbeing, while welfare contexts appear to lift overall CASP levels. Reducing child poverty and strengthening social protection are therefore lifelong wellbeing policies.

data.title: Preprint: Development and psychometric evaluation of the Severity of Myalgic Encephalomyelitis Scale (SoMES) and the Myalgic Encephalomyelitis Occupational Status Scale (MEOSS)
data.authors: Tyson, S. F.; Fleming, R.
data.abstract: Objective: To develop and psychometrically evaluate two new brief assessments measuring disease severity (the Severity of ME Scale, SoMES) and occupational status (the ME Occupational Status Scale, MEOSS) in myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS) Methods: Draft SoMES and MEOSS were co-produced from relevant literature and lived experience. An online survey completed by adults with ME/CFS and was repeated two weeks later to assess reliability. The SF-36 (physical function) assessed criterion-related validity (Spearmann correlations) and discriminant validity (Kruskal-Wallis tests). Weighted kappa co-efficients assessed test-retest reliability and measurement error calculated minimal detectable difference (MDD). Results: 995 adults with ME/CFS participated and 579 completed the retest survey. Construct validity was confirmed from feedback. Criterion related validity was moderate-good (SoMES r = 0.663, MEOSS r=0.472, both p<0.001). Discriminant validity was demonstrated by significant differences in SF36-PF scores in different levels of SoMES and MEOSS (p=0.003 - 0.0001). SoMES test-retest reliability was moderate (k =0.53, P<0.001) with a MDD of 1.6, and excellent for the MEOSS (k = 0.76 p<.001) and the MDD was 1.4 Conclusions: The Severity of ME Scale (SoMES) and the ME Occupational Status Scale (MEOSS) are valid, reliable, sensitive assessments of ME/CFS severity and occupational status respectively.

data.title: Preprint: Cortical Thinning in Adults with Prader-Willi Syndrome: Distribution Across Functional Networks and Associations with BMI and the GH/IGF-1 Axis
data.authors: Moreno-Armengol, A.; Blanco-Hinojo, L.; Casamitjana, L.; Gimenez-Palop, O.; Cobo, J.; Pujol, J.; Martinez-Vilavella, G.; Deus, J.; Esteba-Castillo, S.; Pareja, R.; Caixas, A.; Pena-Gomez, C.
data.abstract: Prader-Willi syndrome (PWS) is a rare neurogenetic disorder associated with neuropsychiatric, metabolic, endocrine, and physical abnormalities. Although previous neuroimaging studies have identified regional gray matter alterations, cortical thickness (CT) abnormalities and their distribution across large-scale functional brain networks remain poorly characterized in adults with PWS. We investigated cortical morphology in 23 adults with PWS and 22 age- and sex-matched healthy controls who underwent structural MRI. Cortical reconstruction and surface-based morphometric analyses were performed using FreeSurfer. Between-group differences in CT were assessed using age, sex, and intracranial volume as covariates. Associations between CT and clinical, cognitive, anthropometric, and endocrine measures were examined using Spearman correlations. Significant cortical regions were further mapped onto an a priori functional network atlas. Adults with PWS showed reduced CT in a left-hemispheric cluster involving the inferior precentral gyrus, insula, inferior temporal cortex, and orbitofrontal cortex. This cluster overlapped predominantly with the somatomotor, auditory, cingulo-opercular, language, and frontoparietal networks. Within the PWS group, lower CT was associated with higher body mass index and poorer global functioning. CT was positively associated with IGF-1 levels and was greater in participants with a history of growth hormone therapy during childhood. These findings indicate cortical thinning across regions belonging to multiple functional networks involved in sensorimotor, attentional, language, and executive processes, extending previous volumetric findings. The associations with body mass index, functional measures, and the GH/IGF-1 axis suggest that cortical morphology may reflect an interplay between genetic vulnerability and potentially modifiable metabolic and endocrine factors, raising the possibility of a neuroprotective role for GH/IGF-1 signaling.

data.title: Preprint: Beyond Haploinsufficiency: Protein Domain and Variant Class Shape Language Outcomes in SYNGAP1-DEE
data.authors: Kiwull, L.; Schmeder, V.; Zenker, M.; Mengual Hinojosa, M.; Kluger, G.; Eschermann, K.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Paracelsus Medical University, EURAS Project, Salzburg, Austria
data.abstract: Background SYNGAP1-related developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (SYNGAP1-DEE) is generally considered a haploinsufficiency disorder, yet language development varies considerably between affected individuals. With targeted therapies, including antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs), approaching clinical evaluation, understanding genotype-specific differences is increasingly important. We investigated whether expressive language and functional communication are associated with SynGAP protein domains and variant class. Methods We analyzed cross-sectional caregiver-reported data linked to genetic reports from the international PATRE SYNGAP1 registry. Of 440 participants, 334 had variants that could be assigned to a protein domain and classified as missense (n=79) or truncating/splicing (n=255). Variants were mapped to seven predefined SynGAP protein regions. The primary outcome was a five-level current expressive language score. Secondary outcomes included acquisition of two-word phrases and CFCS-derived functional communication. Each domain was compared with all other regions within the same variant class using nonparametric tests and age-adjusted ordinal or logistic regression. Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction was applied. Results Missense variants in the C2 domain (aa248-392; n=28) were associated with markedly poorer expressive language (median score 1 vs. 2; age-adjusted OR 0.16, 95% CI 0.06-0.46; q=0.0025). Only 7.1% had acquired two-word phrases compared with 52.0% of individuals with missense variants outside C2 (OR 0.07; q=0.0023). Functional communication was also significantly impaired (OR 0.23, 95% CI 0.09-0.56; q=0.0052). Conversely, truncating/splicing variants in the PH domain (aa103-247; n=50) were associated with better expressive language (median 3 vs. 2; OR 3.52, 95% CI 1.99-6.24; q<0.001) and more frequent acquisition of two-word phrases (62.0% vs. 31.5%). No corresponding language association was observed for C2 truncating/splicing variants or for variants in the RasGAP domain. Conclusions Language outcomes in SYNGAP1-DEE are associated with both variant class and protein location. The marked impairment associated with C2 missense variants contrasts with the relatively preserved language abilities observed in PH truncating/splicing variants, suggesting that SYNGAP1-related disease cannot be fully explained by a uniform haploinsufficiency model alone. These findings support considering protein domain and variant class in future ASO trials, particularly for patient stratification, endpoint selection, and interpretation of treatment outcomes.

data.title: Preprint: Clinician Counseling and Patient Storage and Disposal Practices for Opioids Prescribed for Acute Pain: A Multicenter Prospective Cohort Study
data.authors: Taherifard, E.; Ahadpour, M.; Bellolio, F.; Chang, N.; Allen, S.; Elie-Turenne, M.-C.; Fillmore, W. J.; Gilbert, G. H.; Heckmann, R.; Koussis, P.; Lee, C.; Lipkind, H.; Mallama, C.; Meyer, T. E.; Nuckols, T. K.; Ritchie, J. D.; Pacanowski, M. A.; Page, D. B.; Soukup, M.; Tamang, S.; Torbati, S.; Wallace, D.; Walter, L.; Zhao, Y.; Shah, N. D.; Ross, J. S.; Jeffery, M. M.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Emergency Medicine, Mayo Clinic, Rochester, MN, USA
data.abstract: BACKGROUND: Opioids prescribed for acute pain frequently remain unused, creating opportunities for unintended use, accidental ingestion, or diversion. Little is known about counseling patients receive from prescribers or pharmacists on storage and disposal of opioids. OBJECTIVE: To characterize clinician counseling on opioid disposal and patient-reported storage, use, and disposal practices among opioid-naive patients prescribed opioids for acute pain. DESIGN: Multicenter prospective cohort study with participant recruitment between September 2020 and March 2023. PARTICIPANTS: Opioid-naive patients prescribed opioids for acute pain in emergency departments, primary care or urgent care clinics, inpatient settings, and dental practices. MAIN MEASURES: Patient-reported receipt of counseling on the importance of opioid disposal and appropriate disposal methods; opioid storage practices; use and disposition of prescribed opioids; disposal methods; and reasons for keeping or disposing of leftover opioids. KEY RESULTS: Among 1708 participants, the median age was 38 years (IQR, 28-52); most were recruited from emergency departments (n=915; 53.6%) and primary care or urgent care clinics (n=307; 18.0%). Among 1233 participants who answered the question on counseling about the importance of opioid disposal, 811 (65.8%) reported receiving no counseling. Among 1220 participants who answered the question on counseling about appropriate disposal methods, 832 (68.2%) reported receiving no counseling. Among 812 participants who answered the question about storing opioids in a locked location, 610 (75.1%) reported never doing so. Among 929 participants providing information on opioid leftovers and disposition, 618 (66.5%) did not use all prescribed opioids. Among these 618 participants, 258 (42.8%) kept leftover opioids and 345 (57.2%) disposed of them. Among 256 participants who reported reasons for keeping leftover opioids, 159 (62.1%) wanted medication available for the same condition, 70 (27.3%) wanted medication available for a different condition, and 36 (14.1%) did not know how to properly dispose of the medication. CONCLUSIONS: Among opioid-naive patients prescribed opioids for acute pain, counseling about opioid disposal was uncommon, secure storage was infrequent, and leftover opioids were frequent, with many patients keeping leftover opioids for possible future use. These findings suggest opportunities to improve counseling on opioid storage and disposal and encourage safe disposal of unused opioids after acute pain treatment.

Among 1220 participants who answered the question on counseling about appropriate disposal methods, 832 (68.2%) reported receiving no counseling. Among 812 participants who answered the question about storing opioids in a locked location, 610 (75.1%) reported never doing so. Among 929 participants providing information on opioid leftovers and disposition, 618 (66.5%) did not use all prescribed opioids. Among these 618 participants, 258 (42.8%) kept leftover opioids and 345 (57.2%) disposed of them. Among 256 participants who reported reasons for keeping leftover opioids, 159 (62.1%) wanted medication available for the same condition, 70 (27.3%) wanted medication available for a different condition, and 36 (14.1%) did not know how to properly dispose of the medication. CONCLUSIONS: Among opioid-naive patients prescribed opioids for acute pain, counseling about opioid disposal was uncommon, secure storage was infrequent, and leftover opioids were frequent, with many patients keeping leftover opioids for possible future use. These findings suggest opportunities to improve counseling on opioid storage and disposal and encourage safe disposal of unused opioids after acute pain treatment.

data.title: Preprint: Figure format and the accuracy of AI-assisted reconstruction of Kaplan-Meier survival data
data.authors: Li, S.; Xing, X.; Te, B.; Han, H.; Ji, H.; Yu, Y.; Siegel, L.; Lin, L.
data.abstract: Reconstructing participant-level data from published Kaplan-Meier curves supports meta-analysis and other secondary survival analyses when original trial records are unavailable. Researchers may use original PDF figures or screenshots, which can look alike but retain different information. We assessed how converting vector figures to images affects reconstruction by a language model that can inspect files and execute code. We generated 64 independent two-arm datasets across four scenarios combining 100 or 1,000 participants per arm with proportional or crossing hazards. Each figure was supplied as a native vector PDF and a matched 300-dpi PNG to Opus 5.5 through Claude Code under the same instructions. Outcomes compared reconstructed records with the original observed records: time-averaged absolute curve error through 24 months, error in the between-group restricted mean survival time difference, and error in the Cox log-hazard ratio. Native PDFs had lower curve error in all 64 completed pairs, including replacements for incomplete runs. Mean errors were 0.000029 and 0.1047 percentage points for PDF and PNG, respectively; the paired difference was -0.1047 (95% confidence interval, -0.1194 to -0.0909). PNG errors in the restricted mean survival time difference and log-hazard ratio were small: mean absolute errors were 0.0084 months and 0.0027. Lower resolution and compression increased curve errors; embedding unchanged pixels in a PDF did not restore vector accuracy. Some PNG runs exceeded the instructed revision limit, so results describe the implemented workflow rather than performance under a strictly enforced limit. Preserving vector information improved reconstruction fidelity in this workflow, but the observed differences do not establish clinically consequential changes in treatment estimates. Validation against reported survival summaries and event counts remains necessary. Generalization to published clinical figures and other model workflows requires further evaluation.

data.title: Preprint: A five-day Mindfulness Based Intervention to reduce burnout and psychological distress in UK Medical Students
data.authors: Cromie, A.; Kaur, M.; Powell, N.; Brown, M.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Swansea University College of Medicine: Swansea University Medical School
data.abstract: Background Medical professionals face significant work overload, with excessive job demands often strongly associated with attrition and burnout. Consequences of burnout include reduced job satisfaction, absenteeism, reduced patient care, lower patient satisfaction and increased healthcare costs. UK Medical students are also at high risk of burnout. Mindfulness-based interventions are effective individual-level treatments, however more research is required to investigate the efficacy of mindfulness for healthcare professionals and students.   Method Four cohorts of second-year medical students at Cardiff University participated in a five-day, in-person mindfulness-based intervention. Pre (T1) and post (T2) intervention and follow-up (T3) survey data were collected online using validated outcome measures for burnout, psychological distress and wellbeing. Results Statistical analysis of data from 69 participants found a statistically significant improvement post intervention (T2) for current energy, calmness, focus and stress (all P=0.001). Statistically significant improvements in psychological distress (Core-10, P=0.001), Burnout (OLBI, P=0.023), and Wellbeing (WHO5, P=0.37) with small, large and small effect sizes respectively; maintained at follow-up (T3). Satisfaction ratings were consistently high, and completion rate was 100%. Discussion Medical schools should consider implementing mindfulness-based interventions into medical curricula, as a feasible and acceptable student selected preventative tool to address burnout and incorporate student perspectives on delivery; to prevent mental ill health in medical professionals.

data.title: Preprint: Divergent Causes of Death After Ischemic and Hemorrhagic Stroke in the Reperfusion Era: A Contemporary Cohort Study
data.authors: Kadiyala, V.; Simpkins, A. N.; Chugh, H.; Czarny, R.; Uy-Evanado, A.; Bosson, N.; Tatonetti, N.; Reinier, K.; Chugh, S. S.
data.abstract: Background: Contemporary data on long-term, cause-specific mortality among stroke survivors are sparse, and much of the existing evidence derives from studies performed before the modern reperfusion era. We sought to characterize long-term cause-specific mortality among stroke survivors to discharge (differentiated by stroke subtype) when compared to in-hospital stroke decedents treated under contemporary standards of care. Methods: Using a hybrid billing-code/imaging and large language model-assisted chart-review pipeline, we identified adults hospitalized for ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke in the Observational Study of Cardiac Arrest Risk (OSCAR) cohort (Cedars-Sinai Health System, Los Angeles) between 2017 and 2020, followed through June 30, 2025. Cause of death was determined and classified into 10 categories. Results: Among 1,344 stroke patients (mean age 74.0 {+/-} 14.9 years; ischemic n=1,036 [77.1%], hemorrhagic n=308 [22.9%]), 203 (15.1%) did not survive the index stroke. Of the 1,141 discharged survivors, 625 (54.8%) died over a median follow-up of 5.2 years. Cerebrovascular causes predominated during index stroke hospitalization (36.0%) but accounted for only 15.5% of post-stroke discharge deaths. Among ischemic stroke survivors, cardiac disease was the leading cause of death (31.6%), with sudden cardiac arrest alone accounting for 10.9% of deaths. Among hemorrhagic stroke survivors, cancer (38.9%) was the leading cause of death. Despite these divergent cause-of-death profiles, overall survival did not differ significantly by subtype (median 5.5 vs 5.8 years; P=0.90). Conclusions: In this contemporary, reperfusion-era cohort, causes of death shifted from cerebrovascular predominance in the acute phase to heart disease/cardiac arrest after ischemic stroke, and malignancy after hemorrhagic stroke. These findings argue for development of subtype-specific post-stroke surveillance, including structured longitudinal cardiac and sudden-death risk assessment for ischemic stroke survivors.

data.title: Preprint: Cumulative Multidomain Vulnerability and Early Mortality After Heart Transplantation: Development and Temporal Evaluation of the RIGHT-HTx Framework
data.authors: Balakrishnan, K. R.; Kemundel Genny, S. R.; Tungatru, M.; Davidson, N.; Sahayaraj, A.; Aravind, A.; Vanga, S.; Singh, N.; Nallamuthu, N.; Jegdish, A.; Krithika, K.; Ratnagiri, R. K.; Chandrasekaran, R.; RAMASWAMY, R. K.; Manikala, V.; Kumar, A.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Institute of Heart and Lung Transplant & Mechanical Circulatory Support, MGM Healthcare
data.abstract: BACKGROUND Risk models from high-income transplant programmes may not generalise to resource-constrained settings with different recipient acuity, donor characteristics and access to mechanical circulatory support. We developed RIGHT-HTx, a parsimonious framework integrating clinical and physiological vulnerabilities, and evaluated its prognostic performance in a subsequent same-centre cohort. METHODS This retrospective single-centre study included 436 consecutive adult heart transplant recipients (2012-2026). Of 357 development recipients, 341 (95.5%) were score-evaluable. RIGHT-HTx incorporated three vulnerability domains: clinical acuity (INTERMACS 1-2), graded renal dysfunction (eGFR 30-59 or <30 mL/min/1.73 m2) and haemodynamic-donor mismatch (TPG >12 mmHg combined with donor-to-recipient weight ratio <1.0). A seven-point Cox-derived score underwent internal validation using 1,000 bootstrap resamples and was applied unchanged to 79 subsequent recipients. Low-, intermediate- and high-risk categories represented zero, one and 2 affected domains, respectively. RESULTS Among development recipients, 75/341 (22.0%) died within one year. Mortality increased across low-, intermediate- and high-risk categories (8.1%, 20.3% and 55.6%; log-rank P<0.001). Elevated TPG was not significantly associated with mortality individually, whereas its combination with donor undersizing was independently associated with mortality (adjusted HR 2.87, 95% CI 1.53-5.40; P=0.001). The full model improved discrimination beyond renal dysfunction alone (optimism-corrected C-index 0.067), and the simplified score achieved an optimism-corrected C-index of 0.732. The temporal cohort more often had 1 affected domain (75.9% versus 60.4%; P=0.010). Discrimination was comparable (C-index 0.738, 95% CI 0.643-0.833), although observed Kaplan-Meier one-year mortality exceeded original predictions (35.4% versus 25.4%; calibration slope 0.929). In pooled analyses (n=420), mortality increased from 8.4% (13/154) with no affected domain to 57.3% (47/82) with two or more. CONCLUSIONS RIGHT-HTx identifies cumulative multidomain vulnerability associated with early mortality after heart transplantation. Temporal discrimination was comparable, but absolute-risk calibration differed. The framework may support risk recognition and mitigation, not transplant eligibility or allocation; independent multicentre validation is required before clinical implementation.

data.title: Preprint: A Reproducible Decomposed Large Language Model Pipeline for Structured Abstraction of Multimodal Neuroimaging Reports: Development and Independent Validation in 1,669 Emergency Department Encounters for Dizziness and Vertigo
data.authors: Shahani, J.; Ousta, A. R.; Shaulov, S.; El-Sherif, Y.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Neurology, Staten Island University Hospital, Northwell Health, Staten Island, NY, USA; Zucker School of Medicine at Hofstra/Northwell, Hempstead,
data.abstract:
ObjectiveTo develop and independently validate a decomposed, modality-specific large language model (LLM) pipeline that abstracts structured variables from the free-text neuroimaging reports of a multimodal stroke workup, and to validate the resulting structured dataset for reuse in downstream research.

Materials and MethodsA frozen pipeline (temperature 0) extracting 22 variables across CT head, CT angiography, CT perfusion, and MRI brain was applied to 1,669 ED encounters for dizziness or vertigo; 11 variables were pre-specified as primary (Tier 1). Reproducibility used three same-session runs and a nine-week re-run; three frontier models (Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.4, Gemini 3.5 Flash) measured cross-model agreement (Cohens/Fleiss {kappa}). Accuracy was assessed in an independent 200-encounter cohort (150 random, 50 enriched for rare findings); 100 were double-read by two blinded reviewers with discordances adjudicated.

ResultsTest-retest reproducibility was high (Tier 1 Fleiss {kappa}=0.993; 99.8% exact) and stable nine weeks later ({kappa}=0.992); inter-model agreement was {kappa}=0.962. Against the adjudicated reference, pooled Tier 1 accuracy was 0.971 to 0.988 across models (Cohens {kappa} 0.959 to 0.982), comparable to inter-reviewer agreement ({kappa}=0.932). Accuracy was 0.980 to 0.983 in random and 0.955 to 0.977 in enriched encounters (agreement on model-flagged findings, not sensitivity).

DiscussionA decomposed LLM pipeline produced reproducible, model-portable, stable, and accurate multimodal abstraction. Because schema design and validation are up-front costs, such pipelines scale to larger research cohorts.

ConclusionThe quantified per-field error rates support reuse of this dataset with field-specific review, and such pipelines offer a practical path to large-scale, reproducible research datasets.

data.title: Preprint: Prevalence and Determinants of the Double Burden of Malnutrition among Adolescents: A Cross-Sectional Study in Urban Schools of Nepal
data.authors: Sunuwar, D. R.; Shrestha, A.; Kiwanayo, A.; Karki, S.; Shrestha, M.; Sunuwar, S.; Singh, D. R.; Karki, K.; Chaudhary, N. K.; K.C., D.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Public Health Promotion and Development Organization
data.abstract:
BackgroundThe double burden of malnutrition (DBM), characterised by coexisting undernutrition and overnutrition, remains a public health concern among adolescents especially in low- and middle-income countries. Adolescents in Nepal are nutritionally vulnerable, yet evidence on the coexistence of stunting and overweight/obesity is limited. This study assessed the prevalence and associated factors of DBM among school-going adolescents in urban Kathmandu Valley, Nepal.

MethodsA school-based cross-sectional study was conducted to assess factors associated with the double burden of malnutrition among adolescents in Kathmandu Valley, Nepal from 25th April, 2022 up to 25th July, 2025. A multi-stage cluster random sampling technique, using the Probability Proportional to Size method, was employed to ensure the selection of the desired number of participants. Students from grades 8 to 10 were randomly selected for face-to-face interviews and anthropometric measurements (height and weight were collected to calculate Body Mass Index (BMI)-for-age Z-scores (BAZ)), using tools adapted to the local context. Bivariate and multivariable models examined the associations between the dependent and independent variables.

ResultsThis study revealed that 15.3% of the students were stunted, 5.5% were underweight, 16.9% were overweight/obese, and 3% of students with the coexistence of DBM.

In the fully adjusted model, the odds of stunting were significantly higher among adolescents aged 15-19 years (aOR = 2.03, 95% CI: 1.35-3.06), salty-snack consumers (aOR = 1.53, 95% CI: 1.00-2.36), those with low nutritional knowledge (aOR = 3.17, 95% CI: 2.17-4.66), and low diet quality (aOR = 7.27, 95% CI: 4.96-10.65). Conversely, fatty-food consumption was associated with lower odds of stunting (aOR = 0.65, 95% CI: 0.42-1.00). For overweight/obesity, older adolescents had significantly lower odds (aOR = 0.49, 95% CI: 0.35-0.67). Regarding the double burden of malnutrition (DBM), low nutritional knowledge (aOR = 2.16, 95% CI: 0.99-4.71) and low diet quality (aOR = 5.27, 95% CI: 2.42-11.48) were significantly associated with higher odds.

ConclusionThe double burden of malnutrition exists among adolescents in urban Kathmandu Valley, highlighting a critical public health challenge. Socio-demographic, dietary, and behavioral factors significantly influence its prevalence. Comprehensive school- and community-based interventions are crucial for addressing this dual nutritional burden.

data.title: Preprint: A Global Atlas of Immune Alleles Reveals Health-Relevant Variation Across Groups
data.authors: Harvey, W. T.; Emde, A.-K.; Kakembo, F. E.; Hamid, I.; Clarke, W. E.; Apriyana, I.; Babiker, H.; Rakotoarivony, R.; Hendershott, M.; Kasina, P.; Kalungi, A.; Ojewunmi, O.; Pascart, T.; Rosso, S.; Verdugo, R. A.; Ferreccio, C.; Dessein, A.; Kusuma, P.; Priliani, L.; Malik, S. G.; Fabian, J.; Ramsay, M.; Wasik, K. A.; Fox, K.; Merriman, T. R.; Fatumo, S.; Sudoyo, H.; Yerges-Armstrong, L.; Castel, S. E.
data.abstract: Immune allele frequencies inform disease association mapping, pharmacogenomic guidance, and vaccine design, yet such data are missing for most of the worlds groups. Here we present the Global Atlas of Immune Alleles (GAIA), applying benchmarked genotyping tools across the Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA), Immunoglobulin Heavy Chain Constant (IGHC), and Fc Gamma Receptor (FCGR) loci to whole-genome sequencing data from 20,248 individuals, oversampling sub-Saharan African, Island Southeast Asian, and Pacific groups. Despite representing fewer than 0.5% of observations in the Allele Frequency Net Database, GAIA expands the databases catalogue by 38%, demonstrating that representation matters more than sample size. We identify HLA alleles at group-specific frequencies that challenge pharmacogenomic screening recommendations and document disease-risk alleles common in groups lacking clinical guidance. Finally, we introduce majority allelic diversity (MAD-X), which counts the alleles required for X% of individuals in a group to carry at least one, and show that reaching 90% HLA-B coverage for vaccine design requires up to 2.7 times more alleles in underrepresented groups than in those of Northwest European ancestry.

data.title: Preprint: Effect of protocolized MAGNesium replacement in critically ill patients On mortaLIty and Atrial fibrillation: protocol for the MAGNOLIA randomized controlled trial
data.authors: Yarnell, C. J.; Bruce-Kemevor, S.; Burns, K.; Burry, L.; Craig, J.; Fernando, S. M.; Fowler, R.; Gunaratne, K.; Haskings, J.; Lamontagne, F.; Liu, K.; Prakash, V.; Sibley, S.; Soliman, K.; Tomlinson, G.; Wei, L.; Bodley, T.; Canadian Critical Care Trials Group,
data.category: intensive care and critical care medicine
data.abstract:
Abstract {1b}O_ST_ABSBackgroundC_ST_ABSMeasurement of serum magnesium levels, and administration of supplemental magnesium when levels are below target, is a common element of routine care for critically ill patients. However, targets for replacement vary, and the targets that lead to the best outcomes are unknown.

MethodsMulti-center open-label parallel group randomized controlled superiority trial of adult critically ill patients receiving protocolized magnesium replacement, comparing a higher target (>0.95mmol/L) to a lower target (>0.7mmol/L). The trial will be embedded into the electronic health record (EHR) at 6 hospitals across 2 health networks in Ontario, Canada, with a shared EHR. We will include patients aged 16 years or older who have ICU admission orders, including an order for the magnesium replacement protocol. data.title: Preprint: Balancing Analgesic Effects and Abuse Liability in Older Adults: A Randomized, Placebo-Controlled Trial of Oral and Vaporized Δ9-Tetrahydrocannabinol
data.authors: Costa, G. P. A.; Gueorguieva, R.; Riggs, M. M.; Dunlap, T.; Sofuoglu, M.; De Aquino, J. P.
data.abstract: Cannabis use is rising fastest among older adults in the U.S., and pain is among the most common reasons they use it. No trial, however, has measured the trade-off between the analgesic and abuse-related effects of {Delta}9-tetrahydrocannabinol ({Delta}9-THC) in this population. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 20 adults aged 65 and older were assigned to oral {Delta}9-THC (placebo, 5, 10 mg) or vaporized {Delta}9-THC (placebo, 2, 4 mg) across three eight-hour sessions in counterbalanced order. We assessed laboratory-evoked pain sensitivity using quantitative sensory testing, abuse liability using subjective drug effects and reinforcement value, and also sampled plasma {Delta}9-THC and 11-OH-THC. Analgesia and abuse liability outcomes were measured repeatedly within each session. On a pain sensitivity index, oral 5 mg relieved pain relative to placebo (p=.040), although the oral arms overall dose effect was not significant (p=.108); oral 10 mg and both vaporized doses did not differ from placebo. Subjective effects increased with dose and were greatest after vaporization, whereas reinforcement value increased only after vaporized 4 mg. After oral 5 mg, analgesia exceeded placebo at every assessment (60-360 min), while its pleasurable effects peaked at 150 min. Vaporized {Delta}9-THC produced pleasurable effects within 30 min but did not significantly change thermal pain sensitivity. While abuse liability tracked {Delta}9-THC exposure, analgesia showed no significant association, and all adverse events occurred at vaporized 4 mg. These findings suggest dose and route selection may help maximize {Delta}9-THC analgesia while minimizing abuse liability, a strategy that warrants evaluation in clinical populations.

data.title: Preprint: Understanding, Confidence and Usefulness of Effect Size and Certainty of Evidence: A Cross-Sectional Survey Among Australian Dietitians
data.authors: Ghosh, N. R.; Neale, E. P.; Johnston, B. C.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Nutrition, College of Agriculture and Life Sciences, Texas A&M University, College Station, Texas, USA; Department of Surgery, Houston Methodist H
data.abstract:
PurposeInterpreting treatment effect size is essential for evidence-sinformed dietetic care, yet dietitians understanding remains unestablished.

MethodsWe conducted a web-based cross-sectional survey of Australian dietitians (October 2024-February 2025). The survey assessed their understanding of effect size, presented using three absolute estimates (risk difference [RD], risk in treatment vs. risk in control groups, number needed to treat [NNT]) and two relative estimates (relative risk [RR], odds ratio [OR]). We also assessed dietitians confidence in determining correct effect size, their perceived usefulness of effect estimates and corresponding certainty of evidence.

ResultsApproximately 7,697 dietitians received the survey link; 27 participated and 13 completers were analyzed. Correct understanding was higher for absolute than relative estimates (30.0% vs. 18.2%). Risk in treatment vs. risk in control groups was understood the most (41.7%) and RD, RR and OR the least (18.2% each). Confidence was highest for RR [mean (SD): 4.18 (1.25)] and lowest for NNT [3.40 (1.17)]. Perceived usefulness was highest for OR [4.69 (1.18)] and lowest for NNT [3.75 (1.76)]. Certainty of evidence was rated useful [5.69 (1.03)].

ConclusionBased on a small sample, preliminary evidence suggests limited understanding of effect size, highlighting the need for further training and assessment in larger sample.

data.title: Preprint: Clinical and Social Determinants of Guideline-Directed Medical Therapy Optimization in Heart Failure with Reduced Ejection Fraction
data.authors: Nelson, M.; Kwon, M.; Driscoll, K.; Kaiwan, O.; Dunlap, M. E.; Murad, K.; Rybinska- Campbel, A.; Gunzler, D. D.; Nandar, P. P.
data.abstract:
BackgroundHeart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) is associated with high morbidity and mortality. Guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) for HFrEF has been shown to improve outcomes, with higher GDMT scores at hospital discharge being associated with lower mortality, fewer rehospitalizations and reduced healthcare costs. Yet, disparities in the utilization of GDMT remain. In this study, we examined the effect of various clinical, demographic, and socioeconomic factors on the utilization of GDMT in HFrEF patients referred to Cardiology in a tertiary care safety net hospital, using a standardized GDMT scoring system.

MethodsWe conducted a single-center cross-sectional retrospective analysis of patients who had an index HFrEF [≤] 40% diagnosis between January 1, 2024, to December 31, 2024, and who were referred to Cardiology at a tertiary care safety net hospital. Baseline characteristics, laboratory investigations, health care utilization, and GDMT score data were extracted at the ambulatory care visit nearest to 90 days from the index HF diagnosis. GDMT score ranges from 0 to 9 factored in doses of beta-blocker (BB), angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor/angiotensin receptor blocker (ACEi/ARB), mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (MRA), sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor (SGLT2i), angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI), isosorbide dinitrate/hydralazine (ISDN/HYD). Multivariable logistic regression was performed to examine associations between low GDMT scores (0-4) nearest to 90 days from new onset HFrEF diagnosis and several clinical, demographic, and socioeconomic variables.

ResultsIn 200 patients meeting entry criteria, mean age was 62.7 years, 64.0% were male, 47.5% were classified as white and 42.0% as Black. 39.5% had a low GDTM score (<5). The following were less likely to be associated with low GDMT score: diabetes mellitus (adjusted OR: 0.41, 95%CI=0.18-0.91) and frequent medical appointments (adjusted OR: 0.37, 95% CI=0.25-0.54), while higher serum eGFR was more likely to be associated with low GDMT score (adjusted OR: 1.02, 95%CI=1.00-1.03). There was no significant association between GDMT score and age, sex, race, or payer status.

ConclusionIn patients with HFrEF referred to Cardiology in our safety net tertiary care center, higher utilization of GDMT at 90 days was achieved in those who have diabetes mellitus, more frequent medical appointments, or lower serum eGFR. There was no difference in GDMT utilization according to age, sex, race, or payer status predictive of lower GDMT scores. Contrary to findings from previous studies, no significant differences were observed across demographic or payer groups, emphasizing the role of healthcare access and utilization.

data.title: Preprint: The origin of the MV Hondius Andes outbreak
data.authors: Ulloa-Zepeda, L.; Parker, E.; Gangavarapu, K.; Castillo, A.; Pavez, C.; Fernandez, J.; Vilches, M.; Vial, P.; Rambaut, A.; Andersen, K. G.; Vial, C.
data.abstract: In April-July 2026, Andes virus (ANDV) caused an outbreak aboard the MV Hondius cruise ship resulting in 12 confirmed cases and three deaths. Before symptom onset, the index case had travelled through hantavirus-endemic regions of Chile and Argentina, leaving the geographic origin of infection unresolved. We conducted phylogenetic and phylogeographic analyses using newly generated ANDV genomes from human cases and rodent reservoirs to investigate the likely origin of the outbreak. Through phylogenetic analyses, we show that the outbreak genome falls within a geographically structured lineage spanning southern Chile and Argentine Andean Patagonia. Using phylogeographic reconstructions across all three segments, integrated with the index cases travel itinerary, we identified the Tolten-Lanco area of southern Chile as the most likely geographic origin of the outbreak genome, with two candidate locations accounting for >98% of the posterior support. However, the index case visited this area 62-66 days before symptom onset, exceeding the conventionally reported ANDV incubation period of 7-42 days. Thus, while genomic evidence supports a southern Chilean origin of the outbreak genome, the timing and circumstances of transmission to the index case remain unresolved.

data.title: Preprint: Spatial distribution and factors associated with unmet need for family planning among women of reproductive age in Zambia: Evidence from the 2024 Zambia Demographic and Health Survey
data.authors: Sibeso, P.; Tembo, N.; Jacobs, C.
data.abstract: Unmet need for family planning contributes to unintended pregnancies, unsafe abortions, and preventable maternal and child deaths, and remains high in sub-Saharan Africa. In Zambia, national estimates may conceal important geographic inequalities. We assessed the spatial distribution of unmet need for family planning among women of reproductive age in Zambia and the factors associated with it. We conducted a cross-sectional analysis of the 2024 Zambia Demographic and Health Survey (ZDHS), including 12,133 women aged 15-49 years. We used survey-weighted logistic regression, accounting for the stratified two-stage cluster design, to estimate adjusted odds ratios (AOR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Global spatial autocorrelation was assessed with Morans I, local hotspots with the Getis-Ord Gi* statistic, and spatial clusters with a purely spatial Bernoulli scan statistic in SaTScan. The weighted prevalence of unmet need was 27.0% (95% CI: 25.7-28.3%), ranging from 23.8% in Central to 31.6% in North-Western Province. Unmet need was spatially clustered (Morans I = 0.142, p = 0.018), with hotspots mainly in Lusaka, Southern, North-Western, and Northern provinces; SaTScan detected a primary cluster in Lusaka (observed-to-expected ratio 1.42, p < 0.001). Women in union (AOR 2.33, 95% CI: 1.90-2.86) and never-married women (AOR 2.20, 95% CI: 1.69-2.86) had higher odds of unmet need than formerly married women, as did women with five or more children compared with none (AOR 3.05, 95% CI: 2.25-4.13). Lower odds were observed among women aged 35-49 years (AOR 0.65, 95% CI: 0.52-0.83), women in the richest wealth quintile (AOR 0.62, 95% CI: 0.45-0.86), employed women (AOR 0.73, 95% CI: 0.64-0.84) and urban residents (AOR 0.80, 95% CI: 0.68-0.95). Unmet need for family planning in Zambia is high, geographically clustered and socially patterned. Family planning programmes should prioritise hotspot areas, particularly Lusaka, Southern and North-Western provinces, while targeting younger, higher-parity and poorer women.

data.title: Preprint: Knowledge, attitudes and behaviours related to tick awareness and prevention among users of urban green spaces: insights from stakeholder focus groups
data.authors: Taylor-Egbeyemi, J. L.; Masterton, S.; Robin, C.
data.abstract:
BackgroundTicks in the UK can transmit pathogens that lead to diseases in humans, including Lyme disease and tick-borne encephalitis. Expanding tick populations and increasing human use of urban green spaces may elevate exposure risk. Public health advice exists, but little is known about how this guidance is understood and applied by users of urban environments.

MethodsFour stakeholder focus groups were conducted with professionals involved in tick fieldwork in urban green spaces. Discussions explored interactions with the public, perceived awareness, behaviours, and views on communication. Data were analysed thematically using an approach informed by the Framework Method.

ResultsStakeholders reported substantial variation in public awareness of ticks, influenced by prior exposure to rural environments and local knowledge. Misinformation, particularly around tick removal, was common. Signage was rarely observed in urban green spaces, and views on its effectiveness were mixed. Participants emphasised the need to balance risk communication with reassurance and highlighted the importance of age-appropriate education.

ConclusionsInsights from stakeholders underline the importance of targeted, context-specific public health messaging in urban settings. Priorities include identifying groups with lower awareness, addressing misinformation, designing balanced communication materials, evaluating the effectiveness of signage, and integrating education for children and families.

data.title: Preprint: Effects of Weighted Seated Core Exercises on Immediate Postural Stability in Healthy Young Adults: An Exploratory Study
data.authors: Fujino, F.; Yamakawa, M.; Kono, T.; Higaki, T.; Maeda, K.
data.abstract:
ObjectivesThis exploratory study investigated whether low-load, seated core exercises could produce immediate improvements in standing balance among healthy young adults, aiming to provide a foundation for safe, early-stage rehabilitation protocols.

MethodsTen healthy males performed seated core exercises consisted of alternating hip flexion 5 times per side while seated and maintaining bilateral shoulder flexion at 120{degrees} shoulder flexion under four load conditions: upper-limb weight only, a 400-g empty box, a 1-kg ball, and a 2-kg ball. Immediately following the exercise, participants performed a 10-s single-leg stance. Transversus abdominis (TrA) thickness was measured via wireless ultrasound at baseline, post-exercise, and during the stance. Center of pressure (CoP) sway was recorded concurrently to evaluate postural stability.

ResultsLeft-side TrA thickness during stance increased significantly under the 1-kg and 2-kg load conditions compared to baseline (p < 0.05), although substantial missing data for the left-side measurements limited the robustness of this finding. No significant load-dependent effects were observed for CoP sway parameters (p > 0.05). A moderate positive correlation ({rho} = 0.43, p = 0.002) was found between right-side TrA thickness and CoP sway velocity during the single-leg stance.

ConclusionsLow-load, seated core exercises do not yield immediate enhancements in standing stability in healthy populations. The results suggest that increased TrA thickness during a balance task may correlate with heightened postural instability rather than improved balance control. Further research is needed to determine whether these findings translate to clinical populations with impaired physical fitness.

data.title: Preprint: Beyond Perinatal Mood: Breadth of Psychiatric Symptoms and Delay Discounting as Correlates of Mothers' Relational Reports from Pregnancy Through Adult Children
data.authors: DeLauder, R.; Hebert, M.; Rhodes, S.; Lang, E.; Lee, M.; Riddle, A.; Margary, A.; Basso, J. C.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University
data.abstract: Maternal mental illness affects roughly one in five mothers in the United States, yet most evidence linking it to the mother-child relationship comes from the first postpartum year and relies on self-report measures of depression, anxiety, and stress. In 613 women spanning five family contexts - pregnancy and mothers whose youngest child was aged 0-2, 3-12, 13-17, or 18 and older - we examined twelve psychological constructs as correlates of mothers' relational reports. Eleven were associated with relational reports individually; entered together, only three retained independent associations surviving false discovery rate correction: cross-domain psychiatric symptom burden (beta = 0.38), delay discounting (beta = -0.11), and orienting sensitivity (beta = 0.10). To our knowledge, this is the first peer-reviewed study linking delay discounting to maternal relational reports. Depression, anxiety, anger, perceived stress, and negative affect fell to non-significance, and the symptom composite that displaced them contains none of those domains, indicating that breadth of psychiatric symptoms, not their type, tracked relational reports. A person-centered analysis converged: the latent profile with the poorest relational reports was defined by symptoms across multiple domains rather than by elevated stress alone. Associations varied across family contexts, though because each context used a different relational instrument, differences cannot be attributed to child age. These cross-sectional findings suggest that the psychological dimension most closely tied to maternal relational reports is broader than the perinatal mood constructs around which research and screening are organized, and that cross-domain symptom assessment warrants prospective evaluation as a complement to mood screening.
data.summary: Maternal mental illness affects roughly one in five mothers in the United States, yet most evidence linking it to the mother-child relationship comes from the first postpartum year and relies on self-report measures of depression, anxiety, and stress. In 613 women spanning five family contexts - pregnancy and mothers whose youngest child was aged 0-2, 3-12, 13-17, or 18 and older - we examined twelve psychological constructs as correlates of mothers' relational reports. Eleven were associated with relational reports individually; entered together, only three retained independent associations surviving false discovery rate correction: cross-domain psychiatric symptom burden (beta = 0.38), delay discounting (beta = -0.11), and orienting sensitivity (beta = 0.10). To our knowledge, this is the first peer-reviewed study linking delay discounting to maternal relational reports. Depression, anxiety, anger, perceived stress, and negative affect fell to non-significance, and the symptom composite that displaced them contains none of those domains, indicating that breadth of psychiatric symptoms, not their type, tracked relational reports. A person-centered analysis converged: the latent profile with the poorest relational reports was defined by symptoms across multiple domains rather than by elevated stress alone. Associations varied across family contexts, though because each context used a different relational instrument, differences cannot be attributed to child age. These cross-sectional findings suggest that the psychological dimension most closely tied to maternal relational reports is broader than the perinatal mood constructs around which research and screening are organized, and that cross-domain symptom assessment warrants prospective evaluation as a complement to mood screening.

data.title: Preprint: Individualised and Time-Dependent Prediction of Recurrence After Colorectal Cancer Liver Metastases Resection
data.authors: Viljamaa, A.; Baumgartner, R.; Strandberg, R.; Sterner, J.; Drejian, S.; Aghayan, D.; Fernandez Moro, C.; Sparrelid, E.; Osterlund, P.; Edwin, B.; Fretland, A. A.; Geyer, N.; Engstrand, J.; Gerling, M.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Clinical Science, Intervention and Technology, Division of Surgery and Oncology, Karolinska Institutet, Stockholm, Sweden
data.abstract: Introduction: Treatment strategies for colorectal cancer liver metastases (CRLM) are increasingly complex, driving interest in advanced prognostic tools. Externally validated benchmarks based on established clinical risk scores are needed to contextualise emerging models. However, existing scores remain difficult to apply and compare, because they provide categorical risk strata rather than individualised probabilities, and because model parameters are rarely published. Here, we validate and recalibrate seven established risk scores to derive individualised recurrence probabilities for future score benchmarking. Method: Patients undergoing index CRLM resection from two tertiary centres were included: Karolinska University Hospital (retrospective KaroLiver cohort [2013-2021, follow-up to 2025, n=709]) and Oslo University Hospital (OSLO-COMET trial cohort [2012-2016, follow-up to 2022, n=198]). Performance of the GAME, m-CS, Fong, Nordlinger, Nagashima, Konopke and Helsinki scores was assessed using recurrence-free survival as the primary outcome. Results: Among 709 patients in KaroLiver (median age 67 years [IQR 59-74]; 434 men [61%]), 422 (60%) had synchronous metastases and 444 (63%) received neoadjuvant chemotherapy. All scores significantly stratified recurrence risk (log-rank P<0.001; time-dependent AUC 0.63-0.74 at 3 years), albeit with performance differences across time points. Recalibrated models showed good agreement between predicted and observed recurrence and were externally validated in OSLO-COMET with broadly comparable net benefit. Models were implemented in the online tool PLATO (Personalised Liver metastases risk AssessmenT in Oncology). Conclusion: Established CRLM risk scores can be translated into individualised probabilistic recurrence estimates at clinically relevant time points, supporting patient communication, risk-adapted surveillance and transparent benchmarking of next-generation prognostic models.

data.title: Preprint: PlanetDiet: Sustainable diets and cardiometabolic health, study protocol for a six-month parallel-group randomized controlled trial in middle-aged adults at cardiovascular risk
data.authors: Trius-Soler, M.; da Costa-Seco, T.; Rewers, A.; Cuparencu, C.; Raabyemagle, A. M.; Tetens, I.; Guasch-Ferre, M.
data.abstract: Background: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains the leading cause of death worldwide. Diet plays a key role in CVD prevention while linking human health with environmental sustainability. The EAT-Lancet Commission proposed the Planetary Health Diet (PHD), a predominantly plant-based dietary pattern emphasizing high-quality foods and reduced meat consumption. Despite growing interest in the PHD, no randomized controlled trial (RCT) has evaluated its effects using the PHD index on established and novel cardiometabolic biomarkers. Methods: The PlanetDiet study is a six-month, three-arm parallel RCT investigating the effects of sustainable diets on traditional and novel cardiometabolic risk factors in 180 Danish adults aged 45?70 years at high cardiovascular risk. Participants are randomized to a PHD, an ovo-lacto-vegetarian diet, or their habitual diet (control). The primary outcome is changes in a composite cardiometabolic health score, with secondary outcomes including changes in metabolomic and proteomic profiles. Clinical assessments include the analysis of urine, blood, and faecal samples; continuous glucose monitoring; anthropometry and body composition measurements; dietary records; and self-reported questionnaires assessing physical activity, quality of life and dietary acceptance. To support adherence, participants receive four individualized dietary counselling sessions, two group sessions, seasonal food boxes tailored to their assigned diet, and access to a personalized digital application with recipes, individualized timelines, and visit scheduling. Conclusions: PlanetDiet will provide evidence on the effects of sustainable dietary patterns on cardiometabolic health. It will also investigate molecular pathways linking diet to cardiometabolic disease. Ultimately, the study may inform the development of effective, personalized dietary interventions that promote both human and planetary health. Trial registration: Sustainable Diets and Cardiometabolic Health (PlanetDiet): NCT07189676 [ClinicalTrials.gov] [registered before inclusion start; 2025-09-15]; Unique identifier: H-25030722.

data.title: Preprint: Multi-Modal Wearable and Biological Data Integration Reveals Physiological Signatures of Weight Variation in Overweight and Obese Adults: An AI4Food Machine Learning Study
data.authors: Attioui, H.; Lacruz-Pleguezuelos, B.; Carrillo de Santa Pau, E.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Computational Biology Group. IMDEA Nutrition Institute, Madrid, Spain
data.abstract: This study is part of the AI4Food project, which aims to identify the physiological and behavioral factors influencing weight variation in overweight and obese individuals through integrative analysis of multi-source data. A 30-day crossover intervention was conducted on 93 participants at IMDEA Nutrition Institute, combining a traditional phase (questionnaires, food diaries) and a digital phase (Fitbit Sense Smartwatch, FreeStyle Libre 2 glucose sensor). The collected data encompassed sleep, glucose, skin temperature, nutrition, and gut microbiome information. After rigorous preprocessing and alignment by intervention days, unsupervised clustering, association analysis, and machine learning models were applied to uncover physiological patterns linked to weight dynamics. Results showed greater weight reduction during the digital phase in Group 2, while between-group differences were not significant. Significant associations were observed between nocturnal respiratory rate, skin temperature, and weight variation. Under participant-level five-fold cross-validation, Random Forest models achieved mean accuracies of 64.3% for thermoregulation and 61.7% for glucose phenotype prediction, with RMSSD, restlessness, and nocturnal respiratory rate among the most influential predictors. In contrast, microbiome composition remained almost stable over the short intervention period. These findings support the potential of AI-driven integration of wearable and nutritional data to stratify metabolic phenotypes and advance personalized nutrition strategies in obesity management.

data.title: Preprint: KNOWLEDGE, ATTITUDES AND PRACTICES OF REFUSE DISPOSAL IN OKELELE, ILORIN, NIGERIA
data.authors: IBRAHIM, M.; ALATARE, A. S.; ADEWUNMI, M. O.; ADEYEMO, A. O.; PRECIOUS, D.-O. J.; ADEGOKE, M. O.; ADELEKE, A. O.; AKINDEJI, I. O.
data.author_corresponding_institution: COLLEGE OF HEALTH SCIENCES, UNIVERSITY OF ILORIN
data.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: Improper refuse disposal remains an environmental health concern in many Nigerian communities. This study assessed knowledge, attitudes and practices relating to refuse disposal among adult residents of Okelele community, Ilorin East Local Government Area, Kwara State, Nigeria. METHODS: A descriptive cross-sectional community-based study was conducted among 180 adults. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire covering sociodemographic characteristics, knowledge, attitudes and disposal practices. Descriptive statistics summarised responses, and chi-square tests assessed associations between categorical variables at a 5% significance level. RESULTS: Of 180 respondents, 102 (56.7%) had good knowledge, while 87 (48.3%) had negative attitudes and 99 (55.0%) had poor refuse-disposal practices. Commonly reported practices included incineration (50.6%), disposal into drains (30.6%) and open burning (21.7%). Absence of waste containers (37.2%) and distance to available containers (28.9%) were the leading reported barriers. Knowledge was associated with practice (chi-square=22.122; p<0.001) and attitude (chi-square=8.221; p=0.016); practice was also associated with attitude (chi-square=5.970; p=0.015). CONCLUSION AND IMPLICATIONS FOR TRANSLATION: Despite generally good knowledge, poor disposal practices were common. Improving access to reliable waste-collection infrastructure, alongside community education and enforcement of local waste-management measures, may help translate knowledge into safer practices. Keywords: Solid waste; Waste management; Knowledge; Attitude; Health behavior; Nigeria
