data.title: Preprint: Real-World Use, Dosing, and Reported Side Effects of BPC-157 and TB-500 for Musculoskeletal Injury: An Analysis of Online Communities
data.authors: Cassinat, J. J.; Callan, C.; Liggett, C.; Wright, V.
data.author_corresponding_institution: University of Colorado School of Medicine
data.abstract: Objective: To describe how people use the unapproved peptides BPC-157 and TB-500 for tendon, ligament and muscle injury and what side effects they report. Methods: Using a large language model validated against physician review, we analyzed 92,254 posts and comments from 28,652 users in Reddit's peptide communities from 2021 to 2026. We compared side effects with those reported by users of four other peptides in the same communities. Results: In all, 5,588 users described using BPC-157 and/or TB-500 for a specific musculoskeletal injury, most often a chronic tendon problem of the shoulder, knee or elbow. Only 3.8% of users described physician involvement, and 90.9% of those naming a source bought from research-chemical vendors. The median BPC-157 dose (366 mcg per injection) was about 2.7 times the human-equivalent dose of the 10 mcg/kg rat regimen, and among new users it rose from 300 mcg in 2024 to 500 mcg in 2025. Of those stating an outcome, 79.3% reported improvement, and 36.6% of all users were also in physical therapy. Overall, 27.2% described at least one side effect, most often fatigue, anxiety, anhedonia and insomnia. Anhedonia was more common than among users of the four other peptides (10.2% versus 1.3% of those with side effects). Conclusion: Use of these unapproved peptides for musculoskeletal injury is largely unsupervised, relying on grey-market products at self-selected, rising doses without established safety or efficacy.

data.title: Preprint: A healthy donor kidney aging signature estimable from PAS histology and its association with progression of diabetic kidney disease
data.authors: Hong, S. G.; Ryu, D.; Ku, H.; Ko, A.; Oh, J.-I.; Lee, J.; Kang, M.-W.; Kim, M.; Shin, Y.; Lee, H.; Han, S. S.; Kim, Y.; Kwon, J.; Lee, J.; Lee, J.; Park, J. I.; Park, J. T.; An, J. N.; Kim, H. J.; Moon, K.-C.; Kim, Y.-G.; Park, S.; Kim, D. K.; KORNERSTONE investigators,
data.author_corresponding_institution: Division of Nephrology, Department of Internal Medicine, Seoul National University Hospital, Seoul, Republic of Korea
data.abstract: Background. As kidneys age, their cells change in arrangement and gene expression. Whether these changes are also present in diabetic kidney disease (DKD), and whether they relate to how quickly kidney function is lost, is not known. Methods. Zero-time biopsies from 24 healthy living kidney donors (aged 36-66 years) and biopsies from 28 patients with DKD were profiled by single-cell-level spatial transcriptomics with a 5,101-gene panel. data.title: Preprint: Electric and Magnetic Source Imaging in Epilepsy: Anatomical Insights from Realistic Simulations
data.authors: Sdoukopoulou, G.; Jahromi, S.; Corona, L.; Partamian, H.; Lim, J.; Afnan, J.; Grova, C.; Papadelis, C.
data.abstract: Neurosurgery is an effective treatment for drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE), but its success depends on the accurate delineation of the epileptogenic focus, approximated noninvasively by electric and magnetic source imaging (ESI/MSI) of high-density electroencephalography (HD-EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG). These modalities have distinct sensitivity profiles; consequently, epileptiform activity detected by one modality may remain undetected by the other. However, the implications of these differences for spike detectability and localization accuracy, and the added value of combined electromagnetic source imaging (EMSI), remain insufficiently characterized under clinically realistic conditions. Here, we characterize HD-EEG and MEG sensitivity profiles and compare ESI, MSI, and EMSI, using realistic simulations with known ground truth. We generated HD-EEG and MEG datasets from cortical, insular, and hippocampal sources across multiple orientations, activated using patient-derived intracranial EEG spike waveforms. Spike sensitivity and localization accuracy were evaluated using dipole scanning, dynamic statistical parametric mapping (dSPM), and linearly constrained minimum variance (LCMV). EEG demonstrated higher spike detection rates and sensitivity for radially cortical sources at gyral crowns and sulcal bottoms (p<0.001), while MEG detected more spikes from tangential cortical sources along sulcal walls (p<0.001). MSI localized tangential sources more accurately than ESI across all methods (p<0.001), while dipole scanning outperformed dSPM and LCMV for cortical and insular sources (p<0.001). EMSI outperformed ESI (p<0.001) but did not improve localization over MSI. These findings suggest that complementary anatomical sensitivities of HD-EEG and MEG may improve epileptogenic source characterization, supporting simultaneous acquisition during the presurgical evaluation of patients with DRE.

data.title: Preprint: Circulating insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) and short-term functional change in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS): exploratory evidence for systemic trophic-metabolic reserve.
data.authors: Lim, C. K.; Brocardo, M.; Hunter, J.; Heads, J. A.; Rowe, D. B.; Furlong, S.; Atkin, J. D.
data.author_corresponding_institution: MND Research Centre, Faculty of Medicine, Health and Human Sciences, Macquarie University
data.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) exhibit heterogeneous functional decline, potentially influenced by systemic metabolic reserve. We investigate whether circulating insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) is associated with subsequent functional change in ALS. Serum IGF-1 was measured in 37 participants with ALS and 25 healthy controls. Baseline levels were compared between groups, and across disease-duration defined progression categories. Lagged regression assessed whether prior visit IGF-1 level predicted change in Revised ALS Functional Rating Scale (ALSFRS-R) on the next visit, adjusting for inter-visit interval, body mass index, age and sex. Mixed-effects and sensitivity analyses assessed robustness. Baseline IGF-1 did not differ significantly between controls and ALS (mean + SD: 107.3 + 54.3 vs 132.2 + 68.3 ng/mL, p = 0.12), or across progression categories (F(2, 34) = 0.13, p = 0.88). Across 48 intervals from 23 ALS participants, each 1-SD higher IGF-1 from prior visit was associated with 1.40-point less subsequent {Delta}ALSFRS-R decline (95% CI: 0.03 to 2.77, p = 0.045). Generalised estimating equations yielded a similar association ({beta} = 1.50, p = 0.030), whereas small-cluster robust inference showed wider uncertainty (p = 0.084). Repeated IGF-1 showed an intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.69, and the lagged association remained positive in all 23 leave-one-participant-out analyses. The IGF-1-by-time interaction was not significant in a random-slope mixed model (p =0.254). Higher circulating IGF-1 may reflect systemic trophic-metabolic reserve associated with short-term functional preservation in ALS, but limited precision precludes definitive prognostic or causal conclusions.

data.title: Preprint: Optimized phase-targeted auditory stimulation reduces nocturnal spikes in childhood epilepsies
data.authors: Schmidt, E. C.; Wapp, N.-A.; Alessandri, B.; Eberhard, R.; Lederberger, D.; Moser, K.; Imbach, L.; Boelsterli-Heinzle, B.; Ramantani, G.; Fattinger, S.; Huber, R.
data.abstract: Interictal epileptiform discharges, so called spikes, are often strongly activated during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep in childhood epilepsies. In children with pronounced spike activation during NREM - sleep, spike burden can be associated with lifelong impaired cognitive functions. This spike activation is also related to alterations in sleep oscillations, specifically slow waves and spindles, which play essential roles in brain maintenance and maturation. These observations suggest that spikes may disrupt sleep-dependent brain processes that are critical for the development of cognitive functions. Phase-targeted auditory stimulation during NREM sleep delivers brief, non-arousing tones at specific phases of ongoing slow waves to modulate sleep oscillations. Recently, our group showed that isolated, less frequent, and thus less expected, tones engage widespread thalamocortical networks, whereas repetitive, regular trains of tones promote habituation and engage more local corticocortical networks. In this study, we use these contrasting stimulation patterns for a targeted modulation of sleep oscillations and examine their interaction with epileptic spikes. In an initial exploratory study (N = 10; age range: 7.3 - 16.2 years), we used a within-night block design to directly compare responses to the different stimulation patterns. Isolated tones delivered at long interstimulus intervals induced a transient increase in spike rate, whereas down-phase stimulation delivered in trains at short, regular intervals was associated with a significant reduction. We subsequently optimized the train-based paradigm and evaluated stimulation delivered throughout the night in a proof-of-concept study using a counterbalanced, between-night design (N = 5; age range: 4.4 - 10.7 years). Spike density decreased locally in all patients, providing convergent evidence for the effects observed in the exploratory study. With this mechanistically guided approach, we demonstrate that repetitive down-phase auditory stimulation of slow waves results in a local reduction of epileptic spikes. This framework may provide a rational basis for targeted interventions aimed at reducing spikes and related cognitive impairments.

data.title: Preprint: Food-Group Intakes and Depression in Tangerang, Indonesia: An Exploratory Case-Control Study
data.authors: Cipta, D. A.; Saputra, A.; Suryadinata, N.; Siregar, R. U. P.; Rivami, D. S.
data.abstract: Background: Diet may be associated with depression, but evidence on locally consumed food groups in Indonesia is limited. Objectives: To compare food-group intake between people with and without a formal diagnosis of depression in Tangerang, Indonesia, and to explore whether BMI modifies any association. Methods: In this case-control study, cases were psychiatric outpatients with a formal diagnosis of depression. Controls had no formal diagnosis and were recruited through university and community networks. Daily intake of ten food groups was estimated with a semi-quantitative food frequency questionnaire. Intakes were compared with independent-samples t-tests (Welch's test when variances were unequal), overall and stratified by BMI group. Logistic regression estimated the odds of depression per 100 g/day of sweetened beverage intake, adjusted for BMI group, sex, and age, with a sweetened beverage and BMI group interaction term. Results: There were 257 participants: 104 cases and 153 controls. Sweetened beverages were the only food group whose intake differed significantly between groups (approximately 214 vs. 153 g/day; mean difference 61 g/day; 95% CI 18-103; p=0.005). Each additional 100 g/day was associated with higher odds of depression after adjustment (OR 1.29; 95% CI 1.09-1.52). The association appeared stronger in underweight/normal-weight participants (ratio of ORs for overweight/obese vs. underweight/normal 0.70; 95% CI 0.49-0.99; p for interaction=0.046). Conclusions: Higher sweetened beverage intake was associated with depression in this sample, and there was modest evidence that the association differed by BMI group. Because the study is cross-sectional in timing, the case-control samples were selected differently, and many comparisons were made, these findings are exploratory. They do not establish causality.

data.title: Preprint: Communication without dialogue? Framing patient-professional interaction in UK institutional discourse on pregnancy loss
data.authors: Nuttall, L.; Malory, B.
data.abstract: Communication failures are repeatedly implicated in harmful experiences and outcomes in pregnancy care, especially in contexts of loss, yet little is known about how communication itself is represented in the institutional texts that shape expectations of care. This study examines the extent to which communication is discussed, and how patient-healthcare professional interaction is framed, in publicly accessible UK discourse about pregnancy loss. Two corpora comprising texts from seven medical organisations (120,383 words) and eight charities (224,481 words) were divided into healthcare professional-facing and patient-facing sub-corpora. Frequency, semantic keyness, keyword and concordance analyses were conducted using Wmatrix7. In medical discourse, language and communicative interaction were underrepresented, while speech acts associated with unidirectional professional activities such as advising, recommending and referring were overrepresented. Compared with charity texts, medical outputs foregrounded clinical evidence, policy, risk and professional knowledge. Characteristic forms including 'confirmed', 'advised', 'recommended' and 'offered' frequently occurred in passive or agentless constructions that positioned patients principally as recipients of information; patient agency was most visible in 'reporting' symptoms or concerns. Charity discourse more often foregrounded talking, listening, feelings, preferences, wording, lived experience, and patient knowledge; representing communication as active and bidirectional. We argue that UK medical discourse constructs communication primarily as the transmission of authorised knowledge rather than as relational clinical practice, reinforcing a paternalistic distribution of communicative agency. Medical institutions should embed listening, reciprocal dialogue, sensitivity to language preferences, and checks on understanding as core standards of safe pregnancy care.

data.title: Preprint: Hidden overweight and adverse birth outcomes among Asian mothers in the United States, 2016-2023: a population-based repeated cross-sectional study
data.authors: Tasnim Jahan, J.; Afrose, S.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Epidemiology and Biostatistics, University at Albany, State University of New York, Albany, New York, USA
data.abstract: Background: Standard body mass index (BMI) categories may understate risk in Asian individuals. Lower Asian action points exist, but their relevance to birth outcomes is unclear. Objectives: To estimate the proportion of normal-weight Asian mothers with BMI 23.0-24.9 kg/m2 and its association with birth outcomes, overall and by Asian subgroup, and to compare Asian and White mothers. Methods: Repeated cross-sectional study of US singleton live births, 2016-2023 (National Vital Statistics System). Outcomes were hypertensive disorders, caesarean delivery, preterm birth, and low birthweight. Modified Poisson regression, adjusted for confounders and Asian subgroup, estimated risk ratios (RRs), standardized risks, and risk differences (RDs). We tested for a change in slope at 23.0 kg/m2, subgroup heterogeneity, and race x BMI interaction. Results: Among 1,758,116 non-Hispanic Asian mothers, 314,510 (17.9%) had BMI 23.0-24.9 kg/m2, 30.4% of normal-weight mothers. Compared with BMI 18.5-22.9, standardized risk of hypertensive disorders was 4.5% versus 3.2% (RD 1.4 percentage points, 95% CI 1.3, 1.5; RR 1.44, 95% CI 1.40, 1.47), and of caesarean delivery 32.4% versus 28.6% (RR 1.14, 95% CI 1.13, 1.14). Preterm birth risk was 7.2% versus 6.6% (RR 1.08, 95% CI 1.06, 1.10); low birthweight risk was not higher (7.1% versus 7.5%; RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.93, 0.97). The hypertensive-disorder slope showed no evidence of change at 23.0 (ratio of per-unit RRs 0.99, 95% CI 0.98, 1.01); the hypertensive-disorder RR ranged from 1.24 (95% CI 1.18, 1.29) among Asian Indian to 1.70 (95% CI 1.60, 1.81) among Chinese mothers. BMI-outcome associations differed between Asian and White mothers. Conclusions: Nearly one in three normal-weight Asian mothers had BMI 23.0-24.9 kg/m2, associated with higher risks of hypertensive disorders and caesarean delivery but not low birthweight. The hypertensive-disorder gradient showed no evidence of change at 23.0 kg/m2, and associations varied across Asian subgroups.

data.title: Preprint: Genomic epidemiology reconstructs the pre-detection transmission and establishment of chikungunya virus in Guangdong, China
data.authors: Peng, X.; Chen, Z.; Jia, P.; Zhang, C.; Zhang, M.; Zhong, Y.; Sun, A.; Huang, S.; Li, W.; Zhang, X.; Cai, J.; Liu, Z.; Luo, J.; Su, J.; Sun, C.; Yu, Q.; Tan, Q.; Zheng, Z.; Zou, L.; He, J.; Li, B.; Faria, N. R.; Yu, H.
data.abstract: In 2025, a chikungunya outbreak in southern China resulted in more than 25,000 confirmed cases, but its origins and transmission history remain unresolved. As part of the public health investigation, we generated 1,264 near-complete chikungunya virus (CHIKV) genomes from Guangdong Province and integrated genomic, epidemiological, entomological, and human mobility data to reconstruct the emergence and spread of this outbreak. Our analyses traced the outbreak to a single dominant introduction of a Reunion-associated East/Central/South African (ECSA) virus lineage and dated the origin of the sampled Guangdong outbreak lineage from late April to early May 2025. The interval between the estimated origin of the outbreak lineage and the first reported case was consistent with a period of undetected local transmission and exposed limitations in passive surveillance for early arboviral outbreak detection. Spatiotemporal reconstruction showed two distinct epidemic waves with contrasting transmission dynamics. The Foshan wave involved frequent medium- to long-distance viral movement, while the Jiangmen wave remained relatively localized. Together, these findings reconstruct the early establishment and spatially heterogeneous spread of the largest documented CHIKV epidemic in southern China to date and demonstrate the necessity of expanding active genomic surveillance in areas at the fringe of CHIKV endemic transmission for timely detecting and characterizing emerging epidemics.

data.title: Preprint: Association Between Anorexia Nervosa Severity and Social and Occupational Functioning across Adulthood
data.authors: Zhang, Z.-P.; Larsen, J. T.; Clausen, L.; Agerbo, E.; Bulik, C.; Petersen, L. V.; Yilmaz, Z.
data.abstract: Importance: Severe anorexia nervosa (AN) carries substantial mortality risk, but its consequences associated with social and occupational functioning remain poorly characterized, limiting the development of targeted interventions to improve functioning, prevent and reduce long-term social disadvantage. Objective: To determine whether AN severity is associated with educational attainment, employment, income, and cohabitation status. Design: Cohort study following social and occupational outcomes across adulthood until age 55. Setting: Population-based. Participants: All individuals born in Denmark from 1963 to 1994, alive and residing in Denmark at age 30. The AN group had a first AN diagnosis between ages 10 and 25 years, excluding those who died or emigrated within 5 years. The comparison group had no AN diagnosis. Exposure: Illness severity of AN, measured by the AN Register-based Severity Index 5 years after the first AN diagnosis. Main Outcomes and Measures: Educational attainment was assessed at age 25 (upper secondary education) and at age 30/35 (highest completed education). Employment status, income deficiency, and cohabitation status were assessed annually from age 30 to 55. Results: Among 2,442,916 individuals, 9,465 were diagnosed with AN, of whom 1,996 (21.1%) were classified as severe AN cases. At age 25, individuals with severe AN had increased odds of non-completion of upper-secondary education compared to the general population (odds ratio [OR]=3.07; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 2.72-3.46), and those with less severe AN (OR=1.39; 95% CI: 1.29-1.50). data.title: Preprint: Classical machine learning versus transformers for predicting daily psychological distress from passive smartphone sensing and self-report: a prospective cohort study
data.authors: Griss Salas, I.; Lam, W.-Y.; Kilshaw, R. E.; Baucom, B. R. W.; de Lacy, N.
data.abstract: Objective: We test whether data collected from daily passive smartphone sensing and self-reports can predict daily significant psychological distress with meaningful potential clinical utility, comparing across best-in-class machine learning algorithms. Methods: In this prospective cohort study, 169 community-dwelling adults completed baseline surveys followed by 7 days of passive smartphone sensing (accelerometer, GPS, power state) and end-of-day Brief Symptom Inventory-18 (BSI-18) assessments. Cases were defined as days (total n = 1,062) where participants' psychological distress measured with the sex-specific BSI-18 Global Severity Index T-score was [≥]63 (prevalence 11.2%). Four classical models (artificial neural network, elastic net, support vector machine [SVM], extreme gradient boosting [XGB]) and four transformers (sensor-only or multimodal; standard or fusion architecture) were tuned, Platt-calibrated and evaluated on held-out participants (210 records, 25 cases) with participant-level bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Results: The SVM (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUROC] 0.84; 95% CI 0.71-0.93), the multimodal fusion transformer (0.84; 0.69-0.95) and XGB (0.82; 0.63-0.94) discriminated best; sensor-only transformers performed at chance (0.49-0.50). At the default threshold of 0.50, elastic net logistic regression was the best classifier (sensitivity 0.56, positive predictive value 0.64). At 0.12 (near the outcome prevalence), the SVM detected all cases (negative predictive value 1.00), but positive predictive values were low for all models (0.13-0.26). Decision-curve analysis favored most models over treat-all and treat-none lines at thresholds between 0.05 and 0.25. Baseline survey items, mainly on functional impairment, had the largest feature importance. Conclusions: Compact classical models performed as well as transformers, which were considerably more computationally intensive. Decision-curve analysis supports further clinical exploration of these tools for triaging daily psychological distress, though our results suggest the relative value of psychosocial assessments and digital data should be carefully analyzed. External validation is needed before clinical use.

data.title: Preprint: Determinants of Prehospital Management of Superficial Burns in Pediatric Patients at Health Facilities in Mazabuka District: A Cross-Sectional Study
data.authors: KASOMA, D.; Rosen, H. E.; Machona, P. K.; Jacobs, C.; Musonda, P.
data.abstract: Background Burn injuries in children are common in low-resource settings, yet little is known about how they are managed before reaching health facilities in Zambia. Early care at home plays a key role in recovery, but harmful practices are still widely used. We examined how caregivers manage superficial burns in children and identified factors linked to good prehospital care in Mazabuka District. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional study between September and December 2025 among 337 caregivers of children aged 0-15 years presenting with superficial burns. The study was conducted at three health facilities in Mazabuka District. Data were collected using structured interviews and clinical records. Prehospital burn care was classified as good or poor based on the recommended first-aid practices. Associations were assessed using Firth penalised logistic regression, and results are reported as adjusted odds ratios (AORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Results Only 13.1% (44/337) of caregivers provided good prehospital burn care. Urban residence was associated with lower odds of good management (AOR 0.22; 95% CI: 0.05-0.92; p=0.038). Older caregiver age reduced the odds of good care (AOR 0.92; 95% CI: 0.86-0.98; p=0.011), while increasing child age improved it (AOR 1.25; 95% CI: 1.10-1.43; p<0.001). Longer time to reach a facility was also associated with poorer care (AOR 0.96; 95% CI 0.94-0.98; p<0.001). Conclusion Good prehospital burn care was uncommon. It was associated with time to the health facility, caregiver age, child age, and urban versus rural residence, rather than with proximity to a facility alone. Programmes should promote cooling with running water, avoidance of harmful home applications, and prompt care-seeking. Messages in routine child health services may reach caregivers of young children; additional approaches are needed for older caregivers and urban communities.

data.title: Preprint: Longitudinal Participation and Cognitive Score Interpretation in the J-TRC Webstudy
data.authors: Sato, K.; Niimi, Y.; IHARA, R.; Suzuki, K.; Iwata, A.; Iwatsubo, T.
data.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Web-based registries support remote cognitive assessment for Alzheimer's disease research, but participant-driven reassessment raises questions about long-term data yield and interpretation of repeated scores. We evaluated data contribution, selective observation, and retest-dependent estimates of cognitive change in the Japanese Trial-Ready Cohort (J-TRC) Webstudy. METHODS: We analyzed over six years of J-TRC Webstudy data (launched October 2019; registrations through March 31, 2025; assessments through May 31, 2026). We examined data contribution, inactivity, reactivation, score-associated observation, first-exposure contrasts, and sensitivity to retest models and estimators. RESULTS: Among 14,912 registered accounts, 10,863 participants were eligible; 10,645 (98.0%) completed the Cognitive Function Instrument (CFI), 6,419 (59.1%) completed Cogstate, and 5,792 (53.3%) contributed assessments on multiple days. Among those with sufficient opportunity, 19.4% and 14.1% contributed data at or beyond three and five years. After 365 days without assessment, the estimated probability of resuming within two years was 7.2%. Worse prior cognitive scores were associated with lower odds of subsequent assessment (adjusted odds ratios per standard deviation: CFI, 0.952; Cogstate, 0.845). By assessment 12, returnee changes were +0.43 and +1.14 favorable baseline standard deviations (CFI, Cogstate), versus -0.06 and +0.08 in first-exposure contrasts. Marginal CFI time estimates differed under categorical versus flexible retest adjustment (+0.080 versus -0.227 standard deviations/year). DISCUSSION: High initial completion was accompanied by limited long-term data contribution. Subsequent assessment was associated with prior scores, and estimated time trends varied by retest model. Reporting assessment histories and testing model sensitivity are important for interpreting repeated online cognitive scores.

data.title: Preprint: Cognitive Performance in Prodromal Neuronal α Synuclein Disease
data.authors: Anis, S.; Zimmerman, E.; Sperling, S. A.; Alberts, J. L.; Weintraub, D.; Simuni, T.; Siderowf, A.; Fernandez, H. H.; on behalf of the Parkinson's Precision Medicine Initiative,
data.abstract: Importance: Cognitive abnormalities may emerge during prodromal neuronal a-synuclein disease (NSD), but their domain specificity and longitudinal course are uncertain. Objective: To characterize baseline cognition and longitudinal change in prodromal NSD compared with healthy controls, NSD-negative genetic carriers, and sporadic Parkinson disease (PD). Design: Longitudinal cohort study using Parkinson's Precision Medicine Initiative (PPMI) data, with first visits from July 2010 through April 2026 and up to 4 years of follow-up. Setting: Multicenter cohort. Participants: Healthy controls (HC; n=244), GBA1 or LRRK2 nonmanifesting carriers without NSD (n=323), prodromal NSD participants recruited through hyposmia or isolated rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder cohorts (n=1640), and sporadic PD (n=824). Exposures: NSD status and clinical cohort. Main Outcomes and Measures: Cognitive summary scores for verbal memory, executive function, processing speed, language, and visuospatial function, and PPMI-defined mild cognitive impairment (MCI). Models adjusted for age, sex, education, and APOE {varepsilon}4 status. Results: Among 3031 participants (mean [SD] age, 66.6 [7.0] years; 1322 female [43.6%]), prodromal NSD participants had lower baseline verbal-memory performance than HC (adjusted difference, -0.20 SD; 95% CI, -0.34 to -0.07; adjusted P = .007); NSD-negative genetic carriers did not differ from HC. No other cognitive domain was lower than HC at baseline or longitudinally. In the primary age-adjusted analysis, verbal-memory trajectory differed from HC over 4 years (P = .009), whereas in a smaller age-matched sensitivity subset through year 3, it did not (P = .62); the baseline difference persisted (adjusted difference, -0.28 SD; 95% CI, -0.46 to -0.10; P = .003). Adjusted MCI probability increased from 10.2% to 15.1% in prodromal NSD, compared with 8.4% to 5.0% in HC and 13.4% to 17.7% in PD. The increase was greater than in HC (ratio of annual odds ratios, 1.28; 95% CI, 1.04 to 1.58; adjusted P = .04) but not PD (P = .62). Conclusions and Relevance: Prodromal NSD was associated with modestly lower verbal memory and increasing MCI probability relative to HC, without lower performance in other cognitive domains. The baseline verbal-memory difference was robust, whereas the longitudinal trajectory finding was not reproduced in the smaller age-matched sensitivity subset.

data.title: Preprint: Benchmarking Structural Variant Detection in Whole-Exome Sequencing of 67 Multiple Myeloma Cell Lines
data.authors: Pugalenthi, L. S.; Nanduri, R.; Hong, R.; Ylagan, M.; Prasad, R.; Arasappan, D.; Kowalski-Muegge, J.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Oncology, Dell Medical School, University of Texas at Austin
data.abstract: Background. Although the majority of structural variant (SV) workflows have been derived based on whole genome sequencing (WGS) data, they continue to be applied to whole exome sequence (WES) data for which many studies have evaluated their performance in cancer. An equally important consideration that has not been well studied is the impact of cancer context specific features among WGS-derived SV callers applied to WES data. Similar to personalized medicine, not all SV callers are alike and optimal for use with all cancer types and sequence data types. In addition to sequencing related data features, cancer types have embedded features withing the sequencing data that should be considered. Herein, we performed an analysis of SV heterogeneity among WGS-derived SV callers to WES data in multiple myeloma (MM), a cancer known for its genetically heterogeneous nature. Using WES data derived from a panel of 67 Multiple Myeloma (MM) cell lines, we evaluated seven WGS-derived SV detection tools (Delly, SvABA, BreakDancer, Smoove, LUMPY and Manta) for their ability to identify cytogenetically known genetic abnormalities and to characterize overall differences in the number, length, type, and runtime of SVs called among them. Results. Among the seven tools, Smoove and Manta both had the shortest runtime, processing files in less than 2 minutes, in contrast to tools that required more than two hours to run such as SvABA and Pindel. Smoove was the only SV caller to identify a range of SV types, while SvABA was the most restrictive, calling only breakends. All tools differed in the length of SVs called, with SvABA's unfiltered output including the shortest length of less than 10 base pairs (bps), and Delly and BreakDancer's output including the longest, with SVs of less than 1,000 bps. At the chromosome level, SvABA's unfiltered output and Delly's output included 78% and 27.5% of known SVs, respectively, with the remaining tools (including SvABA's filtered output) achieved recall rates of less of less than 10%. By comparison, at the genomics coordinate level, no tool identified more than 20% of known SVs. Conclusions. As all evaluated SV detection tools achieved poor recall rates on this comprehensive catalog of MM cell lines, this study implies SVs detected by WGS-based SV callers on WES data should be confirmed experimentally before being declared legitimate. Heterogeneity in these tools' output lends support to their combined use in practice. Considering that many clinical grade sequencing panels continue to expand their repertoire of rearrangements with therapeutic implications, our results prompt the potential need for cancer type-matched workflows to evaluate the calling of such rearrangements.

data.title: Preprint: Agentic Pipeline for Large-Scale Clinical Data Queries in Enterprise Electronic Health Records
data.authors: Pawar, K.; Tavabi, N.; Kalepalli, A.; Kalepalli, N.; Blackmon, M.; Williamson, A.; Kiapour, A.
data.abstract: Using electronic health record (EHR) data to answer clinical research questions is challenging. It requires understanding the research question, finding relevant information across different sources, and combining that information to produce meaningful results. We developed an agentic large language model (LLM) pipeline that decomposes investigator-authored requests into source-specific tasks, generates and executes SQL on EHR, integrates structured and unstructured EHR evidence, and applies study-specific clinical note adjudication. We evaluated this workflow against data analyst-identified cohorts across 50 pediatric orthopedic clinical data query requests. Of these, 43 were included in manual-review-adjusted performance analyses. The median adjusted positive predictive value, sensitivity among patients identified by either approach, and corresponding F1 score were 0.93 (95% CI, 0.88-0.98), 0.92 (95% CI, 0.90-0.95) and 0.90 (95% CI, 0.87-0.94), respectively. These findings support the feasibility of translating natural-language research intent into executable, autonomous multi-stage EHR workflows.

data.title: Preprint: Additional tuberculosis case detection through repeat household contact investigation at 6 and 12 months: a retrospective cohort study in Kasama, a peri-urban district in Zambia
data.authors: Mwaba, P. B.; Mukupa, M.; Sakala, J.; Mwaba, I.; Siameka, D.; Maimbolwa, M. M.; Chanda, C.; Mputu, M.; Zimba, K. M.; Kasese-Chanda, N.; Chimzizi, R.; Mubanga, A.; Muyoyeta, M.; Kagujje, M.
data.author_corresponding_institution: CIDRZ: Center for Infectious Disease Research in Zambia
data.abstract: Background: Tuberculosis contact investigation (TBCI) facilitates early detection of TB among household contacts. However, evidence on the additional contribution of repeat TBCI in high-burden settings remains limited. We assessed the contribution of repeat TBCI at 6 and 12 months to TB case detection in Kasama District, Zambia.   Methods: We conducted a retrospective observational cohort analysis of routinely collected programme data from five purposively selected high-volume TB diagnostic facilities. Household contacts of bacteriologically confirmed TB patients notified between January 2023 and April 2024 underwent symptom-based TB screening at baseline and at 6 and 12 months. We estimated round-specific TB detection yields, the cumulative proportion diagnosed with TB, and the contribution of repeat investigations to overall case detection.   Results: Among 1,250 index TB patients, 3,648 household contacts were identified and screened at baseline. TB was diagnosed in 143 (3.9%) contacts at baseline, 31 (0.9%) at month 6, and 25 (0.7%) at month 12. Overall, 199 (5.5%) contacts were diagnosed with TB across the three screening rounds, of whom 159 (79.9%) had bacteriologically confirmed disease. Repeat investigations identified 56 additional cases, representing 28.1% of all TB diagnoses.   Conclusions: Repeat TBCI at 6 and 12 months identified additional TB cases beyond baseline screening, although detection yields declined across successive rounds. These findings support further evaluation of risk-based follow-up strategies and more sensitive baseline screening approaches to optimize TB case detection and resource utilization in high-burden settings.

Overall, 199 (5.5%) contacts were diagnosed with TB across the three screening rounds, of whom 159 (79.9%) had bacteriologically confirmed disease. These findings support further evaluation of risk-based follow-up strategies and more sensitive baseline screening approaches to optimize TB case detection and resource utilization in high-burden settings.

data.title: Preprint: Natural History Of Oral Human Papillomavirus In Nigerian Mothers And Youth With And Without HIV: A Prospective Cohort Study
data.authors: Kumar, A.; Peter, O. J.; Osagie, E.; Liu, J.; Byrd, M. C.; Chen, J.; Akhigbe, P.; Idemudia, N. L.; Abulude, I. J.; Kavecky, P.; Obuekwe, O.; Eki-Udoko, F. E.; Schlecht, N. F.; Bromberg, Y.; Osazuwa-Peters, N.; Coker, M.
data.abstract: Objectives: HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancer is rising, yet the natural history of oral-HPV, particularly persistence remains poorly characterized in sub-Saharan Africa and in people living with HIV (PLWH). We characterized oral HPV prevalence, incident detection, persistence, and clearance over four visits in a Nigerian mother-youth cohort with and without HIV and quantified the genotype distribution relative to vaccine coverage. Methods: Within the prospective HOMINY cohort, 1075 participants (404 mothers and 671 youth) were followed across four visits at 6-month intervals. Oral rinses were genotyped with the Seegene Allplex HPV28 assay (28 genotypes). Persistence was defined as detection at [≥]2 visit (not necessarily consecutive), with type-specific and visit 2-4 sensitivity definitions. We used modified-Poisson models for visit-level detection, Markov multistate models for acquisition and clearance, and a permutation test for mother-youth genotype concordance. Results: Oral HPV was detected at least once in 112 participants (10.4% overall; 11.1% mothers and 10% youth); incident detection was around 6% in both groups. Persistence was uncommon (1.9%), and only 3 had oral HPV DNA detected at all four visits. Clearance predominated across every visit interval. In Markov models, clearance was slower in PLWH (HR 0.42, 95% CI 0.22-0.77) with no difference in acquisition (HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.39-1.5). Persistence concentrated among PLWH. Only 31.2% of ever-positive participants carried a Gardasil-9 preventable strain of HPV; HPV16 and HPV39 were most frequent. Mother-youth genotype concordance exceeded chance (permutation p =0.009). Conclusion: Oral HPV was common but transient; persistence was confined to a small PLWH minority and was dominated by high-risk non-vaccine genotypes, leaving most infections beyond the reach of current vaccines.

data.title: Preprint: EIN-RECAP: Evidence-Grounded Multi-Agent Summarization and Retrieval of Infectious-Disease Expert Discussions
data.authors: Choudhuri, A.; Zhong, Y.; Beekmann, S.; Hodges, J.; Jha, K.; Segre, A. M.; Adhikari, B.; Polgreen, P. M.
data.abstract: Infectious disease experts exchange practical knowledge through clinical discussions, but identifying relevant information across years of conversations is difficult. These discussions often contain differing opinions and emerging observations that are not yet reflected in published evidence. We present EIN-RECAP, an AI-assisted platform developed with Emerging Infections Network (EIN) experts and deployed in beta to summarize and search historical discussions. The system combines retrieval-grounded summarization, citation validation, and hybrid search while distinguishing published evidence from community experience. We evaluated summarization methods across 3,185 threads and conducted blinded expert review on a recent subset. Although a multi-agent workflow achieved stronger automated scores, experts favored a simpler generation pipeline and identified repetition, inaccuracies, and overconfident recommendations in the more complex system. This feedback motivated an ensemble that improved discussion coverage and key clinical points on nine high-disagreement threads, although retrieval relevance remained a limitation. Our findings demonstrate the importance of expert involvement in clinical AI development and show why automated evaluation alone is insufficient to guide system selection.

data.title: Preprint: Routine CBC-Derived Markers of Systemic Inflammation Are Associated With Growth of the Dilated Ascending Aorta During CT Surveillance
data.authors: Murad, B.; Campello Jorge, C. A.; George, G. C.; Queiroz, I.; Karnam, Y.; Spahlinger, G.; Hofmann Bowman, M. A.; Burris, N. S.
data.abstract: Background: Ascending aortic surveillance relies on diameter thresholds, yet most dissections occur below them. Inflammation drives aortic wall remodeling independent of diameter. Inflammation drives aortic wall remodeling independent of diameter. Inflammatory indices derived from routine blood counts, such as neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), red cell distribution width (RDW), and systemic immune-inflammation index (SII) have been show to predict adverse cardiovascular outcomes, but their association with ascending aortic growth is unclear. Methods and Results: We retrospectively studied adults with 2 computed tomography (CT) scans of the native ascending aorta 6 months apart at a single center (2000-2023), excluding those with aortitis or no complete blood count during follow-up. Markers were summarized as 95th percentile values per patient and per scan interval. Growth was defined as a 2-mm increase in mid-ascending aortic diameter. Patient-level logistic regression and interval-level generalized estimating equation models were adjusted for age, sex, body mass index, baseline diameter, systolic blood pressure, diabetes, and heritable thoracic aortic disease. Among 3,262 patients, data were available in 1,882 for RDW, 1,471 for NLR, and 1,468 for SII; 192 (10.2%) met criteria for growth. Only RDW was independently associated with growth in the overall cohort (patient level: odds ratio [OR] 1.071, 95% CI 1.002-1.144, p=0.043; interval level: OR 1.075, 95% CI 1.012-1.141, p=0.019); NLR (p=0.080) and SII (p=0.164) were not. Among patients with guideline-defined ascending aortic dilation (40 mm), all three markers were associated with interval growth (RDW OR 1.14, NLR OR 1.05, SII OR 1.01 per 100 units; all p 0.014), whereas none were among aortas <40 mm; effect modification was significant for NLR (p=0.01). Conclusions: RDW was modestly associated with ascending aortic growth overall, and all three markers were associated with interval growth in patients with guideline-defined aortic dilation, suggesting that systemic inflammation may contribute to progression of aortic dilation. Prospective studies with more specific inflammatory markers are needed.

data.title: Preprint: Late-Stage Concentration of Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic Syndrome Burden in US Adults: Disability-Adjusted Life Years Across AHA Stages, 2005 to 2023
data.authors: Wang, X.; Qiao, Y.; Sun, H.; Wang, Y.; Zhou, H.; Zhang, T.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Beijing University of Chinese Medicine Dongfang Hospital
data.abstract: Background: Cardiovascular prevention is increasingly prioritised using burden estimates, yet disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) reward late-stage treatment by construction. Whether that bias is large for cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome, and where the population is accumulating relative to where the burden sits, is unknown. Methods: We pooled nine National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey cycles (2005-2023) and assigned CKM stages 0-4 from measured blood pressure, adiposity, glycaemia, lipids, kidney function, urine albumin, self-reported cardiovascular disease, and 10-year PREVENT risk. Years lived with disability used GBD disability weights. Years of life lost combined national death counts, stage-specific mortality from linked mortality files (1999-2018), and period life tables. A second aim attributed burden to smoking and physical inactivity, two exposures outside the CKM definition. Results: In 2021-2023, 13.8% of adults were stage 0, 21.3% stage 1, 49.1% stage 2, 6.5% stage 3, and 9.3% stage 4. CKM accounted for 20.0 million DALYs annually (7,881 age-standardised per 100,000), of which 4.1 million were YLD and 15.9 million attributable YLL. Stages 3-4, 15.8% of adults, generated 76% of attributable YLL; stage 4 alone generated 65% of YLD and 49% of attributable YLL. Adjusted mortality rose from stage 2 (hazard ratio 1.39) through stage 4 (3.22), while stage 1 did not differ from stage 0 (0.99; 95% CI, 0.78-1.25). Between 2006 and 2016, stage 0 prevalence fell 2.3% per year and stage 1 rose 3.1% per year. Smoking and physical inactivity accounted for 30.5% of burden (95% CI, 25.7-35.1). Conclusions: CKM burden is concentrated in stages 3-4, where excess mortality begins, while the population has been shifting into stage 1, where mortality is normal. DALY-based prioritisation will therefore systematically underfund the stage in which the next generation of patients is being created.

data.title: Preprint: Association Between Parental Nativity and Mental Health Among U.S. Adolescents: Findings from the National Health Interview Survey, 2022 - 2024
data.authors: Ndhlovu, S.; Zhang, D. S.; Li, L.; Liu, Z.
data.author_corresponding_institution: NYU Grossman Long Island School of Medicine
data.abstract: Introduction: Studies have shown a high prevalence of mental health problems among immigrants, but findings for their children are mixed. We examined the association between parental nativity and mental health among U.S. adolescents and assessed whether these associations varied by sex and race/ethnicity. Methods: We analyzed pooled cross-sectional data from the 2022-2024 National Health Interview Survey, including 12,540 adolescents aged 12-17 years. The exposure was parental nativity. The outcomes were adolescents' mental health, including anxiety, depression, behavioral difficulties, and peer relationships. Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) and nearest neighbor matching were used to control confounders. Survey-weighted logistic regression was used to estimate the association between parent nativity and each outcome. Subgroup analyses were conducted by sex and race/ethnicity. Results: Compared with adolescents with U.S.-born parents, adolescents with at least one foreign-born parent had lower odds of anxiety (Odds Ratio [OR]=0.62, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.54-0.71), depression (OR=0.71, 95% CI: 0.60-0.84), and behavioral difficulties (OR=0.56, 95% CI: 0.43-0.72), but not relationship difficulties (OR=0.97, 95% CI: 0.74-1.26), in the IPTW analysis. Findings from nearest-neighbor matching were consistent. In exploratory stratified analyses, inverse associations were observed among Hispanic adolescents and adolescents classified as other race/ethnicity. Conclusion: Parental nativity was associated with adolescent mental health, with adolescents of at least one foreign-born parent showing lower odds of anxiety, depression, and behavioral difficulties. Future studies are needed to clarify the underlying mechanisms and identify protective factors that help inform interventions to promote adolescent mental health.

data.title: Preprint: Epidemiological Modeling of Seasonal Influenza Through Periodic Mean-Reverting Stochastic Processes
data.authors: Mostafa, F.; Allen, L.
data.abstract: Seasonal influenza follows annual cycles, but variation in epidemic magnitude and timing complicates preparedness. We applied periodic mean reverting stochastic differential equations (SDEs) to seven seasons of weekly Texas influenza surveillance data. Missing observations were imputed using MissForest and compared with four alternative methods. Stochastic variability was modeled using {sigma}X(t) dW(t), with p = 1/2,2/3,5/6, and 1, representing square root, intermediate sublinear, and multiplicative diffusion. Each specification was evaluated for direct influenza modeling and within a susceptible, exposed, infectious , and recovered model incorporating waning immunity, where the SDE governed transmission. Parameters were estimated using least squares and approximate maximum likelihood for direct models and sample-proportion weighted least squares for stochastic SEIR models. Model-based parametric bootstrap assessed direct-model parameter uncertainty. For direct modeling, p = 1/2 achieved the lowest RMSE (712.8) and AIC (5383.0), with similar AIC for p = 2/3 (5383.2). For stochastic SEIR modeling, p = 1 achieved the lowest RMSE (0.02926), compared with 0.03506 for p = 1/2. The deterministic SEIR model yielded R = 1.158. Transmission peaked approximately 10 weeks before infectious prevalence, while stochastic transmission generated variation in epidemic peak timing. Bootstrap analysis identified dependence between mean-reversion and diffusion parameters. Overall, the appropriate diffusion structure depended on the epidemiological quantity modeled, supporting flexible characterization of seasonal transmission variability while requiring prospective validation before operational forecasting.

data.title: Preprint: Development and Preliminary Evaluation of a Brief Health Chatbot Acceptability Scale (CAS): A Pilot Study
data.authors: Ownby, R. L.; Caballero, J.; Thomas-Purcell, K.
data.abstract: Background. Conversational agents (chatbots) are increasingly used to deliver health information to middle-aged and older adults, a population in which the determinants of technology acceptance are known to diverge from those of younger users. However, acceptability is inconsistently defined and typically measured with ad hoc, unvalidated instruments. The psychometrically sound chatbot measures that exist assess usability rather than acceptability or were validated in student samples. Objective. To develop and conduct an initial psychometric evaluation of a brief, 10-item health chatbot acceptance measure grounded in the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB). Methods. Twenty adults (mean age = 52.8 years, range 28-81; 85% aged 40 or older; 75% female) enrolled in a sleep-application pilot usability study completed the 10 candidate items, the System Usability Scale (SUS), and sleep measures (PROMIS Sleep Disturbance 8a; Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index). We examined item performance, internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha), dimensionality (exploratory factor analysis with oblique rotation), and convergent validity (correlations with the SUS). Results. A two-factor structure emerged and was invariant across rotation methods, resulting in an Information Quality factor and an Acceptance factor (interfactor r = .39). All items loaded [≥] .60 on their primary factor; mean communality was .83. Subscale reliabilities were high (Information Quality  = .96; Acceptance  = .94; full scale  = .93). Both subscales correlated with the SUS in the expected direction (r = .69 and r = .59), providing preliminary support for convergent validity. Conclusions. The measure shows a coherent and theory-consistent two-factor structure and shows preliminary evidence of reliability and convergent validity. Given the small pilot sample, these results must be viewed as provisional but identify the measure as a candidate for formal validation in a larger, independent sample.

data.title: Preprint: The cognitive profile of the schizophrenia-associated 3q29 deletion syndrome and the reciprocal 3q29 duplication syndrome
data.authors: Pollak, R. M.; Bishop, D. V.; Harner, M. K.; Khan, A.; Purcell, J. R.; Wheeler, M.; Irving, T.; Moore, T. M.; Ruparel, K.; Gur, R. C.; Gur, R. E.; Mulle, J. G.
data.abstract: 3q29 deletion syndrome (3q29del) and the reciprocal 3q29 duplication syndrome (3q29dup) are associated with a range of neuropsychiatric phenotypes, including impaired cognition. However, previous sample sizes have been small, and cognitive performance has not been systematically compared between 3q29del and 3q29dup. For both disorders, the impact of familial background on cognition is unknown. 3q29del is associated with high risk for schizophrenia; in the general population individuals at Clinical High Risk (CHR) for psychosis exhibit impaired cognition, but the relationship between CHR status and cognition in 3q29del is unexplored. Here we address these questions in the largest sample of 3q29del and 3q29dup ever evaluated. Individuals with 3q29del (n=103, 58.3% male), 3q29dup (n=38, 55.3% male), and controls (n=54, 42.6% male) were assessed with the Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test, 5th Edition (PPVT-5) and the Penn Computerized Neurocognitive Battery (Penn-CNB). Total PPVT-5 scores and global, domain-level, and task-level Penn-CNB scores were compared across groups. Compared to controls, 3q29del participants scored an average of 24.6 and 22.9 points lower on the PPVT and Penn CNB, respectively (p<3E-16); 3q29dup participants scored an average of 18.8 and 14.2 points lower on the PPVT and Penn CNB (p<4E-6). In addition, 3q29del and 3q29dup exhibit unique profiles of cognitive deficits. To assess the impact of familial background on cognition, we evaluated unaffected relatives of 3q29del (n=140, 38.6% male), 3q29dup (n=25, 24.0% male), and controls (n=45, 11.1% male). The average familial shift on the Penn-CNB was 22.4 points for 3q29del and 16.7 points for 3q29 dup. Individuals with 3q29del+CHR exhibited greater cognitive deficits than 3q29del-CHR. These results demonstrate that both 3q29del and 3q29dup are associated with significant cognitive impairment and indicate that cognitive testing should be standard of care for individuals diagnosed with 3q29del or 3q29dup.

data.title: Preprint: Diagnostic Value in Discarded Reads: Re-evaluating Multi-Mapping cfDNA Fragmentomics and GC Bias in Early-Stage Cancer.
data.authors: Kadali, N.; UPPALURI, K. R.; Challa, H. J.; Vempati, K. K.
data.abstract: Background. Low-coverage plasma cell-free DNA (cfDNA) sequencing is an inexpensive substrate for cancer detection. Standard pipelines discard fragments with low mapping quality, which originate mostly from repetitive DNA, although pericentromeric satellite repeats are frequently hypomethylated in cancer. We asked whether the fraction of multi-mapping cfDNA fragments differs between early-stage cancer and matched healthy controls, and how it compares with conventional fragmentomic features under strict control of technical factors. Methods. We analysed public plasma cfDNA whole-genome sequencing from 25 patients with stage I to III breast cancer and 25 healthy controls matched 1:1 for age, sex, smoking and alcohol use, each pair processed in the same library and sequencing batch, and from 8 early-stage hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) cases with 8 matched controls. For every sample we computed the fraction of autosomal fragments with MAPQ < 30 and the share of these fragments located in centromeric and heterochromatic cytobands, and related them to stage, grade and copy-number deviation as proxies of tumour burden. Classifiers were evaluated by leave-one-pair-out cross-validation in breast cancer and, trained on breast cancer only, applied unchanged to HCC. Robustness to GC content and sequencing depth was tested by within-fold residualisation and by fragment-level GC weighting. Conventional fragmentomic features (fragment length, end motifs, copy number, DELFI-like profiles and window features at transcription start sites) were evaluated under four GC-handling analyses. Results. The multi-mapping fraction was higher in breast cancer than in matched controls (median 5.38 % vs 5.19 %; higher in 19/25 pairs; paired p = 0.0006; cross-validated AUC 0.81, 95 % CI 0.67 - 0.94), in stage I (9/10 pairs), stage II (7/10) and stage III (3/5) disease and in every sequencing batch. The excess was concentrated in centromeric and heterochromatic bands, whose share of multi-mapping fragments rose from 22.0 % to 23.4 % (19/25 pairs; p = 0.004). Both signals persisted after within-fold adjustment for GC content and/or depth (AUC 0.64 - 0.76 for the multi-mapping fraction, 0.71 - 0.76 for the heterochromatic share) and under fragment-level GC weighting (18/25 pairs; p = 0.003). The multi-mapping difference was largest in stage I and decreased with stage (Spearman {rho} = -0.42, p = 0.04), and neither feature was associated with grade or copy-number deviation. In public tissue methylomes, satellites were hypomethylated in breast tumours to a similar extent as other late-replicating DNA, but the bin-level association between tumour hypomethylation and the cfDNA excess was weak and was explained by GC content. In HCC, the pre-specified endpoint, the breast-trained multi-mapping model, was not met (AUC 0.73; 5/8 pairs; sign test p = 0.36). In an exploratory analysis that was not pre-specified, the heterochromatic share was higher in 7/8 HCC pairs (p = 0.016; locked AUC 0.86, 95 % CI 0.62 - 1.00); across all 33 pairs, including the discovery pairs, it was higher in the cancer case in 26 (post hoc sign test p = 0.0007). In contrast, conventional fragmentomic features reached AUC 0.71 (breast) and 0.77 (HCC) only without fragment-level GC control; they tracked the per-sample coverage GC dependence and fell to chance under each of three GC-controlled analyses, including one that preserves promoter-specific signal. Conclusions. Multi-mapping cfDNA fragments, which are routinely discarded, differed between early-stage breast cancer and batch-matched controls, largely independently of GC content and sequencing depth, with an excess in centromeric and heterochromatic DNA. The signal did not scale with stage, its biological origin is unproven, and a read-quality contribution cannot be excluded from fragment files. It is a candidate marker that requires confirmation in larger cohorts with raw reads and tumour-fraction estimates.

data.title: Preprint: The Lived Experiences of Long-Term Users of Copper-T Intrauterine Devices: A phenomenological Qualitative Study among women at Kawempe National Referral Hospital in Uganda
data.authors: pious, I. S.; Beyeza-Kashesya, J.; Namagembe, I.; Twesigemukama, S.; Godfrey James, A.; Saad Sessimba, K.; Balikudembe, K.; Andrew, B.; Mary, M.; Mwanje, D.; Musanje, K.; Sekikubo, M.
data.abstract:
BackgroundThe Copper-T intrauterine device (Cu-T IUD) is a highly effective, non- hormonal, long-acting reversible contraceptive that can protect against pregnancy for up to 12 years, with a failure rate under 1%. Despite its clinical efficacy, early discontinuation remains a substantial challenge in Uganda, where discontinuation is approximated at 29% within the first year of use. Understanding the experiences of women using the Cu-T IUD is important to predict factors associated with discontinuation and to inform practice.

MethodsBetween September and November 2025, we conducted twenty in-depth interviews with women of reproductive age (15-49 years) who had used a Cu-T IUD for at least two years, recruited from the family planning clinic of Kawempe National Referral Hospital, Kampala, Uganda. Data were analysed thematically, guided by the Social-Ecological Model and Lazarus and Folkmans Transactional Model of Stress and Coping.

ResultsLong-term Cu-T IUD users reported both positive and negative experiences shaped by individual, interpersonal, and community factors. Two themes were identified at the individual-level domain: experiences during insertion and post-insertion experiences. Negative experiences, particularly heavy menstrual bleeding, anxiety, and abdominal pain, were common and distressing. Participants employed coping strategies, including taking painkillers, using home remedies, and resting, to manage these challenges with Cu-T IUD use.

ConclusionsNegative experiences of Cu-T IUD are common among long-term users; womens coping strategies such as taking painkillers lead to continued use. Client-centred pre- insertion counselling addressing both anticipated side effects and common misconceptions, alongside accessible follow-up services, may facilitate long-term Cu-T IUD use.

data.title: Preprint: Suvorexant Inversely Affects Phosphorylated Tau in Human Cerebrospinal Fluid and Plasma
data.authors: Pedersen, T. J.; Yu, J.; Li, A.; Ibanez, L.; Bubu, O. M.; Lucey, B. P.
data.abstract: Alzheimer disease (AD) is characterized by amyloid-{beta} plaques and neurofibrillary tangles of tau. Suvorexant, a dual orexin receptor antagonist, was previously shown to acutely reduce the ratio of phosphorylated tau-181 to unphosphorylated tau-181 (pT181/T181) in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). However, its effects on plasma pT181/T181 and broader proteomic networks remain unknown. Here, we conducted a secondary analysis of samples from a randomized, placebo-controlled trial of 25 participants receiving placebo or suvorexant 20 mg. Paired CSF and plasma samples were collected longitudinally via indwelling intrathecal and intravenous catheters. Plasma AD biomarkers were quantified by mass spectrometry, and proteomic profiling was performed using the SomaScan 11K assay on samples from hours 0, 16, and 24. Suvorexant increased pT181/T181 in plasma while decreasing it in CSF between 08:00-16:00. At the pathway level, suvorexant increased the extracellular abundance of proteins associated with translation, RNA binding, cytoskeletal organization and endosomal sorting, centrally at 16 hours and peripherally at 24 hours, and decreased cytokine and receptor-ligand signaling and serine protease activity in plasma at 24 hours. As plasma biomarkers are increasingly used for clinical screening and trial enrollment, factors that influence their levels, including medications, must be identified and their effects on interpretation understood.

data.title: Preprint: Prediction of elective surgical red blood cell transfusion reveals surgeon-level variation
data.authors: Turkulainen, E.; Arvas, M.; Koskinen, M.; Ilmakunnas, M.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUNDPreoperative prediction of red blood cell (RBC) transfusion in elective surgery serves two complementary purposes: enabling patient blood management (PBM) interventions before surgery and supporting blood product supply planning for elective lists. Beyond patient risk factors, individual surgeon practice may also contribute to transfusion rates, but this effect has not been fully quantified.

STUDY DESIGN AND METHODSIn a retrospective cohort of 279,905 elective surgical procedures at Helsinki University Hospital (2021-2025), we trained four gradient-boosted tree (CatBoost) models crossing patient factors with procedure group and pseudonymised surgeon identity. All predictors were restricted to data available seven or more days before scheduled surgery. The primary outcome was any allogeneic RBC transfusion from operating-room entry through seven postoperative days. Discrimination was assessed by the area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) on a held-out 20% test set. Surgeon-level effects were characterised by Shapley additive explanation (SHAP) values.

RESULTSThe transfusion rate was 2.2%. The patient-only model achieved AUPRC 0.261 (no-skill baseline 0.022). Adding surgeon identity to the procedure-adjusted model increased AUPRC from 0.440 to 0.472 (+0.032; 95% CI 0.020-0.044), raising lift from 20.3 to 21.7. Surgeon identity was the third most important of 72 features by permutation importance.

DISCUSSIONThe operating surgeon was associated with RBC transfusion beyond patient and procedure factors, and surgeon identity was the third most important predictor in a deployment-realistic model using only data available a week before surgery. This information is readily available from routine records and could support PBM audit and blood supply planning for elective surgery.

data.title: Preprint: Uncovering Distinct Phenotypes of Early Onset Heart Failure in Women
data.authors: Khorsandi, J.; Yu, Y.; Tinnium, D.; Ganesh, S.; Alahapphan, R.; Oyinloye, P.; Mueller, K.; Ardekani, S.; Taylor, C. O.; Greenstein, J. L.; Ndumele, C. E.; Michos, E. D.; Bairey Merz, C. N.; Barrett, R. B.; Minhas, A. S.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine
data.abstract:
BackgroundHeart failure in younger women is understudied and may reflect heterogeneous pathways and risk not adequately captured by conventional classifications. We aimed to identify clinically distinct phenotypes of early-onset heart failure in women, assess their prognostic significance, and evaluate their transportability in an independent national cohort.

MethodsWe identified women aged 18-55 years with heart failure using electronic health record data from a large multi-hospital system. A variational deep embedding model incorporating 283 clinical features was used for unsupervised phenotyping. Associations with subsequent inpatient hospitalization, emergency department utilization, and mortality were evaluated using age-stratified Cox models. Phenotype transportability was assessed by both applying the institutionally trained model and by independent de novo clustering as a replication analysis in the All of Us cohort.

ResultsAmong 1,407 young women with heart failure (median age, 45 years), four phenotypes were identified: hypertensive pregnancy (n=494), cardiorenal (n=276), autoimmune (n=394), and cardiometabolic-ischemic (n=243), with a bootstrap adjusted Rand index of 0.65 and silhouette score of 0.45. Compared with the hypertensive pregnancy phenotype, risks of inpatient hospitalization were highest for the cardiorenal (HR 2.86 [95% CI, 2.35-3.49]) and autoimmune (HR 2.25 [95% CI, 1.87-2.70]) phenotypes; mortality risks were similarly elevated (HR 4.65 [95% CI, 3.17-6.82] and HR 4.38 [95% CI, 3.03-6.31], respectively) in these two groups. In All of Us participants (n=682), transferred phenotypes retained their principal clinical characteristics and continued to stratify hospitalization risk. Independent clustering most strongly reproduced the cardiorenal phenotype (Jaccard index, 0.744).

ConclusionsEarly-onset heart failure in women comprises distinct cardio-obstetric, cardiorenal, autoimmune, and cardiometabolic-ischemic phenotypes with divergent clinical outcomes. These findings support a life-course approach to heart failure classification in women that complements conventional frameworks and incorporates pregnancy history and female-predominant systemic conditions.

Clinical PerspectiveO_ST_ABSWhat Is New?C_ST_ABSUnsupervised machine learning identifies distinct clinical phenotypes of heart failure among young women, highlighting heterogeneity in a population that remains understudied.
These phenotypes captured differing cardiometabolic, cardiovascular, and pregnancy-related characteristics, suggesting potentially distinct pathways contributing to heart failure development.
External validation in the All of Us cohort supported external validity and demonstrated the potential for identifying these patterns across diverse healthcare populations.


What Are the Clinical Implications?Heart failure in young women is clinically diverse, underscoring the importance of comprehensive assessment beyond traditional heart failure classifications, including cardiometabolic risk factors and pregnancy history.
Recognition of distinct clinical phenotypes may help clinicians identify women with differing risk profiles and inform more individualized approaches to cardiovascular evaluation, risk factor management, and longitudinal follow-up.
Further studies are needed to determine whether phenotypes differ in treatment responses and whether phenotype-guided management can improve outcomes.

data.title: Preprint: Community health workers experiences with a digital clinical decision support system for longitudinal hypertension and diabetes care in rural Lesotho: a mixed-methods study
data.authors: Gerber, F.; Raeber, F.; Moruthoane, M.; Khaemba, A.; Bhandari, N.; Kunwar, L.; Sanchez-Samaniego, G.; Gupta, R.; Williams, A.; Tahirsylaj, T.; Mathulise, M.; Kabi, T.; Mokaeane, M.; Maphenchane, M.; Molulela, M.; Khomolishoele, M.; Sematle, M. P.; Sao, L.; Tlahali, M.; Shankar, U.; Basler, D. B.; Kindler, K.; Grimm, P.; Labhardt, N. D.; Amstutz, A.
data.abstract:
Community health workers (CHWs) are increasingly delivering chronic care in resource-constrained settings but require support to manage complex longitudinal clinical workflows. In the Community-Based chronic Care Lesotho (ComBaCaL) project in rural Lesotho, CHWs provide longitudinal hypertension and diabetes care, supported by the ComBaCaL Community Health Toolkit (CHT) application. The application combines longitudinal participant management and task coordination with clinical decision support for screening, diagnosis, treatment initiation and adjustment, cardiovascular risk management, referral, and follow-up for hypertension and diabetes care. This model of care has demonstrated improved or maintained clinical outcomes compared to facility-based care only. We conducted a mixed-methods study among all 103 participating CHWs to evaluate their experiences with the application.

All CHWs completed a 38-item questionnaire, and 22 participated in qualitative interviews or focus group discussions. Overall usability was high, with a mean System Usability Scale score of 75.6 (SD 13.0), and 98 (95%) CHWs were satisfied or very satisfied with the application. General application functions and diagnosis and treatment tasks were rated easy or very easy by 98% of participants. The most frequently reported benefits were task reminders (92%), structured clinical guidance (87%), overview of allocated participants (81%), and retention of participant information (81%). Main challenges were lengthy questionnaires, difficulties charging tablets, and limited internet connectivity. Qualitative findings showed that ease of use increased with experience, supported by training and supervision. Participants described how algorithmic guidance and task reminders supported care delivery, while also identifying tensions between standardized workflows and flexibility in day-to-day care.

The ComBaCaL CHT application was highly usable and valued by CHWs. High perceived usability extended from general application functions to complex clinical workflows. CHT demonstrated suitability as a configurable framework for implementing such context-specific workflows for hypertension and diabetes care when accompanied by appropriate workflow design, training, and supervision.

Author summaryHigh blood pressure and diabetes require repeated follow-up and treatment decisions, which is difficult where healthcare professionals are scarce. Community health workers (CHWs) may help expand access to this care, but they need appropriate tools to manage complex clinical tasks. We evaluated a digital application designed to support CHWs in delivering hypertension and diabetes care in rural Lesotho. Overall, 103 CHWs used an application built with the Community Health Toolkit to support hypertension and diabetes care. The application helped manage participants and follow-up tasks and provided step-by-step guidance for screening, diagnosis, treatment, referral, and repeated care visits. All 103 CHWs completed a survey, and 22 participated in interviews or focus group discussions.

CHWs found the application easy to use and useful for their work. Frequently reported benefits included reminders, procedural guidance, better participant oversight, and retention of participant information over time. Ease of use improved with experience and was supported by training and supervision. Challenges included lengthy research questionnaires, difficulties charging tablets, limited internet connectivity, and standardized digital workflows that did not fit day-to-day circumstances.

Our findings show that a configurable open-source digital application can support CHWs in delivering complex, longitudinal hypertension and diabetes care in a remote rural setting.

data.title: Preprint: Scleral Allograft-Reinforced Cyclodialysis Combined with Phacoemulsification or Performed as a Standalone Procedure: 24-Month Outcomes from the Multicenter CREST Study
data.authors: Weinreb, R. N.; Provencher, L.; Huang, A. S.; Yadgarov, A.; Rouse, M.; Francis, B.; Ianchulev, T.; Chang, R.
data.author_corresponding_institution: New York Eye and Ear of Mount Sinai, New York, NY, USA
data.abstract:
IntroductionAcellular scleral allograft-reinforced cyclodialysis is a bio-interventional surgery (BIOS) to lower intraocular pressure (IOP). We report 2-year efficacy and safety outcomes when the procedure is performed in combination with phacoemulsification and as a standalone procedure in eyes with open-angle glaucoma.

MethodsAnalysis of the multicenter CREST real-world evidence study of eyes undergoing allograft-reinforced cyclodialysis with AlloFlo Uveo (Iantrek, Inc., White Plains, NY; NCT05506423). Eyes attending the Month-24 visit were analyzed: 176 eyes undergoing phaco-combined surgery (Cohort 1) and 32 standalone eyes (Cohort 2). Values recorded after secondary procedures censored. Cohort 1 only was stratified by low, moderate, or high baseline IOP ([≤] 15, 16-20, [≥] 21 mmHg).

ResultsA total of 176 eyes in Cohort 1 and 32 in Cohort 2 were analyzed. In Cohort 1, IOP decreased 3.1 mmHg at Month 24 from a baseline of 18.0 (-12.5%; p < 0.001), and medications decreased 0.5 from 1.5 (p < 0.001); medication-free eyes rose from 22.9% to 46.4% (p < 0.001). IOP changes in the low, moderate, and high baseline tiers were +0.9 (+7.8%), -3.0 (-16.3%), and -9.2 (-36.1%) mmHg; medication changes were -0.8, -0.6, and +0.1. In Cohort 2, IOP decreased 6.4 mmHg from 20.0 (-27.1%; p < 0.001), and medications decreased 1.2 from 2.8 (p = 0.004); medication-free eyes rose from 4.3% to 30.4% (p = 0.031). Secondary IOP-lowering procedures were performed in 5.1% of Cohort 1 eyes and 28.1% of Cohort 2. Kaplan-Meier freedom from reoperation was 98.9% and 84.4%. No eye developed clinically significant hypotony or choroidal effusion, and there were no allograft-related vision-threatening adverse events.

ConclusionAllograft-reinforced cyclodialysis effectively lowered IOP and medication use through 24 months.

Trial RegistrationClinicalTrials.gov NCT05506423.

Plain Language SummaryGlaucoma damages the optic nerve, usually because pressure inside the eye is too high. A newer operation opens a small channel to a natural drainage route inside the eye and holds it open with thin pieces of biocompatible donor tissue. It spares the surface of the eye, so other operations remain possible later. We asked how well the procedure works after two years. We studied 208 eyes at 17 centers that returned for their two-year visit: 176 done with cataract surgery and 32 done as a standalone procedure. We measured eye pressure and drop use and checked for long-term safety. With cataract surgery, pressure decreased from about 18 to 15 mmHg (millimeters of mercury, the standard measurement for eye pressure) and drop use by about half a drop; eyes starting at the highest pressures improved most, falling about 9 mmHg. Done alone, pressure decreased from about 20 to 14 mmHg and drop use by about one drop. The share of eyes needing no drops at all roughly doubled with cataract surgery, from about a quarter to about a half, and rose from almost none to about a third when done alone. No eye developed dangerously low pressure or fluid behind the retina. About one-in-four eyes treated alone needed a further pressure-lowering procedure within two years, against about one-in-twenty treated with cataract surgery. The procedure meaningfully lowered pressure and drop use over two years without the complications that ended earlier versions of this promising surgery.

Key Summary PointsO_ST_ABSWhy carry out this study?C_ST_ABSO_LIEyes needing cataract surgery with better pressure control, and eyes needing pressure control alone, are managed very differently, yet 2-year data on allograft-reinforced cyclodialysis in both settings have not been reported together.
C_LIO_LIWe asked: how much do pressure and medication burden fall by 24 months in each setting, how often further surgery is needed, and how safe is it?
C_LI

What was learned from the study?O_LIWhen performed at the same time as cataract surgery, pressure decreased 3.1 mmHg and medications by 0.5, and the reductions rose steeply with baseline pressure. The proportion of eyes on no glaucoma medication doubled, from 22.9% to 46.4%.
C_LIO_LIWhen performed as a standalone procedure, pressure decreased 6.4 mmHg and medications by 1.2, and medication-free eyes rose from 4.3% to 30.4%, reflecting promising outcomes in refractory eyes.
C_LIO_LINo eye developed clinical hypotony, choroidal effusion, or corneal decompensation, and endothelial cell loss was confined to the phacoemulsification-combined cohort. Freedom from reoperation at 24 months was 98.9% with cataract surgery and 84.4% standalone.
C_LI

data.title: Preprint: Vitamin D supplementation to prevent tuberculosis infection and disease: systematic review and individual participant data meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
data.authors: Jolliffe, D. A.; Middelkoop, K.; Ganmaa, D.; Irmuun, B.; Sluyter, J. D.; Sudfeld, C. R.; Fawzi, W. W.; Martineau, A. R.
data.abstract:
BackgroundSeveral randomised controlled trials of vitamin D supplementation for prevention of tuberculosis infection and disease have been conducted, but no individual participant data (IPD) meta-analysis has been conducted.

MethodsWe conducted a systematic review, one-stage and two-stage IPD meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD420251173446) of double-blind, placebo-controlled randomised trials of vitamin D supplementation for prevention of tuberculosis infection or disease. We searched MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Cochrane and ClinicalTrials.gov from inception to October 29, 2026. The co-primary outcomes were incident tuberculosis infection (evidenced by tuberculin skin test or Interferon Gamma Release Assay conversion) and incident tuberculosis disease. Mixed-effects models estimated adjusted odds ratios (aORs), accounting for trial and prespecified covariates. Prespecified subgroup analyses investigated effect modification by sex and age, body-mass index, vitamin D status, and BCG vaccination status.

FindingsFour trials contributed IPD for 14,619 participants. Vitamin D did not reduce risk of incident tuberculosis infection (9,557 participants; aOR 0.97, 95% CI 0.81-1.18; p=0.79) or incident tuberculosis disease (14,533 participants; aOR 0.78, 95% CI 0.56-1.10; p=0.15). There was no evidence of effect modification by participant characteristics investigated in sub-group analyses, including in participants with 25-hydroxyvitamin D <25 nmol/L (infection: aOR 0.95, 95% CI 0.67-1.34; disease: 1.01, 0.45-2.30). Serious adverse events and mortality were unaffected.

InterpretationVitamin D supplementation did not reduce the risk of incident tuberculosis infection or disease in the populations studied, either overall or within sub-groups. The 95% confidence interval of the effect estimate for prevention of tuberculosis disease remains compatible with a potentially important benefit, and further trials for this indication may be warranted.
