data.title: Preprint: A five-day Mindfulness Based Intervention to reduce burnout and psychological distress in UK Medical Students
data.authors: Cromie, A.; Kaur, M.; Powell, N.; Brown, M.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Swansea University College of Medicine: Swansea University Medical School
data.abstract:
BackgroundMedical professionals face significant work overload, with excessive job demands often strongly associated with attrition and burnout. Consequences of burnout include reduced job satisfaction, absenteeism, reduced patient care, lower patient satisfaction and increased healthcare costs. UK Medical students are also at high risk of burnout. Mindfulness-based interventions are effective individual-level treatments; however, more research is required to investigate the efficacy for healthcare professionals and students.

MethodFour cohorts of second-year medical students at Cardiff University participated in a five-day, in-person mindfulness-based intervention. Pre (T1) and post (T2) intervention and follow-up (T3) survey data were collected online.

ResultsAll outcome measures saw a statistically significant improvement (N=69) post intervention, current energy, calmness, focus and stress (all P=0.001); Psychological distress (Core-10, P=0.001), Burnout (OLBI, P=0.023), and Wellbeing (WHO5, P=0.37) with small, large and small effect sizes respectively; maintained at follow-up. Satisfaction ratings were consistently high, and completion rate was 100%.

DiscussionMedical schools should consider implementing mindfulness-based interventions into medical curricula, as a feasible and acceptable student selected preventative tool to address burnout and incorporate student perspectives on delivery; to prevent mental ill health in medical professionals.

data.title: Preprint: Cumulative Multidomain Vulnerability and Early Mortality After Heart Transplantation: Development and Temporal Evaluation of the RIGHT-HTx Framework
data.authors: Balakrishnan, K. R.; Kemundel Genny, S. R.; Tungatru, M.; Davidson, N.; Sahayaraj, A.; Aravind, A.; Vanga, S.; Singh, N.; Nallamuthu, N.; Jegdish, A.; Krithika, K.; Ratnagiri, R. K.; Chandrasekaran, R.; RAMASWAMY, R. K.; Manikala, V.; Kumar, A.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Institute of Heart and Lung Transplant & Mechanical Circulatory Support, MGM Healthcare
data.abstract:
BACKGROUNDRisk models from high-income transplant programmes may not generalise to resource-constrained settings with different recipient acuity, donor characteristics and access to mechanical circulatory support. We developed RIGHT-HTx, a parsimonious framework integrating clinical and physiological vulnerabilities, and evaluated its prognostic performance in a subsequent same-centre cohort.

METHODSThis retrospective single-centre study included 436 consecutive adult heart transplant recipients (2012- 2026). Of 357 development recipients, 341 (95.5%) were score-evaluable. RIGHT-HTx incorporated three vulnerability domains: clinical acuity (INTERMACS 1-2), graded renal dysfunction (eGFR 30- 59 or <30 mL/min/1.73 m2) and haemodynamic-donor mismatch (TPG >12 mmHg combined with donor-to-recipient weight ratio <1.0). A seven-point Cox-derived score underwent internal validation using 1,000 bootstrap resamples and was applied unchanged to 79 subsequent recipients. Low-, intermediate- and high-risk categories represented zero, one and [≥]2 affected domains, respectively.

RESULTSAmong development recipients, 75/341 (22.0%) died within one year. Mortality increased across low-, intermediate- and high-risk categories (8.1%, 20.3% and 55.6%; log-rank P<0.001). Elevated TPG was not significantly associated with mortality individually, whereas its combination with donor undersizing was independently associated with mortality (adjusted HR 2.87, 95% CI 1.53-5.40; P=0.001). The full model improved discrimination beyond renal dysfunction alone (optimism-corrected {Delta}C-index 0.067), and the simplified score achieved an optimism-corrected C-index of 0.732.

The temporal cohort more often had [≥]1 affected domain (75.9% versus 60.4%; P=0.010). Discrimination was comparable (C-index 0.738, 95% CI 0.643-0.833), although observed Kaplan- Meier one-year mortality exceeded original predictions (35.4% versus 25.4%; calibration slope 0.929). In pooled analyses (n=420), mortality increased from 8.4% (13/154) with no affected domain to 57.3% (47/82) with two or more.

CONCLUSIONSRIGHT-HTx identifies cumulative multidomain vulnerability associated with early mortality after heart transplantation. Temporal discrimination was comparable, but absolute-risk calibration differed. The framework may support risk recognition and mitigation, not transplant eligibility or allocation; independent multicentre validation is required before clinical implementation.

data.title: Preprint: Greater Stress Response Network (SRN) Connectivity is Associated with Higher Worry in Men and Women Especially in Later Life
data.authors: Hudson, E.; Chae, C.; Tudorascu, D. L.; Butters, M. A.; Thurston, R. C.; Andreescu, C.; Karim, H. T.
data.abstract: Background: Late-life anxiety is common and disabling, with pathological worry as a core feature. The Stress Response Network (SRN: amygdala, bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, paraventricular nucleus), which modulates threat and stress reactivity, and its interaction with the Executive Control Network (ECN), anchored by the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, which supports emotional regulation via top-down cognitive control, may underlie individual differences in worry severity. We hypothesize higher SRN connectivity to be associated with greater worry severity and that this relationship may be moderated positively by older age, and female sex. Methods: We recruited older adults with varying worry. Resting-state fMRI was used to compute SRN connectivity and SRN-ECN connectivity. Regression models tested associations between connectivity and worry (PSWQ), anxiety (HARS), and rumination (RSQ), adjusting for age, sex, race, and education. Exploratory models examined age and sex moderation and associations with emotion regulation/suppression and cognitive function. Results: Among 131 participants who were [≥] 50 years old, with varying levels of worry severity, SRN connectivity was significantly associated with greater worry severity (B=23.51 (SE = 12.12), p<0.05), whereas SRN-ECN connectivity was not. SRN connectivity was lower with greater age (B=-0.003 (SE=0.001), p=0.04), yet older individuals reported greater worry than younger with comparable connectivity. Greater language domain cognitive function was associated with lower SRN connectivity but higher SRN-ECN connectivity, while greater overall cognitive function was associated with lower SRN-ECN connectivity. Women reported lower use of daily expressive suppression and higher performance across cognitive measures than men. Higher daily use of expressive suppression was not significantly associated with either connectivity measure. Discussion: SRN connectivity, rather than SRN-ECN connectivity, may serve as the primary neural correlate of worry, shaped by age and cognitive function.

data.title: Preprint: Midlife mobility assessment from the pocket: agreement and consistency between smartphone placement configurations
data.authors: Keren, D.; Hayek, R.; Gutman, I.; Nudelman, Y.; Springer, S.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Ariel University School of Health Sciences
data.abstract: Subtle declines in mobility may emerge during midlife and can be detected using smartphone-based motion measures. Instrumented assessment of balance and functional tasks commonly uses lower-back placement, which requires device fixation and may limit convenient real-world monitoring. This study compared mobility outcomes obtained from a practical front-pocket/thigh placement with those from a standardized lower-back placement during static balance, sit-to-stand (STS), and Timed Up and Go (TUG) tests. Forty-six adults aged 40-64 years completed static balance, 30-second STS, and TUG assessments during simultaneous smartphone recording at the lower back and pocket/thigh. Outcomes included two- and three-dimensional sway, STS repetition count, average repetition duration, lower limb power, and maximal vertical velocity, as well as TUG total duration and peak yaw angular velocity during both turns. Associations, intraclass correlation coefficients, and Bland-Altman analyses were used to characterize the relationship and agreement between the two placements. Balance outcomes showed strong correlations between placements (rs=0.83-0.93), with moderate-to-excellent consistency for most conditions, although pocket/thigh sway values were systematically higher. TUG total duration showed strong correlation and good absolute agreement (rs=0.895; ICC=0.881), and turning velocity showed good consistency during the first and the second turns. STS repetition count and average repetition duration demonstrated strong correlations between placements (r=0.996 and 0.985, respectively), with excellent absolute agreement for repetition count and excellent consistency for average repetition duration (ICC=0.993 and 0.982, respectively). In contrast, STS power and maximal vertical velocity showed weaker correlations and consistency (r=0.709 and rs=0.382; ICC=0.600 and 0.417, respectively). Pocket/thigh smartphone placement supports practical mobility assessment across balance, STS and TUG. Although some movement-derived measures showed placement-dependent differences in absolute values, relative performance patterns were generally preserved across placements. These findings support the development of pocket-based smartphone assessment for simplified and potentially unsupervised mobility monitoring in midlife, while placement-sensitive outcomes require further validation against external reference measures.

data.title: Preprint: Exercise reshapes cellular immunity toward anti-inflammation and diminishes CCR4 levels on LFA-1αhighCD4+ T cells in multiple sclerosis
data.authors: Proschinger, S.; Wences Chirino, T.; Hoenen, L.; Trebing, S.; Joisten, N.; Walzik, D.; Daube, N.; Ellrichmann-Wilms, G.; Ahmadi, S.; Schneider, M.; Zadora, P.; Frey, D. L.; Meuth, S. G.; Pawlitzki, M.; Masanneck, L.; Kuhle, J.; Ruck, T.; Rehmann, R.; Henneberg, A. L.; Opitz, C. A.; Zimmer, P.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Sports Medicine Research Group, Institute for Sport and Sport Science, TU Dortmund University, Dortmund, Germany
data.abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) represents a multifaceted neuroinflammatory disease for which regular exercise is now recommended by many healthcare institutions. Although preclinical studies indicate robust immunomodulatory effects of exercise, evidence from human studies is lacking. In this randomized controlled trial, persons with MS (pwMS) were assigned to three months of high-intensity interval training or a passive control condition, with outcomes assessed at baseline, after intervention, and a fourweek follow-up. Additionally, a healthy matched control group was included. Besides exercise-induced sustained increases in physical fitness, systemic inflammation was diminished and the Treg-to-TH17.1 ratio improved after exercise. Untargeted proteomic analysis of peripheral blood mononuclear cells covering >7000 proteins revealed an exercise-induced decrease in proteins implicated in inflammatory diseases (i.e., MTHFD2). This was supported by inferred transcription factor activity analysis, which indicated enhanced polarization of immune cells toward anti-inflammatory phenotypes at follow-up. Using flow cytometry, we identified an LFA-1highCD4+ T-cell subset that was associated with disease biomarkers and exhibited increased CCR4 expression compared to healthy matched subjects which was reduced after exercise. data.title: Preprint: Challenges and Health Disparities in Prostate Cancer: Healthcare Access as a Driver of Inequities in a Rural Hospital Network
data.authors: Aguilar-Mogas, A.; Hamilton, J. N.; Ju, A. W.; Lea, C. S.; Shelton, C. H.
data.abstract: Background: Prostate cancer is the most common male cancer, and second most common cause of cancer mortality in the US. Disparities abound in this disease for reasons that need further study, including social and ethnic barriers, geographic barriers, and biological differences. North Carolina is the second largest state by rural population measures (3.5 million), which provides ample geography to study these disparities. Materials and Methods: A dataset containing all patients with a medical record documenting a diagnosis of and/or treatment for de novo prostate cancer within the mostly rural ECU Health 9-hospital system was characterized over a 20-year period for structural inequities, access barriers, and biological differences. Results: Stages and outcomes of prostate cancer changed temporally, reflecting changes in screening, treatment, and inclusion of prognostic factors such as prostate-specific antigen, Gleason score, and other factors. Late stage (4) prostate cancer disproportionately affected our system as a whole and smaller community hospitals, with higher death rates seen in community, mostly rural programs that lack access to all required components of care. Conclusion: Stages of prostate cancer changed considerably over the study period, reflecting changes in screening recommendations, and staging criteria. Late stage (4) disease increased over the analytic period, was higher than NCDB references by period, and disproportionately affected community programs where resources were sparse, correlating with worse outcomes.

data.title: Preprint: Music-Synchronized Gamma Light Stimulation Strengthens Theta-Gamma Coupling in Older Adults with Cognitive Impairment: Results from a Randomized Feasibility Trial
data.authors: Kubit, B. M.; Asthagiri, A.; Lopez, K. L.; Wang, J.; Parrish, C.; Trebour, B.; Zhao, Z.; Yesil, D.; Toivonen, A.; Jacobowitz, A.; Quigley, B.; Wu, X.; Kim, J. C.; Large, E. W.; Loui, P.
data.abstract: Noninvasive clinical innovations for restoring gamma activity via sound and light stimulation have the potential to improve memory and cognitive abilities in Alzheimer's disease. We assessed whether pairing music with theta- and gamma-band light changes memory-supporting neural dynamics, and whether those changes track cognition. In an ongoing randomized feasibility trial, 38 older adults with cognitive impairment completed eight weeks of an audiovisual intervention. The treatment group (n = 19) listened to self-selected music while viewing light stimulation that consisted of a 39-Hz gamma-band signal modulated by delta- and theta-band musical rhythms. The control group (n = 19) listened to podcasts while viewing synchronized lights without the gamma frequency (delta-band only). Before and after the 8-week intervention, participants completed a face-name association task and the Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale-Cognitive (ADAS-Cog). Individuals in the treatment group showed significant improvements on a face-name association task and the ADAS-Cog. Cluster-based permutation testing showed a larger increase in phase-amplitude coupling between acoustic theta phase and frontal EEG gamma amplitude in the treatment group compared to the control group. Across participants, increases in stimulus-driven theta to EEG-gamma phase-amplitude coupling were associated with improvements in memory. These preliminary results suggest that theta-gamma stimulation delivered through music and lights strengthens cross-frequency coupling, and may correspondingly strengthen associative memory.

data.title: Preprint: GLP-1 Receptor Agonists Added to Statin Therapy and Cardiovascular Outcomes in ASCVD A Propensity Score-Matched Cohort Study
data.authors: Tah, S.; Cheshire, M.
data.author_corresponding_institution: West Virginia University School of Medicine
data.abstract: Objective: To evaluate whether GLP-1 RA use added to statins is associated with lower all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction (MI), and ischemic stroke versus statin monotherapy in ASCVD patients with body mass index (BMI) 30 kg/m2. Approach and Results:Using the TriNetX Research Network (108 U.S. healthcare organizations), we identified ASCVD patients with BMI 30 kg/m2 on statins initiating a GLP-1 RA (n=166,278) versus statin-only controls (n=920,176). Propensity score matching on 34 covariates yielded 119,911 matched pairs followed 3 years. Prespecified analyses included a BMI 35 subgroup (62,385 pairs), four washout sensitivity analyses (30-120 days), and a familial hypercholesterolemia exclusion analysis (161,312 matched pairs). Results. GLP-1 RA use was associated with significantly lower all-cause mortality (4.0% vs. 7.5%; HR 0.479; 95% CI: 0.463-0.496; p<0.001), MI (HR 0.762; 95% CI: 0.737-0.788; p<0.001), and ischemic stroke (HR 0.671; 95% CI: 0.588-0.766; p<0.001). Benefits were consistent across the BMI 35 subgroup and all washout analyses. GLP-1 RA users were more likely to achieve LDL <55 mg/dL by risk analysis (17.1% vs. 15.3%; RR 1.118; p<0.001); the Kaplan-Meier analysis was non-significant (HR 1.007; p=0.538). Mortality benefit was preserved in the FH exclusion analysis. Conclusion: ASCVD patients with obesity on statins, GLP-1 RA use was associated with substantially lower mortality, MI, and stroke, suggesting GLP-1 RAs may serve as cardioprotective adjuncts to statin therapy in this population.

data.title: Preprint: A multi-scale cell-type resolved map of trans-regulatory architecture in the aging human brain
data.authors: Cao, X.; Wang, Y.; Sun, H.; Feng, R.; Zhang, H.; Li, Y.; Lee, H.; Karaahmet, B.; Li, B.; Gersbach, C.; Crawford, G. E.; Taga, M.; Beeri, M. S.; Buchman, A. S.; Klein, H.-U.; De Jager, P.; Bennett, D. A.; The Alzheimer's Disease Functional Genomics Consortium,  ; Wang, G.; Dey, K. K.
data.abstract: Mapping genetic effects on distal genes and regulatory programs is essential for understanding how genetic variation influences complex diseases; yet trans-QTL discovery remains limited by weak effect sizes, extensive multiple testing and poor reproducibility. Here, we introduce TransMap, a generalizable computational framework that combines multi-scale trans-QTL mapping with multi-phenotype genetic colocalization to improve the discovery and interpretation of distal regulatory variants. Beyond individual trans-eGenes, TransMap constructs local co-regulatory program phenotypes that account for background expression variation to improve the detection of weak, coordinated distal genetic effects. Across a broad range of simulation settings, TransMap achieved 9.2-36.7% higher trans-QTL discovery power than existing methods while maintaining well-controlled type I error rates. We applied TransMap to bulk and single-nucleus transcriptomic profiles from the aging human brain in the ADSP Functional Genomics Consortium (FunGen-AD), further integrating proteomic, glycoproteomic and metabolomic biomarker measurements (average N=476 donors). Genome-wide fine-mapping of TransMap single-gene and program-level QTL yielded variant annotations with 2.75-2.88x heritability enrichment across 57 complex diseases and traits (average N=307K), with complementary heritability information captured across regulatory scales. Multi-phenotype colocalization identified 49,532 trans-regulatory events supported by shared genetic signals with cis-eQTL or biomarker-QTL, including 1,825 candidate cis-trans-biomarker regulatory configurations. TransMap further revealed an asymmetric cross-cell-type regulatory architecture in which neuronal cis-regulatory signals preferentially associate with coordinated glial trans-regulatory responses, supported by co-culture experiments and spatial transcriptomics. Alzheimer's disease (AD) GWAS-prioritized colocalization identified trans-regulatory associations in 115 AD-associated loci, including a KNOP1 cis-eQTL associated in trans with a microglial regulatory program containing MS4A4E, with additional support from statistical mediation analysis. TransMap provides a multi-scale, cell-type-resolved atlas of trans-regulatory variation and a generalizable framework for elucidating the regulatory architecture of complex diseases.

data.title: Preprint: Computational Modeling of the Acoustic Radiation Force and Viscoelastic Displacement for Transcranial Focused Ultrasound Neuromodulation
data.authors: Plovie, T.; Tanghe, E.; Tarnaud, T.
data.abstract: Objective: In transcranial ultrasound neuromodulation (TUS), simulations of the harmonic pressure are often used for treatment planning. However, other mechanisms of energy transfer, such as acoustic radiation force (ARF) and the resulting tissue displacement, are reported less frequently. Furthermore, there is limited guidance on how these mechanisms should be simulated. This study evaluates the numerical convergence and accuracy of different ARF formulations and investigates the simulation of ultrasound-induced tissue displacement in the context of TUS. Approach: Two simulations steps are used in k-Wave to first simulate the first order acoustic pressure and velocity fields. Subsequently, these fields are used to calculate the ARF using the momentum-flux density tensor, Reynolds stress force, and attenuation force formulations. The ARF is then applied as input for a second viscoelastic simulation to estimate the tissue displacement induced by the ultrasound field. Numerical accuracy and convergence are quantified as functions of the various numerical choices and hyperparameters in the solvers. Main results: Among the investigated formulations, the attenuation-force approach proved to be the most robust and the least susceptible to numerical errors across variable medium types and transducer geometries. Within the parameter space relevant to TUS, it is a valid approximation of the momentum flux density tensor formulation. Similar tissue displacement distributions are found across the different ARF formulations. However, the accuracy of the displacement simulation decreases with increasing pulse duration. Finally, recommendations are formulated on the ARF calculation method and on the numerical hyperparameters for ARF and displacement simulations. Significance: This study offers guidelines for calculating the ARF and simulating tissue displacement. The proposed framework enables a more comprehensive characterization of ultrasound-mediated energy transfer in TUS.

data.title: Preprint: Investigating the potential effect of topiramate on anorexia nervosa and binge eating behaviour using drug-target Mendelian randomization
data.authors: Nguyen, K.-M.; Chang, E. Y.-H.; Kim, B.; Ebert, P.; Chiang, J.-C.; Hwang, L.-D.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Institute for Molecular Bioscience, The University of Queensland
data.abstract: Topiramate is an antiseizure medication used to treat epilepsy and migraine and is commonly prescribed for appetite suppression and weight loss. However, whether its pharmacological actions influence eating disorder risk remains unclear. We applied drug-target Mendelian randomization (MR) to investigate potential causal effects of topiramate on the risk of anorexia nervosa (AN; 24,223 cases and 1,243,971 controls) and binge-eating behaviour (BE; 39,279 cases and 1,227,436 controls) and, exploratorily, eight other psychiatric disorders: attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, anxiety disorders, alcohol use disorder, bipolar disorder, major depressive disorder, panic disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder, and schizophrenia. We used summary-data-based Mendelian randomization (SMR) to investigate genetically predicted pharmacological actions of topiramate using brain- and blood-derived cis-expression quantitative trait loci for genes encoding its molecular targets. Five genetic instruments consistent with topiramate's antiepileptic action were validated: CA4 and CACNB3 expression in the brain and CA4, GRIK1, and GRIK3 expression in the blood. Robustness of the findings was assessed using SMR-multi, HEIDI, and colocalization analyses. After multiple-testing correction, genetically predicted inhibition of CA4 expression in blood was associated with decreased BE risk (OR = 0.867, 95% CI = 0.792 - 0.950, p = 0.002) and remained significant in SMR-multi (p = 0.0049). Colocalization provided moderate support for a shared causal variant underlying CA4 expression and BE (PPH4 = 0.58). No robust evidence was identified for AN or the eight exploratory psychiatric outcomes. Overall, our findings warrant further clinical and functional investigations into mechanisms underlying topiramate-associated appetite suppression and weight loss and their relevance to eating-disorder risk.

data.title: Preprint: Molecular typing and characterisation of antimicrobial resistance determinants of Neisseria gonorrhoeae among symptomatic individuals in the Eastern Cape, South Africa
data.authors: Mdingi, M. M.; Kullin, B.; Jung, H.; Mitchev, N.; Peters, R. P.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Medical Microbiology, University of Pretoria, Pretoria, South Africa
data.abstract: ABSTRACT Background. Antimicrobial resistance in Neisseria gonorrhoeae threatens gonorrhoea treatment, while surveillance is constrained by limited culture capacity. We evaluated multi-antigen sequence typing (NG-MAST) and targeted real-time PCR for molecular epidemiology and detection of antimicrobial resistance-associated determinants directly from clinical specimens. Methods. We analysed 235 N. gonorrhoeae-positive stored DNA extracts from symptomatic individuals in South Africa. NG-MAST sequence types were obtained directly or from whole-genome sequences (WGS) of paired cultured isolates. Real-time PCR targeted quinolone resistance-associated mutations (RAMs) in parC and gyrA and macrolide RAMs in the 23S rRNA gene. Results were compared with WGS and with phenotypic susceptibility results from paired isolates. Results. NG-MAST sequence types were obtained for 200/235 (85.1%) specimens and were diverse, with ST21253 predominating (n=26). At least one gyrA or parC mutation was detected by real-time PCR in 110/193 (57.0%) specimens. Compared with WGS, positive agreement was 81.2% for parC and 97.0% for gyrA, and negative agreement 100% and 95.8%, respectively. Among 65 ciprofloxacin-resistant isolates, RAMs were detected in 60 (92.3%) by real-time PCR and 61 (93.8%) by WGS; four had no RAM detected by either method. The 23S rRNA C2611T mutation was detected by both methods in one isolate (azithromycin MIC, 8 mg/L); no A2059G mutations were detected. Conclusions. Gonococcal sequence types were diverse, quinolone RAMs were common, and the assessed macrolide RAMs were rare. Real-time PCR applied directly to specimen DNA agreed well with WGS, but the targeted markers did not fully predict ciprofloxacin susceptibility, supporting complementary molecular and phenotypic approaches. Key words: Neisseria gonorrhoeae, NG-MAST, Real-time PCR, WGS; quinolone resistance; ciprofloxacin resistance, macrolide resistance

data.title: Preprint: An early activated CD38highCD209highCD36low monocyte phenotype is associated with progression to severe dengue
data.authors: Dissanayake, M.; De Silva, M.; Arulnathan, J.; Bary, F.; Hapuarachchi, T.; Perera, A.; Chathurangika, P. H.; Ranatunga, C.; Idampitiya, D.; Wijewickrama, A.; Perera, M. H. M. T. S. H. M. T. S.; Narangoda, E.; Jeewandara, C.; Ogg, G.; Malavige, G. N.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Institute of Allergology and Immunology, University of Sri Jayewardenepura
data.abstract: Background: Although monocytes are among the principal target cells of dengue virus (DENV) infection we sought to investigate monocyte phenotypic markers associated with disease severity and evaluate their potential as prognostic biomarkers and therapeutic targets. Methods: Differences in monocyte subpopulations and phenotypic markers were assessed by flow cytometry in patients with dengue fever (DF=33) and dengue haemorrhagic fever (DHF=21) and compared to health controls (HCs=20). Further in vitro experiments were done by co-culturing peripheral blood mononucleocytes (PBMCs) of healthy individuals (n=8) with DENV2, DENV3, NS1 antigen of both serotypes and LPS. The changes in expression of CD36 and CD38 in vitro in monocytes were assessed. Results: A significant expansion of intermediate monocytes and a contraction of the classical monocytes was seen in patients with DHF compared to DF and HCs, with no significant differences within the non-classical monocytes. Patients who progressed to develop DHF, exhibited an activated monocyte phenotype characterized by, expansion of CD38high, CD209high, CD86high, HLA-DRhigh, CD36low, intermediate monocyte subset. The highest expression of CD38 and CD86 was seen in non-classical monocytes, and CD209 and HLA-DR in intermediate monocytes. Most significant downregulation of CD36 was observed in non-classical monocytes. CD38 expression on monocytes (especially classical monocytes) positively and significantly correlated with liver transaminases and serum ferritin levels. Co-culture of PBMCs with DENV3 led to significant downregulation of CD36 (p=0.023). Conclusions: These results suggest that early alterations in monocyte activation, antigen presentation, viral entry, and lipid sensing pathways contribute to dengue immunopathogenesis.

data.title: Preprint: Single-cell profiling of human plaques reveals cellular and molecular signatures of symptomatic atherosclerosis
data.authors: Ray, A.; Zivkovic, L.; Zhang, L.; Batool, R.; Marei, A.; Dichgans, M.; Tsilimparis, N.; Georgakis, M. K.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Institute for Stroke and Dementia Research (ISD), LMU University Hospital, LMU Medizin, LMU Munich, Munich, Germany
data.abstract: Atherosclerotic plaque vulnerability drives ischemic cardiovascular events, yet the cellular and molecular signatures distinguishing symptomatic from asymptomatic human plaques remain poorly defined. Here, we compared 53 symptomatic and asymptomatic human carotid plaques using single-nucleus (snRNA-seq; 17 samples, 19,100 nuclei; AtherOMICS biobank) and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq; 36 samples, 68,983 cells; four public datasets), analyzed independently and combined by meta-analysis. Across sequencing approaches, symptomatic plaques showed cell-state shifts toward later or terminal states in osteochondrogenic smooth muscle cells (SMCs) and CD4 T cells, as well as transcriptional changes toward inflammatory and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in endothelial cells (ECs), T cells, and fibroblasts. Nuclear profiling uncovered a depletion of fibroblasts in symptomatic plaques, marked by downregulation of RGS5. Integrating these transcriptomic signatures with genome-wide association data for coronary, cerebrovascular, and peripheral atherosclerotic disease, we found that genetic risk was enriched primarily in vascular wall cells (SMCs, fibroblasts, ECs), rather than immune cell types. The analyses further nominated higher TWIST1 expression in ECs (colocalized with risk across four atherosclerotic phenotypes), lower GUCY1A1 expression in fibroblasts and macrophages, and higher MRAS expression in T cells as candidate driver mechanisms linking genetic risk to symptomatic plaque transition. These findings provide novel insights into cellular and molecular phenotypes associated with plaque vulnerability and identify potential driver mechanisms of symptomatic plaque transformation that could inform therapeutic development.

data.title: Preprint: Insulin resistance reverses despite weight gain with pan-PPAR agonism, revealing its plasma molecular correlates in type 2 diabetes
data.authors: Cao, Z.; Li, J.; Zhang, N.; Chen, H.; Pan, D.; Chen, Q.; Mai, Y.; Yao, X.; Sun, S.; Liu, Y.; Hou, W.; Yu, Y.; An, Y.; Yuan, Z.; Tan, J.; Chen, X.; Zheng, Y.; Wu, H.; Wang, J.; Chang, J.; Ding, C.; Huang, Q.; Wang, Q.; Jiang, B.; Wang, S.; Peng, Q.; Li, W.; Pan, D.; Wang, Y.; Xu, T.; Ji, L.; Jia, W.; Jin, L.; Ning, Z.; Vidal-Puig, A.; Lu, X.; Shi, L.; Zheng, Y.
data.author_corresponding_institution: State Key Laboratory of Genetics and Development of Complex Phenotypes, School of Life Sciences, Department of Pathology, Zhongshan Hospital, Fudan University,
data.abstract: Insulin resistance (IR) and body weight are closely linked in type 2 diabetes (T2D), so their molecular correlates are hard to separate in observational data. Pan-PPAR agonism offers a test, because it improves insulin sensitivity while body weight increases. In the ChiHOPE cohort of 835 T2D patients from two randomized phase 3 trials of chiglitazar, 53% of chiglitazar-treated patients with HOMA-IR-defined IR at baseline no longer met the IR threshold after treatment, compared with 29% with placebo and 32% with sitagliptin, while BMI rose. We integrated plasma metabolomics and proteomics into a molecular estimate of HOMA-IR. It outperformed routine clinical measures, disagreed with HOMA-IR classification in 27% of patients, and identified adverse lipid, liver and inflammatory profiles within each HOMA-IR class. With chiglitazar, the molecular estimate fell despite weight gain, with lower proteoglycan 4 and higher glutamine and glycine. Circulating markers of IR can therefore improve without weight loss.

data.title: Preprint: Accounting for Insulin-on-board in Large Language Model Advice about Pediatric Hyperglycemia
data.authors: Healey, E.; Lee, S.; Astley, C. M.; Mandl, K. D.
data.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can be used by patients and caregivers to answer medical questions and the characterization of safety concerns in LLM outputs for patient-facing applications is an active area of research. In this work, we study LLM responses to caregiver questions about hyperglycemia in pediatric type 1 diabetes. We measure the frequency of a potential safety failure: advice to dose insulin in the absence of a clear warning to account for insulin-on-board. We found occurrences of the potential safety failure across four LLMs tested through programmatic endpoints and two LLMs tested through chat interfaces. The rates of the potential safety failure varied when different context was given about the patient's meal and insulin history and treatment regimen. These results highlight a need for guardrails for patients with diabetes who use LLMs to manage their care.

data.title: Preprint: Persisting inequalities in past-year drug use by sexual identity: trends across England's 2007, 2014 and 2024 Adult Psychiatric Morbidity Surveys
data.authors: Wu, Y.; Das-Munshi, J.; Strang, J.; Roberts, E.; Khanolkar, A.; Becares, L.; McManus, S.
data.author_corresponding_institution: City St George's, University of London
data.abstract: Introduction Sexual minority people experience disproportionate discrimination and minority stress, contributing to poorer health and health-related behaviours, including drug use. Increasing drug potency and adulteration may heighten associated harms. UK evidence on sexual identity inequalities in drug use is dated, and whether inequalities have changed over time is unclear. Methods Adult Psychiatric Morbidity Surveys 2007 (N=7403), 2014 (N=7546) and 2024 (N=6912) provide repeated cross-sectional probability samples of the household population of England. Weighted prevalence of past-year drug use was analysed by sexual identity, sex and age. Logistic regression adjusted for age, sex and area deprivation. Trends focused on 16-64-year-olds. Results In 2024, past-year drug use among adults 16+ was reported by: 9.1% heterosexual, 18.3% gay/lesbian, 26.8% bisexual, 28.3% other identity adults. Among 16-64-year-olds, drug use in sexual minority adults (2007=22.9%, 2014=27.5%, 2024=24.9%) remained at least double that of heterosexual adults (2007=10.3%, 2014=9.9%, 2024=11.6%), with adjusted odds ratios of 2.4 (95% CI:1.7-3.2, 2007), 3.2 (2.2-4.8, 2014) and 2.2 (1.4-3.4, 2024). The gap between sexual minority and heterosexual women appeared to widen, although confidence intervals were wide. Conclusions Sexual identity inequalities in drug use persisted over 17 years in England. Prevention, treatment and policies should address these inequalities and their social determinants including discrimination and exclusion. Routine drug statistics should be reported by sexual identity. Health surveys should collect gender identity and be large enough to enable disaggregation of sexual and gender identities.

data.title: Preprint: Inferring viral variants and fitness advantages from longitudinal wastewater sequencing data
data.authors: Rimaite, A.; Beerenwinkel, N.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Biosystems Science and Engineering, ETH Zurich, Basel, Switzerland
data.abstract: During the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic, wastewater-based epidemiology emerged as an effective tool for monitoring infection dynamics. However, wastewater represents a pooled sample of incomplete viral genomic fragments originating from multiple individuals in the catchment area of a wastewater treatment plant, preventing the assembly of complete viral genomes. Existing computational pipelines are therefore limited in detecting new variants that are absent from clinical sequencing data. We developed FitNMF, an integrated viral dynamics and non-negative matrix factorization model that leverages the temporal structure of wastewater sequencing data and the underlying variant competition to jointly infer mutational signatures, relative abundances, and fitness advantages of circulating variants directly from wastewater next-generation sequencing data. Using simulated data as well as wastewater time-series data collected between 2021 and 2024 across six Swiss wastewater treatment plants, we demonstrate FitNMF's ability to identify and quantify emerging variants de novo, offering a powerful tool for real-time variant surveillance in settings with limited clinical sequencing.

data.title: Preprint: The impact of climate variability on dengue virus case incidence in Sindh, Pakistan: Post-2022 flooding.
data.authors: Tariq, A.; Allana, R.; Shah, S.; Kazi, M.; LaBeaud, D.
data.abstract: Dengue virus is spread primarily by the Aedes aegypti and Ae. albopictus mosquitoes is a self-limiting viral disease primarily present in the tropical and subtropical regions of the world. Temperature and rainfall impact vector development, virus replication, and habitat suitability for Ae. aegypti and Ae. albopictus larvae and pupae. Pakistan, located in Southeast Asia, is one country where DENV is endemic and impacts thousands of lives each year. In recent years, Pakistan has been hardly hit by climate change, with heavy rainfalls and flooding recurring each year, with simultaneous surges of dengue virus across the country. In this paper, we analyze the monthly dengue virus disease data from Sindh Pakistan, from 2020-2025 to understand the impacts of flooding, rainfall, and temperature fluctuations on dengue case incidence in the region. We use parametric generalized linear models and the generalized additive model. Our results indicate that monthly confirmed dengue cases exhibit a strong seasonality, with the great majority of cases concentrated in the post-monsoon months (September-November). A 1-month lag in rainfall was associated with a statistically significant increase in dengue incidence (IRR = 1.008, 95% CI: 1.003-1.012, p = 0.002), corresponding to a 0.8% increase in expected case counts per unit (mm) increase in rainfall one month prior. In contrast, neither lagged temperature term reached statistical significance.

data.title: Preprint: Repeated sleep-medication reporting patterns and cognitive change in HRS and SHARE
data.authors: Wang, S.; Lu, D.
data.author_corresponding_institution: 1 Department of Pharmacy, South China Hospital of Shenzhen University, Shenzhen, China
data.abstract: Background: Self-reported sleep-medication use has been inconsistently linked to cognitive decline, largely because sleep disturbances, affective symptoms, and treatment transitions co-evolve over time. Moreover, whether repeated sleep-medication reports across consecutive survey waves follow a monotonic dose-response gradient with subsequent cognitive aging remains unclear. data.title: Preprint: Co-production of an oral health intervention: Enabling Service Users with Severe Mental Illness to Learn about and Engage (SMILE) with Good Oral Health
data.authors: Mishu, M. P.; Kika, N.; Tkach, E.; Bird, J.; Cupac, J.; Daniel, S.; Horspool, M.; Johnston, G.; Killaspy, H.; Marshman, Z.; Marston, L.; Nafees, S.; Ndwandwe, S.; Pan, S.; Vadgama, E.; Watson, F.; Peckham, E.
data.abstract: Background: People with severe mental illness (SMI) experience poorer oral health than the general population. They are less likely to visit the dentist or brush their teeth and face unique barriers to accessing oral health support. There is a limited number of oral health interventions for people with SMI, and there is no conclusive evidence on their effectiveness. An integrated oral health intervention delivered by mental health professionals in a community mental healthcare setting could offer a scalable option to oral health support for people with SMI. In this paper we report on the process of co-producing such an intervention in England. Methods: The intervention development process was informed by Hawkins co-production framework. In this paper we report on stages 2 (co-production) and 3 (prototyping). Two online and two face-to-face co-production workshops took place (N=22) involving service users with SMI (n=6), mental health professionals (n=8) and dental health professionals (n=8). Two online patient and public involvement consultations, and a professional stakeholder meeting were held during the co-production process to provide feedback on the co-production process. The workshops informed the core components, format and content of the intervention. Results: The co-production process resulted in five intervention components: 1) Initiating a conversation about oral health, 2) providing advice to people with SMI on keeping their teeth and mouth healthy, 3) weekly tooth brushing text reminders, and 4) mental health professionals updating the care record to document the administration of this intervention. To support intervention delivery, we co-produced an intervention flowchart, an intervention leaflet for people with SMI, and a training manual for mental health professionals delivering the intervention. Conclusion: We co-produced an integrated oral health intervention to be delivered to service users with SMI in community mental health settings. The next stage of the research is a single-arm feasibility study to assess whether the intervention is acceptable to people with SMI and feasible to deliver within the NHS.

data.title: Preprint: Rapid antidepressant effects of psilocybin without increased SV2A binding: baseline binding predicts response
data.authors: Yngwe, H.; Plaven Sigray, P.; Andersson, M.; Bolin, M.; Beckman, M.; Ekman, C.-J.; Tiger, M.; Lundberg, J.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Centre for Psychiatry Research, Department of Clinical Neuroscience, Karolinska Institutet, and Stockholm Health Care Services, Region Stockholm
data.abstract: We report a pre-registered [11C]UCB-J PET sub-study of a recently published randomized trial in which a single psilocybin dose produced rapid and sustained antidepressant effects in major depressive disorder (MDD). Synaptic loss has been implicated in MDD, and psychedelics induce synaptic remodeling in preclinical models within 24 hours, raising the possibility that psilocybin's antidepressant effects involve increased synaptic density. We used the PET radioligand [11C]UCB-J targeting synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2A (SV2A) to test this in thirty-five participants with moderate-to-severe recurrent MDD randomized 1:1 to a single dose of 25 mg psilocybin or 100 mg niacin placebo, both with psychotherapeutic support. [11C]UCB-J PET was performed 2-7 days before and 15 (+/-7) days after dosing. Despite significant clinical improvement in the psilocybin group, we found no evidence of a group-level increase in SV2A binding (VT or BPND) relative to niacin in the hippocampus or frontal cortex. In secondary analyses, higher baseline VT was associated with greater subsequent clinical improvement in the psilocybin group; this survived FDR correction at Day 8 and Day 15 (two of three pre-registered timepoints). Change in VT was associated with greater subsequent clinical improvement in unadjusted analyses, but these associations were attenuated after adjustment for baseline VT and baseline MADRS and did not survive FDR correction. These findings indicate that substantial antidepressant improvement after psilocybin can occur without a detectable group-level increase in SV2A binding, while raising the possibility that baseline SV2A binding could help identify individuals more likely to respond.

data.title: Preprint: Investigating Climate-Driven Disruption of Malaria Transmission Following the 2022 Sindh, Pakistan Floods: An Interrupted Time Series Study
data.authors: Tariq, A.; Allana, R.; Shah, S.; Kazi, A. M.; LaBeaud, A. D.
data.abstract: Malaria remains a major global public health challenge in developing countries, with climate change intensifying its impact, particularly in vulnerable populations. Rising temperatures can expand the geographic range and local abundance of malaria vectors, Anopheles mosquitoes, which thrive in warm climates, with 25C representing the optimal temperature for malaria transmission. In Pakistan, malaria is primarily spread through P. falciparum and P. vivax. Pakistan is one of the seven countries in the Eastern Mediterranean Region that accounts for 98% of the total malaria burden in the region. Recently, after catastrophic flooding in Pakistan in 2022 and the subsequent increase in malaria incidence, it has become imperative to estimate the climate change-attributed increase in the risk of malaria. In this study, we analyze the time series malaria case incidence data from the province of Sindh, Pakistan, and the climate data to quantify climate-attributed malaria cases in Sindh, Pakistan. We fit a negative binomial generalized linear model (GLM) to monthly case counts with interrupted time series and seasonality terms. The majority of malaria-confirmed infections were Plasmodium Vivax (40-95%) between 2016-2024, followed by Plasmodium falciparum infections. The positivity rate for malaria remained <10% until June 2022, and increased massively after the July 2022 flooding. After accounting for this case momentum, the onset of the 2022 floods was associated with an immediate, independent increase in malaria cases of approximately threefold (IRR 2.985, 95% CI 1.878-4.751, p < 0.001). These findings suggest that post-flooding malaria surveillance and response in flood-affected settings should anticipate not only an acute environmentally driven surge in cases but also a subsequent period of elevated, self-sustaining transmission that may persist well beyond the resolution of the initiating environmental disruption, in this case the flooding.

Rising temperatures can expand the geographic range and local abundance of malaria vectors, Anopheles mosquitoes, which thrive in warm climates, with 25C representing the optimal temperature for malaria transmission. In Pakistan, malaria is primarily spread through P. falciparum and P. vivax. Pakistan is one of the seven countries in the Eastern Mediterranean Region that accounts for 98% of the total malaria burden in the region. Recently, after catastrophic flooding in Pakistan in 2022 and the subsequent increase in malaria incidence, it has become imperative to estimate the climate change-attributed increase in the risk of malaria. In this study, we analyze the time series malaria case incidence data from the province of Sindh, Pakistan, and the climate data to quantify climate-attributed malaria cases in Sindh, Pakistan. We fit a negative binomial generalized linear model (GLM) to monthly case counts with interrupted time series and seasonality terms. The majority of malaria-confirmed infections were Plasmodium Vivax (40-95%) between 2016-2024, followed by Plasmodium falciparum infections. The positivity rate for malaria remained <10% until June 2022, and increased massively after the July 2022 flooding. After accounting for this case momentum, the onset of the 2022 floods was associated with an immediate, independent increase in malaria cases of approximately threefold (IRR 2.985, 95% CI 1.878-4.751, p < 0.001). These findings suggest that post-flooding malaria surveillance and response in flood-affected settings should anticipate not only an acute environmentally driven surge in cases but also a subsequent period of elevated, self-sustaining transmission that may persist well beyond the resolution of the initiating environmental disruption, in this case the flooding.

data.title: Preprint: Acceptability and feasibility of measles vaccination, small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplementation, and their co-delivery among children aged 6-23 months in northern Nigeria: a qualitative study
data.authors: Ahmad, S. I.; Nabunje, J.; Adamu, S. K.; Sheriff, A. M.; Gwayo, A. G.; Goje, A.; Atanga, I.; Akinyi, A. M.; Ugonna, E. C.; Bahonon, S.; Chiroma, U.; Adam, H. M.; Becquet, R.; Muhammad, N. S.; Goni, B. W.; Cazes, C.; Phelan, K. P. Q.; Plazy, M.
data.author_corresponding_institution: University of Bordeaux, INSERM UMR 1219, IRD EMR 271, Bordeaux Population Health Centre,  Bordeaux, France
data.abstract: Background. Undernutrition and infectious diseases form a vicious cycle that endangers child survival in low-resource settings, including in Northern Nigeria. The NutriVax-Measles trial was designed to evaluate a strategy combining preventive small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplements (SQ-LNS) distributions with community mobilization and routine immunization services for children aged 6-23 months to improve measles vaccination uptake. To inform future programs co-delivering nutrition supplementation and immunization services at scale, we aimed to assess the feasibility and acceptability of measles vaccination, SQ-LNS distribution, and the NutriVax strategy. Methods. A qualitative study was conducted at the end of the trial using in-depth interviews (n=53) and focus group discussions (n=8) with key stakeholders: caregivers, health care workers, community health workers, and community representatives. Thematic analysis was guided by multiple conceptual frameworks. Results. The majority of the participants expressed satisfaction with measles vaccines in both arms, and with SQ-LNS in the NutriVax arm, as they perceived the benefits for their children health. In both arms, community awareness sessions and previous experience of outbreaks were key to motivating caregivers to bring their children to healthcare centres. Although distance to health facilities was identified as one of the main barriers to accessing care, SQ-LNS was perceived as an important source of motivation to bring their child to the clinic where they subsequently received vaccination. All stakeholder groups emphasized the importance of community leaders support and targeted male sensitization to address the prevailing sociocultural norms. Additionally, improved service organization to reduce waiting time was considered crucial to enhance caregivers acceptability of the intervention. Conclusion. Both measles vaccination and SQ-LNS provision were acceptable and feasible, supporting the NutriVax strategy within primary healthcare settings in fragile health systems. Successful implementation depends on sustained community sensitization, continued engagement of fathers and community leaders, and service delivery decentralized as close as possible to beneficiaries.

data.title: Preprint: Deep Learning-based Framework for Rapid, Precise and Fully Automated Localization of Cochlea Landmarks in 3D CT Images
data.authors: Wang, Y.; Kral, A.; Lenarz, T.; John, S.
data.abstract: Manual localization of anatomical landmarks within human cochlea structures in 3D computed tomography (CT) images is labor-intensive. However, despite progress in various studies on automatic localization methods, it remains challenging to jointly achieve rapid, precise, and fully automated landmark localization. Therefore, we propose a deep learning-based localization framework, called MEDICO-YOLO, which bridges speed and precision. It can automatically and simultaneously localize 6 human cochlea landmarks (apex, basal point, round window center of both left and right cochleae) in the full-resolution 3D CT images. The main contributions are: 1) MEDICO-YOLO learns from few manually annotated 3D CT images; 2) Within the framework, a 2D CNN-based network was developed to specifically localize cochlea landmarks in 3D single-scale medical CT images; 3) A novel loss function was designed; 4) The localization model achieved human expert-level precision while ensuring rapid inference. This study employed anonymized 3D pre-operative CT images (0.3 mm, covering the full head or temporal bone region). The evaluation involved comparing four models that were trained using 4 different training set sizes (n=4, 8, 12, 16). Each of them was evaluated on a distinct test set (n=16). The results show that the MEDICO-YOLO framework achieved strong localization performance by learning from few annotated 3D CT images. Trained on only 8 CT volumes, the model already attained a mean localization error of 1.30 mm (approximately 4 voxels). When trained on 16 CT volumes, the model achieved a mean error of 0.71 mm and a successful detection rate (SDR@3.0 mm) of 97.92%. Furthermore, on an Apple M1 laptop, the model achieved a real-time speed (32 ms) for inferencing each 2D slice (608 x 608) and an average latency of 25.43 s for inferencing the full 3D CT image (608 x 608 x 200, including post-processing). The complete methodology for the MEDICO-YOLO framework is presented in this article.

data.title: Preprint: The development and psychometric evaluation of the Post Activity Symptom Scale (PASS) for Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/ Chronic Fatigue Syndrome.
data.authors: Horton, M.; Tyson, S. F.; Fleming, R.
data.abstract: Purpose: To develop and psychometrically evaluate a new scale measuring post-exertional malaise in people with myalgic encephalomyelitis (ME)/ chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS). Methods: A draft scale was co-produced with patient and clinician advisory groups. After extensive pilot testing, adults with ME/CFS completed the Post Activity Symptom Scale online and repeated it two weeks later to assess test-retest reliability and sensitivity to change. Rasch analysis assessed each domain for unidimensionality, targeting, internal reliability, item fit and local dependency. Then Rasch-transformed interval data and parametric statistics were used to assess criterion-related and discriminant validity (by comparison with measures of physical health and ME/CFS severity), test-retest reliability and minimal detectable difference. Results: The item regarding delay in PEM onset was an under-discriminating misfit anomaly which was inconsistent with the remaining PASS items. When this was removed, the PASS was a unidimensional, psychometrically robust scale. Criterion-related validity (r=0.58, p<0.001) was moderate and highly significant, discriminant validity (p<0.001) and test-retest reliability (ICC = 0.81) were excellent. The minimal detectable difference was 1.93/100. Participants found the PASS easy to complete, comprehensive and relevant. Conclusion: The Post Activity Symptom Scale is a valid, reliable, sensitive measure of people of PEM in ME/CFS

data.title: Preprint: Methodological Adherence, Reporting Completeness, and Risk of Bias in AI-Assisted Systematic Reviews: A Matched Meta-Research Study
data.authors: Jay, M.; Esttaifo, M.; Samani, A.; Wilson, E.; Esttaifo, S.; Morgan, M.; Abi-Jaoude, J.; Reszetnik, G.; Chopra, M.; Alrashidi, A.; Monteiro, J. K.; Schemitsch, G.; Karthikeyan, V.; Obi, O.; Emdin, F.; Nguyen, D.-D.; Anni, N. S.; Sutradhar, R.; Dharma, C.; Yu, C.; Straus, S.; Lipscombe, L. L.; Eskander, A.
data.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to accelerate systematic reviews that inform clinical practice and policy. However, evidence on the methodological adherence, reporting completeness, and risk of bias of completed AI-assisted reviews is limited. Objective: To compare methodological adherence, reporting completeness, and risk of bias between published systematic reviews with reported AI assistance and matched reviews with no reported AI use, and to assess AI-use transparency. Methods: We conducted a matched-cohort meta-research study of English-language, peer-reviewed health systematic reviews. AI-assisted reviews published during 2023--2025 were matched 1:2 to reviews with no reported AI use using individualized MEDLINE searches targeting publication timing, clinical domain, review type, and meta-analysis status. When more than two eligible comparators were available, two were randomly selected. AI assistance was defined as reported use during searching, screening, data extraction, risk-of-bias assessment, evidence synthesis, or substantive drafting. Full texts and supplementary materials were examined to classify reported AI use. The primary outcome was a prespecified modified 13-item AMSTAR-2 methodological-adherence score (range 0 -- 13; noninferiority margin &-1 point). Secondary outcomes included PRISMA 2020 reporting completeness and ROBIS risk of bias; AI-use transparency was assessed descriptively. Adapted 13-item AMSTAR-2 confidence categories were summarized descriptively, while critical- and noncritical-domain adherence was examined in exploratory adjusted analyses. Multivariable regression models adjusted for journal impact tier, funding reporting, formal review-group affiliation, review-team size, and review-question type, using cluster-robust standard errors by matched set. Sensitivity analyses included matched-set fixed-effects models. The study was registered on the Open Science Framework (DOI: 10.17605/OSF.IO/Q5JRW). Results: The cohort included 231 systematic reviews: 77 AI-assisted and 154 with no reported AI use. Mean 13-item AMSTAR-2 scores were 7.58 and 9.63, respectively. In multivariable-adjusted analyses, AI-assisted reviews scored 1.64 points lower (95% CI &-2.37 to &- 0.91); noninferiority was not demonstrated. PRISMA adherence was estimated to be 4.7 percentage points lower among AI-assisted reviews in primary adjusted analyses (95% CI &-8.9 to &-0.6) and 6.4 points lower in matched-set fixed-effects analyses (95% CI &-10.7 to &-2.1). Among reviews with assessable ROBIS ratings, 75.0% of AI-assisted reviews and 65.6% of comparators were rated low risk (adjusted difference +17.8 percentage points; 95% CI 2.7 to 33.0). Among AI-assisted reviews, model version or date was reported in 42.9%, prompts or parameters in 55.8%, and data-governance or ethics considerations in 9.1%. Conclusions: Reviews reporting AI assistance had lower methodological-adherence scores and had less complete reporting, despite more favorable risk-of-bias ratings. These findings provide an early warning that AI-assisted systematic reviews may require stronger safeguards, human verification, and transparency to support trust.

data.title: Preprint: Diagnosis Journey and Future Outlook Among Young People Living with HIV in Bangladesh: protocol for a qualitative study
data.authors: Sweety, S. A.; Niaz, S. N.; Sakib, I. A.; Shafique, R. B.; Khalil, M. I.; Patwary, M. A. U.; Iqbal, S.; Shawkat, S. M.; Islam, M.; Bahar, T.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College and Hospital
data.abstract: Introduction Bangladesh is a country with low HIV prevalence, but case detection has more than doubled in 2020-24, reaching 1,891 cases in the most recently reported year, and the number of cases is growing in the 18-24 age group. There is little qualitative evidence that describes the journey from suspected exposure to diagnosis for young people in Bangladesh, and no comparative evidence of this journey between key-population and general-population youth. Objective To explore the pathway to HIV testing and diagnosis, what motivated testing, and the life outlook of people living with HIV in Bangladesh aged 18-30 years, and to compare these between key-population and general-population participants. Methods This qualitative exploratory study uses semi-structured in-depth interviews, guided by the theory of emerging adulthood and the HIV Stigma Framework. Purposive maximum-variation sampling (20-30 participants) will recruit people aged 18-30, diagnosed within that age range and currently on antiretroviral therapy, balanced between key and general populations. Participants will be recruited through Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College Hospital and Ashar Alo Society, Dhaka, and interviewed privately in Bangla. Recordings will be transcribed, translated into English, and analysed with the Framework Method in MAXQDA, with saturation judged within each group. Ethical concerns The study is approved by the Ethical Review Board, Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College Dhaka with written consent from Ashar Alo Society and PLHIV Network Bangladesh. All participants will be asked for written informed consent, identifiers will be removed and distressed participants will be referred for counselling and psychosocial support. Findings will be shared via a technical report, a policy brief for the National AIDS/STD Programme and partner organisations, conference presentations and peer-reviewed publication. Limitations The recruitment process via one gatekeeper organisation in Dhaka and the need for the participants to be on treatment may exclude young people not in care.

data.title: Preprint: On conducting diary-based social contact surveys to inform transmission models of close-contact infections: a systematic review and expert-informed questionnaire
data.authors: Loedy, N.; Lumia, G.; Di Domenico, L.; Suer, J.; Jit, M.; Melegaro, A.; Funk, S.; Backer, J. A.; Grijalva, C. G.; Paolotti, D.; Verbiest, J.; Ratmann, O.; Coletti, P.; Dan, S.; Colizza, V.; Beutels, P.; Willem, L.; Abrams, S.; Hens, N.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Hasselt University and University of Antwerp
data.abstract: Background: Diary-based social contact surveys are widely used to parameterise transmission models of close-contact infections. However, variation in study design, contact definitions, and questionnaire content limits comparability across studies. These challenges became particularly evident during the COVID-19 pandemic, when rapid and repeated data collection was urgently needed, often without harmonised instruments. To address these challenges, we aimed to develop an expert-informed questionnaire and update the recommendations on conducting diary-based social contact studies previously proposed by Hoang et al. (2019). Methods and findings: We conducted a systematic review of diary-based social contact surveys published between 31 January 2018 and 25 September 2025 using PubMed and the Web of Science Core Collection, extracting information on study design, survey methodology, contact definitions, and survey items from available questionnaires. Methodological quality and reporting were assessed using an adapted AXIS tool, with results summarised for each criterion. In total, we identified 129 studies across 62 countries, with most studies conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic (59.7% in 2021-2022). Retrospective reporting (86.0%) and non-probability sampling (77.5%) were largely adopted and became increasingly common during the pandemic, while non-paper-based data collection rose sharply from 2021 onwards. Across 36 retrievable questionnaires from general-population surveys, we identified 54 survey items. An online assessment involving 26 experts informed the classification of these items according to their perceived importance, resulting in an expert-informed questionnaire comprising 22 core items. Based on our findings, we updated previous recommendations on sampling, survey methods, contact definitions, behavioural change, essential contact information, and data governance. Conclusions: This study provides an expert-informed questionnaire and updated recommendations to support harmonised social contact data collection, improve comparability across studies, and strengthen preparedness for future public health emergencies.

data.title: Preprint: Stressful life events recorded in 39.7 million clinical notes: associations with mental disorders, comorbidity, and frailty
data.authors: Peltola, A. A.; Khan, E.; Kaijansinkko, J.; Alexander, N.; Tirkkonen, A.; von Bonsdorff, M. B.; Lin, J.; Jylhava, J.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Faculty of Medicine and Health Technology, Tampere University, Tampere, Finland
data.abstract: Abstract Background: Despite being harmful to both mental and physical health, stressful life events are not recorded in structured electronic health records. They appear sporadically in narrative clinical notes, where they are difficult to analyze at scale. Natural language processing (NLP) has made clinical notes more available for research, but applications to stressful life events remain limited, leaving their documentation patterns and prognostic value understudied. By applying NLP, we identified stressful life events from clinical notes and examined their associations with mental disorders, comorbidity, and frailty. Methods: We analyzed 39.7 million clinical notes, recorded between 2010 and 2023, from 202,988 patients in Central Finland Wellbeing Services County. NLP was applied to identify stressful life events in five categories: grief, divorce, financial distress, violence, and family problems. Associations with the risk of mental disorders (stress-related disorders, anxiety, and depression) were estimated using time-varying Cox proportional hazards models, and associations with physical health outcomes (comorbidity and frailty) using generalized linear mixed models. Results: Stressful life events were identified from clinical notes with high accuracy (F1 scores 0.81-0.95). Event prevalences ranged from 0.5% for family problems to 22.1% for grief. Most individual events were associated with mental disorders, comorbidity, and frailty. The number of different life events was associated with a higher risk of stress-related (hazard ratio [HR], 1.62; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.58-1.67), anxiety (HR, 2.08; 95% CI, 2.03-2.14), and depressive disorders (HR, 1.99; 95% CI, 1.94-2.03), and with higher comorbidity (rate ratio, 1.58; 95% CI, 1.56-1.59) and frailty (mean ratio, 1.57; 95% CI, 1.56-1.58). Conclusions: Stressful life events were accurately identified from clinical notes and were associated with a higher risk of mental disorders, comorbidity, and frailty. Even so, violence and financial distress, the two events with comparable national estimates, were documented substantially less often than those estimates, suggesting underrecording of stressful life events in clinical settings.

Conclusions: Stressful life events were accurately identified from clinical notes and were associated with a higher risk of mental disorders, comorbidity, and frailty. Even so, violence and financial distress, the two events with comparable national estimates, were documented substantially less often than those estimates, suggesting underrecording of stressful life events in clinical settings.

data.title: Preprint: Determinants of Digital Health Pre-Acceptance in Respiratory Care: A Quantitative Irish Study
data.authors: Byrne, T.; Murray, N.; Mc Donnell Naughton, M.; Rowan, N. J.
data.author_corresponding_institution: TUS Midlands: Technological University of the Shannon Midlands Midwest - Athlone Campus
data.abstract: Introduction: Digital health technology (DHT) is increasingly being integrated into healthcare delivery; however, limited research exists exploring the pre-acceptability of DHT among ageing respiratory patients. This study aimed to identify the factors influencing the pre-acceptability of digital health technology in individuals with chronic respiratory disease in Ireland. Methods: A quantitative study was conducted among respiratory service users attending two respiratory centres in the Midlands and West of Ireland. A convenience-based questionnaire was developed and distributed, which was informed by prior Phase 1 qualitative findings that adopted the Technology Acceptance Model and the Health Belief Model.Data were analysed using non-parametric statistical methods, including the Mann-Whitney U test, to explore differences between gender and geographical location (urban/rural). Results: Fifty-eight participants completed the study. Overall, participants demonstrated positive perceptions toward the use of DHT, particularly regarding support for self-management, hospital admission avoidance, increased symptom awareness, and enhanced engagement with healthcare professionals. Perceived usefulness emerged as a significant factor influencing acceptability. Concerns regarding privacy, data security, and digital literacy were less significant than anticipated. Statistical differences were identified between urban and rural participants in relation to perceived usefulness, technology design preferences, feedback functionality, and preference for reduction in face-to-face appointments. No significant differences were identified between male and female participants. Conclusions: This study demonstrates that ageing respiratory patients in Ireland are receptive to the integration of digital health technology provided that technologies are perceived as useful, user-friendly, and supportive rather than replacements for healthcare professionals. The findings highlight the importance of involving service users during the design phase of DHT and recognising geographical differences in perspectives toward technology adoption. These findings may inform future policy, service development, and digital health implementation strategies nationally and internationally

data.title: Preprint: Knowledge and attitudes toward infertility and reproductive health among nursing and midwifery students from selected universities in Accra, Ghana
data.authors: Donkor, E. S.; Osafo, E. K.; Oti-Boadi, E.; Twum-Dei, B.
data.abstract: Introduction        In sub-Saharan Africa, where high societal value is placed on childbearing, infertility prevalence is high and often leads to stigma and psychosocial distress. Nurses and midwives, as frontline reproductive health providers, need adequate preparation to support infertile couples, yet a literature gap exists regarding how well nursing and midwifery trainees are equipped with the knowledge and attitudes needed for this role. This study investigated the knowledge and attitudes regarding infertility among nursing and midwifery students, applying the Knowledge-Attitude-Practice (KAP) model. Materials and methods   A descriptive cross-sectional survey was conducted among a stratified sample of 263 final-year BSc nursing and midwifery students at four universities in Accra, Ghana. Data were collected via a structured questionnaire covering demographics, infertility knowledge, attitudes, and practice intentions; and were analysed using SPSS. Results Respondents demonstrated a high overall level of infertility knowledge (composite knowledge score: M = 18.25/23, SD = 3.17; attitudes toward infertility were largely favourable (composite attitude score: M = 3.812/5, SD = 0.654; female respondents scored significantly higher than males on both knowledge (U = 2800.5, p = .044) and attitude (U = 2777.0, p = .040). BSc Midwifery students demonstrated significantly higher knowledge than BSc Nursing students (U = 2868.0, p = .002). A statistically significant moderate positive correlation was found between knowledge and attitude scores (r = .400, p < .001), and knowledge score was the sole significant predictor of attitude in multiple regression (B = 0.080, p < .001, R{superscript 2} = .178). The large majority of respondents (86.3%) supported expanded infertility content in the curriculum. Conclusion     The significant association between knowledge and attitude supports the KAP framework and suggests that targeted curricular reinforcement of weak knowledge areas may further strengthen students attitudes. The findings will inform curriculum improvements and promote evidence-based practice in nursing and midwifery education.

data.title: Preprint: Negotiating the Social Self in Chronic Spinal Pain: A Qualitative Study
data.authors: Sonjon, Y.; Charriau, A.; Mouhoub, D.; Van der Henst, J.-B.; Chabanat, E.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Centre Hospitalier psychiatrique Saint Jean de Dieu, Federation de recherche, Fondation ARHM, F-69008, LYON, France
data.abstract: Purpose: This study examined how people living with chronic spinal pain experience, interpret and navigate social representations of their condition and the interactions these generate across clinical, occupational, and personal settings. Materials and Methods: Thirty semi-structured interviews were analysed using an approach informed by constructivist grounded theory, through initial, focused and theoretical coding. Results: Five categories emerged, capturing how social representations and relational dynamics threatened the social self and prompted deliberate strategies for restoring agency. Theoretical coding identified a central process (maintaining and rebuilding the social self), describing how participants navigated these threats across social contexts. Notably, approximately half the participants reproduced, without revision, representations of chronic pain typical of the general population, directing judgements of simulation or inadequate effort at others with the condition. These strategies primarily aimed to restore agency and maintain a viable social self, rather than to reduce pain. Conclusions: These findings describe one process through which social environments shape the experience of chronic spinal pain by influencing how the social self is continually negotiated. Recognising these processes may help rehabilitation professionals attend to the social dimensions of chronic pain.

data.title: Preprint: A Framework for Variant Filtering to Improve Diagnostic Outcomes in Genome Sequencing
data.authors: Birnbaum, R.; Lee, K.; Mazor, Y.; Unger, Y.; Yanovsky-Dagan, S.; Grundwag, I.; Chalk, M.; Shaul-Lotan, N.; Greenbaum, L.; Freireich, O.; Klopstock, T.; Dror, T.; Sebbagh, M.; Beeri, R.; Murik, O.; Raved, D.; Rock, R.; Pode-Shakked, B.; Shani, H.; Josefsberg, S.; Harel, T.; Mor, H.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Genetics, Hadassah Medical Center, Jerusalem, Israel.	Faculty of Medicine, Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Jerusalem, Israel. 	Geneyx Genomics, Is
data.abstract: Rare genetic disorders frequently remain undiagnosed despite the use of exome sequencing (ES) and genome sequencing (GS). This study aimed to enhance diagnostic yield by introducing a systematic framework: SMART filtering (Systematic, Multi-step, Automated, Rare variant prioritization Tool), designed to optimize GS analysis, with a particular emphasis on non-coding regions. We retrospectively analyzed 153 cases with previously negative ES and GS results. SMART filtering was applied as a pre-annotation filtering step, integrating conservation metrics, allele frequency thresholds, and splicing prediction scores. Then followed by phenotype-based prioritization and manual review. Application of this framework identified pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in 4.6% of cases, strong variants of uncertain significance (VUS) in 1.3%, and additional candidate variants in 5.2% of cases. Several deep-intronic variants were confirmed by RNA studies and segregation analyses. The framework enabled efficient prioritization of non-coding and regulatory variants that were overlooked by standard analyses. In conclusion, SMART filtering offers a reproducible and scalable strategy to improve diagnostic yield in GS, particularly in cases where conventional analysis methods fall short. Integrating such frameworks into clinical genomic pipelines can enhance variant interpretability and diagnostic performance, ultimately leading to better patient care outcomes.

data.title: Preprint: Pathogenic MYRF ICA Domain Variant is Aberrantly Trafficked in the RPE and Results in Isolated Nanophthalmos
data.authors: Rozumek, G. M.; Lim, R. S.; Presley, W.; Blevins, B.; Guan, B.; Han, J. Y. S.; Ullah, E.; Naik, A.; Hahn, T. E.; Young, R.; Moroi, S. E.; Hufnagel, R. B.; Miller, J. M. L.; Prasov, L.
data.abstract: Purpose: Myelin regulatory factor is a transcription factor essential for RPE development and serves as a critical "GO" signal for eye growth. Pathogenic variants in MYRF manifest in a spectrum of clinical phenotypes ranging from isolated nanophthalmos to severe syndromic disease, in a gene dosage dependent manner. In this study, we aimed to determine the pathogenicity and molecular mechanism of a novel variant in the MYRF ICA domain, c.2083C>T (p.R695C), that leads to isolated nanophthalmos and mild retinal pigment epithelial disruption. Methods: Whole genome sequencing was performed and identified a novel MYRF variant. Pathogenecity and in silico modeling were evaluated using the Ensembl VEP tool and PyMOL. Human primary RPE and/or ARPE-19 cells were transduced with FLAG-tagged variant and wildtype MYRF or double-tagged FLAG-MYRF-MYC proteins to evaluate transcriptional activity, localization, and protein trafficking. Results: In silico modeling supports variant pathogenicity and altered homotrimer conformation. Functional studies in human primary RPE (hRPE) and/or ARPE-19 cells confirmed that MYRF p.R695C is cleavage deficient, mislocalized to the apical surface of polarized RPE, and demonstrated reduced synergistic transcriptional activity with co-factor SOX10 in HEK293T cells. Protein trafficking studies demonstrated that wildtype MYRF is trafficked to the apical cell surface and plasma membrane and that endogenous MYRF requires ER to Golgi trafficking pathways for proper nuclear localization and cleavage dynamics. Conclusions: Together, these results confirm that p.R695C is pathogenic for nanophthalmos, implicate trafficking as a regulatory mechanism of MYRF in the hRPE, and support that RPE disruption as a feature of MYRF-associated nanophthalmos.
