data.title: Preprint: Diagnosing a cardiac cause for palpitations: Five-year service evaluation of a smartphone ambulatory ECG pathway for Emergency Department patients.
data.authors: Morran, C.; Srinivasan, P.; Andrew, R.; Pow, E. A.; Padovani, L.; Thackray, Y.; Murphy, R.; Zangana, G.; Krupej, S.; I'Anson, M.; Findlay, L.; Millar, J.; Watts, F.; Moni, M.; Reed, M. J.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Emergency Medicine Research Group Edinburgh (EMERGE), Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh, Edinburgh, UK; Acute Care Edinburgh, Usher Institute, University of Edinburg
data.abstract: Background: Capturing an electrocardiogram (ECG) during transient symptoms remains challenging in emergency department (ED) patients with palpitations. Following the IPED trial, a smartphone-based ambulatory ECG event recorder pathway was integrated into NHS care. We evaluated this service over five years, assessing diagnostic yield, management, one-year outcomes and predictors of cardiac arrhythmia. Methods: Single-centre service evaluation of consecutive patients referred with palpitations to a smartphone-based ambulatory ECG event recorder clinic between 24th July 2019 and 24th July 2024. Patients underwent event-triggered ECG monitoring using the single-lead Kardia Mobile (AliveCor, Inc.) or their own smartwatch with ECG capability. Clinical characteristics, rhythm recordings, investigations, one-year outcomes and management changes were recorded. Multivariable logistic regression identified independent predictors of one-year cardiac arrhythmia diagnosis. Results: 1750 patients attended the clinic, mean age 44.3 +/- 16.1 years, 58.2% female. 1176 patients (67.2%) underwent monitoring with a cardiac arrhythmia directly captured in 67 patients (5.7% of monitored), including atrial fibrillation (n=39), supraventricular tachycardia (13), atrial flutter (9), atrial tachycardia (5) and ventricular tachycardia (1). By one year, 84 (7.1%) who underwent monitoring received a cardiac diagnosis with 79.8% (67/84) established directly via clinic monitoring. Across the entire cohort (n=1750), 114 (6.5%) had a cardiac cause at one year, 1472 (84.2%) had non-cardiac aetiology and 1569 (89.1%) were discharged back to primary care. Medication changes were initiated in 106 patients (6.1%). Independent predictors of a one-year cardiac diagnosis were increasing age (aOR 1.04 per 1-year increase), prior atrial fibrillation/flutter (aOR 5.57) and a presenting symptom of irregular beating (aOR 2.65). Conclusion: Our service provides an effective model for evaluating ED patients with palpitations. Over five years the service reliably detected actionable cardiac arrhythmias while safely discharging nearly 90% of patients to primary care. Clinical characteristics may guide patient selection to maximise clinic efficiency.

data.title: Preprint: A robust coordinated molecular response following trauma promotes recovery and protects against chronic pain and neuropsychiatric symptoms
data.authors: Winfield, B.; McLean, S. A.; Branham, E. M.; Stanley, N.; House, S. L.; Beaudoin, F. L.; Stevens, J. S.; Neylan, T. C.; Clifford, G. D.; Germine, L. T.; Haran, J. P.; Storrow, A. B.; Lewandowski, C.; Musey, P. I.; Hendry, P. L.; Sheikh, S.; Kessler, R. C.; Ressler, K. J.; Linnstaedt, S. D.
data.author_corresponding_institution: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
data.abstract: The biological mechanisms governing recovery versus chronicity of adverse posttraumatic neuropsychiatric sequelae (APNS) remain poorly understood. Here, we characterized longitudinal molecular changes among trauma survivors across ten APNS domains, including pain, anxiety, and depression. Recovery across these diverse clinical outcomes was associated with a shared, temporally coordinated transcriptional signature, characterized by early innate immune activation, subsequent homeostatic and wound-healing processes, and later adaptive immune responses. In contrast, chronic APNS trajectories exhibited limited transcriptional remodeling. We derived and externally validated an RNA-based Recovery Score (RRS) capturing the shared molecular response underlying recovery. Higher RRS was associated with greater clinical recovery, elevated peritraumatic cortisol, and lower cumulative stress exposure. Drug-response profiling identified candidate compounds predicted to mimic recovery-associated transcriptional changes. Together, these findings support posttraumatic recovery as an active biological process and identify shared molecular pathways that may be harnessed to prevent multiple adverse posttraumatic outcomes.

data.title: Preprint: Effectiveness of AI-Supported Holistic Health Management Through PREVERY's Digital Health Promotion and Prevention Program: A Prospective Before-and-After Observational Study
data.authors: Ringleb, M.; Trampert, T.; Trampert, T.; Bloch, W.
data.abstract: Background: There is an increasing strain on our healthcare system due to rising numbers of diseases related to chronic stress. One approach to combat these stress-related complaints is health coaching. However, personal health coaching is expensive and time costly, while digital offers can complement the already existing health coaching strategies. Therefore, this study investigates the effects of an AI-supported, digital health and prevention program. Methods: 253 participants were included in the study, with 113 being analyzed eventually. General stress experience and self-efficacy were assessed at baseline (T1), after six weeks (T2), and three months after the interventional phase (T3) via a Numerical Analog Scale (NAS) with values ranging from 0 to 10, the Perceived Stress Scale (PSS), and the PsyCap Scale (CPC). Results: A significant time effect was observed for CPC and PSS. CPC increased significantly from T1 to T2 and T3 and remained stable between T2 and T3, while PSS decreased from T1 to T2 and increased again by T3. All pairwise comparisons were significant. There were also significant time effects for self-reported current health status, health literacy, health awareness, and self-efficacy, with values at T3 being higher than at T1 (for health awareness, this was already evident at T2; for self-efficacy, this was additionally evident between T2 and T3), while no time effect was found for motivation. Conclusion: PREVERY seems to be an effective prevention program to increase psychological capital together with self-reported current health status, health awareness, health literacy, and self-efficacy, while at the same time reducing perceived stress.

Therefore, this study investigates the effects of an AI-supported, digital health and prevention program. Methods: 253 participants were included in the study, with 113 being analyzed eventually. General stress experience and self-efficacy were assessed at baseline (T1), after six weeks (T2), and three months after the interventional phase (T3) via a Numerical Analog Scale (NAS) with values ranging from 0 to 10, the Perceived Stress Scale (PSS), and the PsyCap Scale (CPC). Results: A significant time effect was observed for CPC and PSS. CPC increased significantly from T1 to T2 and T3 and remained stable between T2 and T3, while PSS decreased from T1 to T2 and increased again by T3. All pairwise comparisons were significant. There were also significant time effects for self-reported current health status, health literacy, health awareness, and self-efficacy, with values at T3 being higher than at T1 (for health awareness, this was already evident at T2; for self-efficacy, this was additionally evident between T2 and T3), while no time effect was found for motivation. Conclusion: PREVERY seems to be an effective prevention program to increase psychological capital together with self-reported current health status, health awareness, health literacy, and self-efficacy, while at the same time reducing perceived stress.

data.title: Preprint: Neurotransmitter-specific polygenic scores dissect clinical heterogeneity in schizophrenia
data.authors: Ramon-Canellas, P.; Vazquez-Bourgon, J.; Crespo-Facorro, B.; Molto, D.; Escarti, M. J.; Gonzalez-Penas, J.; Arango, C.; Gonzalez-Pinto, A. M.; Fananas, L.; Arias, B.; Bobes, J.; Costas, J.; Martorell, L.; Vilella, E.; Santpere, G.; Muntane, G.
data.abstract: Schizophrenia (SCZ) is a highly heritable psychiatric disorder characterised by substantial clinical heterogeneity. While global polygenic scores (gPGS) capture genetic liability to SCZ, their ability to explain clinical variability remains limited. Pathway-stratified polygenic scores (sPGS) offer a biologically informed approach to patient stratification. In this study, common genetic variants were annotated across five neurotransmitter (NT) signalling pathways - acetylcholine (ACh), dopamine, gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), glutamate (Glu), and serotonin. sPGS adjusted for sex and ancestry principal components, were calculated in two independent cohorts with different available clinical data (N=3,044 and N=645). By clustering top-decile individuals across the five sPGS dimensions, we classified patients into five mutually exclusive patient profiles, which were then evaluated for their associations with Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) symptom dimensions, age at disease onset (AAO), and three-year clinical remission and treatment response. Although gPGS showed no significant association with clinical outcomes, some sPGS-derived profiles captured clinically relevant heterogeneity across cohorts. Patients assigned to the Ach profile exhibited higher overall symptom severity, particularly negative symptoms and general psychopathology. Patients within the Glu profile were characterised by more severe negative symptoms, earlier AAO, reduced three-year remission, and poorer treatment response. Similarly, the GABA risk profile was also associated with three-year remission rates. These findings suggest that NT pathway-specific polygenic profiling may capture clinically relevant variation overlooked by genome-wide approaches. By identifying genetic profiles associated with symptom severity, disease onset, and longitudinal outcomes, this framework could contribute to biologically informed patient stratification and inform future precision psychiatry approaches in SCZ.

data.title: Preprint: Mental Health-related School Provision and Hospital Contacts among Pupils enrolled in Alternative Provision
data.authors: Ni Chobhthaigh, S.; Greenway-Bailey, T.; Musanu, J.; Cox, C.; Neave, C.; Mawi, M.; Buhari, A.; Green, M.; Burgess, R. A.; Devakumar, D.; Jay, M. A.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Institute for Global Health, University College London, UK
data.abstract: Background. Pupils enrolled in Alternative Provision (AP) represent a highly vulnerable population, with heightened mental health need at risk of long-term educational disengagement. Examining AP enrolment in relation to mental health-related school support and hospital contacts may inform early intervention and prevention approaches to address unmet mental health need. Methods. We analysed population-level linked school and hospital administrative data for 1.7m pupils (born 2000-2002) who attended state schools in England. We examined differences by racial-ethnic group and gender in rates and timing of AP enrolment and recording patterns of mental health-related provision and hospital contacts among pupils with AP enrolment. Results. A majority (62.4%) of pupils with AP enrolment had recorded mental health need, highest among Mixed White-Black Caribbean pupils (74.0%). Among those in AP, 52.0% of girls with a mental health-related hospital contact had school provision, compared to 67.3% boys. For some racial-ethnic groups, schools appeared less likely to record need evident in hospital records; 17.5% boys and 36.2% girls from Mixed White-Asian backgrounds enrolled in AP had mental health-related hospital contact without school provision. Conclusion. Among pupils enrolled in AP, documented mental health need is high but unevenly recorded across systems, with inequalities by racial-ethnic group and gender.

data.title: Preprint: MB-CasFire™: A Plug-and-Play, Thermostable CRISPR Enzyme for Precise Nucleic Acid Detection
data.authors: Broughton, J. P.; Alpay, E.; Fantin, N. J.; Ansaloni, S.; Elsener, S.; Jung, J. K.; Zhang, Y.; Madrid, I. Z.; Shiigi, S. A.; Rajan, S.; Jain, I.; Wright, W. D.; Hendriks, C. G.; Tymoshenko, S.; Ratushna, V.; Lee, S.; Warner, M.; Hong, R.; Sui, X.; Panchal, S.; Garske, A. L.; Miao, X.; Chen, J. S.
data.abstract: CRISPR-based detection technologies have the potential to enable precise, rapid, and cost-effective diagnostic and biosurveillance solutions by pairing sensitive and specific nucleic acid detection with a simple workflow. Combining isothermal amplification and CRISPR detection in a single reaction as a "one-pot" detection method can meet these needs, but only if the CRISPR enzyme remains active at the temperatures and salt concentrations that isothermal amplification requires. Here we describe MB-CasFire, a CRISPR-Cas enzyme engineered from a naturally thermostable Cas12a for improved stability and performance, as a "plug-and-play" DETECTR(R) (DNA Endonuclease-Targeted CRISPR Trans Reporter) enzyme for sensitive and specific nucleic acid detection. MB-CasFire remains active at elevated temperatures in amplification buffers and supports one-pot detection with loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) and nicking enzyme amplification reaction (NEAR), eliminating transfers between amplification and readout, and increasing the signal-to-noise to enable precise nucleic acid detection. This method, called OnePot DETECTR, is also compatible with commercially available isothermal master mixes, including those from New England Biolabs, allowing assays to be assembled from standard reagents. Using MB-CasFire, we detected SARS-CoV-2 in nasal swab samples with a LAMP-based OnePot DETECTR assay and Neisseria gonorrhoeae in urine samples with a NEAR-based OnePot DETECTR assay. MB-CasFire also functioned in multiplex detection and single-nucleotide polymorphism discrimination assays for antibiotic resistance genotyping. These results support MB-CasFire as a versatile detection enzyme that simplifies assay architecture for CRISPR-based detection assays that amplify, recognize, and report the presence of nucleic acid targets in a single reaction without thermocycling.

data.title: Preprint: Provider-Level and Specialty Variation in ARNI and SGLT2i Use After Heart Failure Hospitalization
data.authors: Salahuddin, T.; Patten, A.; Chow, C.; Hess, P. L.; Allen, L. A.; Simons, C.; Essien, U. R.; Rodriguez, F.; Scherer, L.; Leonard, C.; Matlock, D. D.; Ho, P. M.; Helfrich, C. D.; Doll, J. A.
data.author_corresponding_institution: VA Eastern Colorado Health Care System
data.abstract: Background: Angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitors (ARNI) and sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) are incompletely utilized in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF). The degree to which use varies at the individual level and within specialties is unknown. We aimed to characterize provider-level and specialty-level variation in ARNI and SGLT2i prescribing after HF hospitalization. Methods: This retrospective cohort study included Veterans Affairs (VA) providers seeing patients within 6 months of HFrEF hospitalization 2017-2023. We used descriptive statistics and site-adjusted multilevel logistic regression to examine prescribing by medical specialty, provider type, and provider sex. Adjusted median odds ratios (mOR) and empirical (unadjusted) provider-level rate ratios (RRs) by percentile were used to describe provider-level variation. Clinical pharmacy visits were assessed as an independent factor and as an interaction with specialty. Results: Among 7,946 providers caring for 76,795 patients across 211,267 outpatient encounters, provider-level variation remained substantial after adjustment for patient characteristics and site-level clustering (mOR 1.45 for ARNI; 1.46 for SGLT2i). Within every specialty, providers ranged from near-zero to near-100% use. Relative to the median provider in the same specialty, RRs ranged from 0-0.31 (5th percentile), 0.37-0.71 (25th), 1.38-1.66 (75th), to 1.8-3.2 (95th). Cardiology visits carried the highest adjusted odds of ARNI (OR 2.30, 95% CI 2.18-2.44) and SGLT2i use (OR 1.99, 95% CI 1.88-2.11) and most new starts. Pharmacist visits were independently associated with greater use of ARNI (OR 1.14, 1.06-1.23) and SGLT2i (OR 1.15, 1.06-1.24), with no effect modification by specialty. In early 2023, 58.4% (ARNI) and 40.2% (SGLT2i) of post-hospitalization HF visits had untreated patients. Conclusions: Provider-level variation in ARNI and SGLT2i use after guideline incorporation was large within every specialty and independent of site effects. Though specific specialties have higher use, individual providers, not specialty alone, may be an important target for efforts to close gaps in therapy.

data.title: Preprint: Human immunodeficiency virus and tuberculosis coinfection prevalence and treatment outcomes in Cameroon: a systematic review and meta-analysis
data.authors: Cheuyem, F. Z. L.; Tchamani, R.; Touko, A. D.; Achangwa, C.; Mapouo, C. J. K.; Fouodjeu, G. C. M.; Nouko, A.; Modibo, S.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Public Health, Faculty of Medicine and Biomedical Sciences, The University of Yaounde 1, Yaounde, Cameroon
data.abstract: Background: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and tuberculosis (TB) form one of the deadliest syndemics, and sub-Saharan Africa bears over 80% of HIV-associated TB deaths. In Cameroon, evidence on HIV/TB coinfection remains unsynthesized across regions and populations, obscuring the national burden. Hence, we estimated the prevalence of HIV/TB coinfection and treatment outcomes in Cameroon. Methods: Following PRISMA 2020 (PROSPERO: CRD420261399169), we searched PubMed, Scopus, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, African Journals Online, and grey literature for English- and French-language studies conducted in Cameroon. Reports were independently screened, their data extracted, and their methodology appraised using Joanna Briggs Institute tools. Random-effects models pooled prevalence, treatment outcomes, and adjusted odds ratios. Heterogeneity was assessed with I2. Results: Seventy studies (1995-2023) were included, 87.1% at low risk of bias. Pooled HIV prevalence among TB patients was 29.2% (95% CI: 26.3-32.3; 67 studies; n=57,169; I2 = 97.8%), with no significant evidence of publication bias. Prevalence was higher from 2007 onwards (29.9%; 62 studies; n=55,358) than before (20.5%; 5 studies; n=1,811). It was highest in the North-West (41.9%; 7 studies; n=6,324) versus Littoral (25.0%; 15 studies; n=10,419) and West (23.8%; 6 studies; n=4,206); and in extrapulmonary TB (42.3%; 3 studies; n=371) versus mixed forms (37.7%; 21 studies; n=37,239) and pulmonary TB (23.9%; 37 studies; n=16,096) (all p<0.05). Among coinfected patients, pooled treatment success was 75.9% (95% CI: 70.4-80.8; 8 studies; n=4,230), mortality 21.1% (95% CI: 11.9-34.7; 10 studies; n=4,403), loss to follow-up 7.7% (95% CI: 4.3-13.3; 5 studies; n=3,103), and treatment failure 0.3% (95% CI: 0.1-1.5; 6 studies; n=3,520). Lack of antiretroviral therapy (ART) increased the odds of unfavorable outcomes (AOR = 1.90; 95% CI: 1.15-3.12; 2 studies). Conclusions: Approximately three in ten TB patients in Cameroon are coinfected with HIV, with marked regional and clinical variation. Treatment success remains below national targets. Strengthening TB-HIV service integration, routine HIV testing, and timely ART initiation and continuation is essential to reduce the HIV-associated TB morbidity and mortality in the country.

data.title: Preprint: Peripheral intravenous catheter fixation splint in pediatrics, FIX I/V: A proof-of-concept study protocol
data.authors: Dube, S.; El-Haouly, A. A.
data.abstract: Project Summary Introduction: Using a fixation splint to maintain a peripheral intravenous device (PIVD) is common practice in pediatrics. However, splints are made from small wooden, plastic, or metal boards, and wrapped with gauze and adhesive fabrics. Accidental removals of the PIVD, mechanical complications (infiltrations/extravasations, occlusions, etc.), and skin injuries related to the splint are frequently observed. They do not always keep the PIVD securely in place. In addition, painful procedures to reinstall the PIVD in the child can worsen the negative experience of hospitalization. Moreover, unplanned PIVDs and fixation splint reinstallation appears to increase nurse workload and, consequently, care costs. New PIVD fixation splints for the hand and arm, adapted for newborns, infants, and children, are available in Quebec: the FIX/IV splints. Field observations suggest these splints show promising safety and efficacy. A prospective interventional proof-of-concept study is being conducted. Objective: This article describes the protocol for a prospective interventional proof-of-concept study on the safety and acceptability of the new pediatric FIX/IV PIVD fixation splints. Method: This protocol describes the implementation process conducted in fall 2023 and winter 2024. We selected 30 children for the experimental group and 22 for the control group. We will conduct descriptive and comparative statistics between groups, as well as a questionnaire on the acceptability of these new splints among nurses and parents. Discussion and conclusion: This proof-of-concept protocol presents the expected safety criteria for these new splints, which will improve the rigour and scientific value of future clinical trial phases with a larger sample.

data.title: Preprint: Automated MRI-Based Segmentation of the Cranio-Cervical Venous System Using a Dedicated Deep Learning Pipeline
data.authors: Duigou, M.; Treguer, T.; Dissaux, B.; Ognard, J.; Seizeur, R.; Capel, C.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Neurosurgery, University Hospital of Brest, Brest, France; Anatomy Department, University of Western Brittany (UBO), Brest, France
data.abstract: PURPOSE To develop an automated magnetic resonance imaging based segmentation pipeline for the cranio-cervical venous system (CCVS), a complex anatomical network for which no dedicated segmentation tool is currently available. MATERIALS AND METHODS A retrospective single-center cohort of 194 contrast-enhanced cranio-cervical MRI examinations acquired between 2019 and 2024 was used. Manual reference segmentations were performed on 50 examinations using 3D Slicer. A nnU-Net v2-based segmentation model was trained through an iterative process combining automatic segmentation, manual correction, and retraining. Segmentation performance was assessed using the Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC). The complete processing pipeline was integrated into an open-source software application, VenousNetworkAnalyzer (VNA). RESULTS The final model achieved a mean DSC of 0.94 (95% CI, 0.93-0.95) in five-fold cross-validation on 106 examinations with manual reference segmentations. Iterative optimization progressively reduced manual processing time from approximately 10 hours of fully manual segmentation to less than 10 minutes of manual correction per patient. Application of the final model to the entire cohort enabled the generation of patient-specific three-dimensional reconstructions of the cranio-cervical venous system. The segmentation workflow was successfully integrated into the VNA software environment, allowing automated processing and visualization of MRI datasets. CONCLUSION This study demonstrates the feasibility of automated segmentation of the cranio-cervical venous system from contrast-enhanced MRI using a dedicated deep-learning pipeline. The resulting reduction in processing time and integration into an open-source software platform provide a foundation for future large-scale anatomical studies of cranio-cervical venous draina

data.title: Preprint: Randomized Trial Protocol: Head-to-Head Comparison of Two Ambient Artificial Intelligence Documentation Tools on Clinician Usability
data.authors: Chin, A. T.; Leung, K.; Vangala, S.; Woo, H.; Kingsley, T.; Sandhu, A.; Jalalian, L.; Cheng, E. M.; Mafi, J. N.; Lukac, P. J.
data.author_corresponding_institution: UCLA Health Information Technology, UCLA Health, University of California, Los Angeles
data.abstract: Abstract Background: Ambient AI documentation reduces documentation burden and electronic health record (EHR) time for ambulatory clinicians. Newer features also queue orders and offer some level of coding support for clinician review. This study compares two commercial products deployed at UCLA Health. Objective: To compare Nabla and Epic Systems, Inc. ambient AI solution among ambulatory clinicians at UCLA Health on usability, documentation burden, perceived note quality, adoption, EHR time and productivity, clinician-reported experience with order queueing and coding support, coding and billing patterns and integrity, work productivity, and patient-reported communication experience. Methods: Two-arm parallel-group randomized trial, 1:1, among 374 ambulatory clinicians at a single academic health system who hold an active license for a standalone ambient application (Nabla). Randomization is covariate-constrained where cohort size permits, balancing age, sex, half-day clinic sessions, specialty group, and baseline System Usability Scale (SUS) score. Intervention runs 11/9/2026 to 1/17/2027, with the first four weeks as lead-in. The primary outcome is SUS score at follow-up, compared between arms. Analysis is by intention-to-treat using mixed-effects models. Ethics and dissemination: Determined exempt by the UCLA Institutional Review Board (IRB-26-2147). Survey completion indicates consent. data.title: Preprint: Exploring Perspectives of Healthcare Staff on Achieving the Healthcare Quality Standards in District Hospitals in Rwanda: A qualitative Study
data.authors: Ntawukuriryayo, J. T.; Woolhead, G.
data.abstract: Background: The World Health Organization (WHO) has recommended that quality of care (QoC) should be timely delivered within safe conditions based on patient needs and preferences. However, low- and middle-income countries face challenges such as understaffing and inadequate infrastructure, resulting in poor QoC. In 2012, Rwanda leveraged the pre-existing performance-based financing (PBF) to introduce continuous quality improvement (QI) towards accreditation recognition of district hospitals (DH). Despite these efforts, no DHs accredited by 2022. Objective: To explore perspectives of healthcare professionals (HCP) on achieving the delivery of standard QoC in Rwandan DHs. Methods: Using an interpretative epistemology, this qualitative study conducted in-depth semi-structured interviews with 14 participants purposively sampled HCPs from Masaka (urban) and Remera-Rukoma (rural) DHs. Interview data were audio-recorded, manually transcribed, and analyzed with thematic content analysis. Results: The analysis revealed three main themes: perceptions about continuous QI towards accreditation recognition, barriers to achieving accreditation, and strategies to achieve the recognition. Participants from both hospitals expressed that the accreditation program required more efforts than the PBF approach. They also highlighted that the DHs were still at the awareness stage and had not clearly implemented the quality standards due to challenges such as low staff involvement and motivation, staff turnover and shortage, and limited budget for accreditation. Recommended strategies to achieve the recognition included staff motivation through increased incentives and salaries, cascaded accreditation rollout, and integrating accreditation program into pre-service curriculum. Conclusions: This qualitative study highlighted the challenges, such as limited budget and low staff motivation, impeding progress towards DH accreditation recognition. Cascaded accreditation rollout, enhanced staff incentives and salaries, and integration of accreditation program into pre-service curriculum were key strategies suggested for Rwanda Ministry of Health and DHs to achieve the required quality standards and recognition.

data.title: Preprint: Investigating Biological Aging Measures, Neurocognitive Performance, and Depressive Symptoms: Moderating Effects of HIV and Childhood Maltreatment
data.authors: Maloka, K. M. S.; Spies, G.; du Plessis, S.; Hemmings, S. M. J.; Letendre, S.; Seedat, S.; Womersley, J. S.
data.abstract: Introduction: Neurocognitive impairment and depression remain common among people with HIV (PWH), and childhood maltreatment (CM) may further increase vulnerability. In this cohort, we previously reported that PWH exhibited shorter absolute telomere length, lower MRI-based brain-predicted age difference, and greater epigenetic age acceleration (AA) compared to controls, with limited associations with CM severity. Building on this, the present study examines whether these markers are linked to neurocognitive performance and depressive symptoms, and whether HIV status or CM severity moderates such associations. Methods: In this study of 238 women (122 PWH), biological aging was assessed using absolute telomere length, mitochondrial DNA copy number, MRI-based brain-predicted age difference, and DNA methylation AA measures, including Horvath, Hannum, PhenoAge, Horvath intrinsic epigenetic, and Hannum intrinsic epigenetic and extrinsic epigenetic AA. Neurocognitive performance was measured using a standardised assessment battery and global deficit scores (GDS) were derived. Depressive symptoms were assessed with the Centre for Epidemiologic Studies - Depression Scale. Linear regression models examined associations with GDS and depressive symptoms, with interaction models evaluating moderation by HIV status and CM severity. Results: Biological aging markers were not associated with either neurocognitive performance or depressive symptoms. Though HIV infection in combination with higher mitochondrial DNA copy number and extrinsic epigenetic AA was nominally associated with higher GDS (p = 0.012 and p = 0.047, respectively), these associations did not survive correction for multiple testing. Neither HIV nor CM moderated the association between biological aging markers and depression scores. Conclusions: Despite accelerated biological aging being evident in PWH, we found limited evidence of association with neurocognitive performance or depressive symptoms, underscoring their multifactorial nature. Larger longitudinal studies are needed to determine whether these markers predict neurocognitive and psychiatric trajectories.

data.title: Preprint: Post-Vaccination COVID-19 Infection and Its Correlates among Residents of Chandra, Gazipur, Bangladesh: A Cross-Sectional Study
data.authors: Al Hasan Pranto, A.; Sushmita Zafar, S.; Fakhruzzaman, M.; Rahman, M. S.; Akter, S.; Taslima Meem, J.; Sultana, R.; Afridi, S.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Saic College of Medical Science and Technology
data.abstract: Background: COVID 19 vaccines are highly effective at preventing severe disease and death but post vaccination (breakthrough) infections are still seen, especially with immune-evasive variants. There is some evidence at the community level from Bangladesh. The aim of this study was to estimate prevalence, clinical profile and correlates of post-vaccination COVID 19 infection in Chandra, Kaliakair, Gazipur, Bangladesh. Methods: This was a community based cross-sectional study that included adults & 8805;18 years of age with at least one dose of a COVID 19 vaccine from March 2021 to December 2022. The respondents were 300 people who were selected by multistage sampling technique and interviewed with a pretested semi-structured questionnaire. Demographic, vaccination history, post vaccination infection, clinical features, preventive behaviours, knowledge and comorbidities data were gathered. The chi square test was used to test the bivariate associations and multivariable binary logistic regression was used to identify independent correlates. A p value of < 0.05 was used to determine statistical significance. Ethical Approval took from the IRB board of SCMST. Results: Among 300 participants (mean age 48.0 17.6 years; 52.0% male), 124 (41.3%) reported COVID 19 infection after vaccination. Of these, 24 (19.4%) were asymptomatic, 67 (54.0%) had mild disease, 24 (19.4%) had moderate disease, and 9 (7.3%) had severe disease; only 12 (9.7%) required hospitalisation. In multivariable analysis, rural residence (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 4.87; 95% CI 2.42 9.79), poor mask use (aOR 2.28; 95% CI 1.31 3.97), poor physical distancing (aOR 2.74; 95% CI 1.55 4.86), poor hand hygiene (aOR 3.61; 95% CI 2.05 6.38), and diabetes (aOR 4.46; 95% CI 1.97 10.14) were independently associated with higher odds of infection, whereas receipt of a booster dose was protective (aOR 0.23; 95% CI 0.13 0.42). Conclusion: P st-vaccination infection was common but largely mild and hospitalisation was rare. The booster vaccination was protective and factors such as rural residence, poor preventive practices and diabetes were risk factors for infection. These results do reinforce the importance of booster doses coupled with ongoing preventive behaviour and targeted interventions for clinically vulnerable populations.

data.title: Preprint: Tuberculosis treatment outcome in Cameroon: a systematic review and meta-analysis
data.authors: Cheuyem, F. Z. L.; Zefack, J. T.; Tchamani, R.; Achangwa, C.; Mapouo, C. J. K.; Tsapi, A. T.; Minkandi, C. A.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Public Health, Faculty of Medicine and Biomedical Sciences, The University of Yaounde 1, Yaounde, Cameroon
data.abstract: Background: Tuberculosis (TB) remains a major public health challenge in Cameroon, yet national evidence on treatment outcomes across the full spectrum of routine care is limited. This systematic review and meta-analysis estimated pooled proportions of treatment success, mortality, treatment failure and loss to follow-up (LTFU) among TB patients in Cameroon, and identified predictors of unfavorable outcomes. Methods: PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, African Journals Online and the Cochrane Library were searched, supplemented by Google Scholar and reference-list screening. Observational studies conducted in Cameroon reporting at least one WHO-defined treatment outcome were eligible. Pooled proportions and adjusted odds ratios (AOR) were estimated with random-effects models meta-analysis. Data were analyzed using R Statistics version 4.6.1. Results: Thirty-two studies (25 cohorts, 7 cross-sectional), conducted between 1998 and 2022 across six of Cameroon's ten regions, were included. Pooled treatment success was 78.2% (95% CI: 73.8-82.1; 27 reports; 71,784 participants; I2= 98.2%), mortality 8.1% (95% CI: 5.5-11.7; 25 reports; 71,870 participants; I2 = 97.8%), treatment failure 0.9% (95% CI: 0.5-1.4; 26 reports; 71,389 participants; I2 = 89.1%) and LTFU 6.8% (95% CI: 5.0-9.1; 26 reports; 70,768 participants; I2 = 98.6%). Mortality was highest in the South-West (16.2%) and among TB/HIV-coinfected patients (30.5%), and lowest among children (5.0%). Treatment success was lowest in the Littoral (71.1%) and among TB/HIV-coinfected patients (60.8%) and highest among multidrug-resistant TB (89.3%) and pediatric patients (86.8%). Treatment failure significantly declined from 2.9% before 2005 to 0.5% from 2020 onward (p < 0.001). Significant predictors of unfavorable outcomes were HIV positivity (AOR = 2.57; 95% CI: 1.86-3.55), previous TB treatment (AOR = 1.99; 95% CI: 1.40-2.84), male sex (AOR = 1.67; 95% CI: 1.45-1.92), age [≤]40 years (AOR = 1.45; 95% CI: 1.06-1.98) and absence of antiretroviral therapy (AOR = 1.71; 95% CI: 1.15-2.54). Conclusions: TB treatment outcomes in Cameroon remain suboptimal, with nearly one in five patients not achieving treatment success and high mortality among TB/HIV-coinfected individuals. Strengthening TB/HIV service integration, early antiretroviral therapy initiation, targeted support for previously treated patients and men, and improved retention in care are needed. Systematic review registration number: CRD420261404490

data.title: Preprint: Sex- and Age-Specific Associations of Blood Lead Levels with Child Growth and Haemoglobin in Bangladesh: A Nationally Representative Study
data.authors: Patwary, M. M.; Ashraf, S.; Islam, M. A.; Browning, M. H. E. M.; Bell, M. L.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Environment and Sustainability Research Initiative, Khulna, Bangladesh
data.abstract: Evidence on sex- and age-specific associations between lead levels and childhood growth remains limited. We analyzed 10,324 children aged 12-59 months from the Bangladesh Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey 2025 using survey-weighted multivariable linear regression to examine sex- and age-specific associations of blood lead level (BLL) with anthropometric measures and haemoglobin levels. The geometric mean BLL was 4.43 {micro}g/dL, and 66.3% of children had concentrations above the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) threshold ([≥]3.5 {micro}g/dL). Higher BLL was associated with lower height-for-age z-score (HAZ) ({beta} = -0.129, 95% CI: -0.182 to -0.076), weight-for-age z-score (WAZ) ({beta} = -0.108, 95% CI: -0.156 to -0.060), and weight-for-height z-score (WHZ) ({beta} = -0.052, 95% CI: -0.101 to -0.002). Higher BLL was also associated with lower HAZ and WAZ among boys (HAZ: {beta} = -0.114, 95% CI: -0.188 to -0.040; WAZ: {beta} = -0.113, 95% CI: -0.179 to -0.046) and girls (HAZ: {beta} = -0.150, 95% CI: -0.225 to -0.075; WAZ: {beta} = -0.104, 95% CI: -0.171 to -0.036), while higher BLL was associated with lower WHZ among boys ({beta} = -0.076, 95% CI: -0.144 to -0.007). Higher BLL was associated with lower HAZ ({beta} = -0.266, 95% CI: -0.408 to -0.125) and WAZ ({beta} = -0.206, 95% CI: -0.326 to -0.086) among boys aged 24-35 months, while among girls aged 36-59 months, corresponding estimates were -0.211 (95% CI: -0.310 to -0.113) and -0.106 (95% CI: -0.191 to -0.022). The findings suggest that longitudinal studies are needed to clarify the temporal and developmental patterns underlying these associations.

data.title: Preprint: Development and pilot evaluation of ACE-T, a nurse-focused delirium initial-response tool, across three health systems
data.authors: Cours, A.; Trabert, J.; Higgins, M.; Saleem, U.; Sampson, E.; Storr-Street, N.; MacLullich, A.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Section of Geriatric Medicine, Primary Care and Population Health, Department of Medicine, Stanford University School of Medicine, Palo Alto, CA, USA
data.abstract: Background A positive delirium screen should trigger timely assessment and care, but the initial bedside response is not always clearly defined. ACE-T (Acute Triggers / Patient Experience / Treatments) is a nurse-led tool (www.theace-t.com) that sets out initial care actions and supports documentation and team communication. Objectives To assess perceived usability and utility, refine the tool, and describe documentation before and after its introduction at three hospitals. Methods In this developmental pilot, 53 multidisciplinary staff completed a structured survey and provided free-text feedback. We also reviewed a non-random sample of 60 records: 10 before and 10 after ACE-T introduction at each site. Prespecified delirium-care actions documented within 48 hours of the first positive delirium screen or documented diagnosis were summarised descriptively by site. Results ACE-T was rated easy or very easy to use by 75% (39/52), clear or very clear by 77% (41/53), and very or extremely helpful for improving delirium care by 71% (37/52). Feedback guided revisions to clarify professional roles, fit clinical workflows and strengthen person-centred prompts. Documentation of delirium or suspected delirium was more frequent after introduction at all three sites: 1/10 before versus 10/10 after in Germany, 0/10 versus 10/10 in the UK, and 3/10 versus 9/10 in the USA. Changes in documentation of other assessments varied by site. Conclusion ACE-T is a promising nurse-led tool for initial delirium care. Positive staff ratings and more frequent delirium documentation support its further development and prospective evaluation. It offers nurses a practical starting point for what to do next when delirium is detected.

data.title: Preprint: Protocol for a controlled human infection with genetically modified Neisseria lactamica expressing the meningococcal vaccine antigens NadA and FHbp: The GM-Nlac Pilot Study
data.authors: Chick, G.; Gbesemete, D. F.; Jump Salcedo, P.; Wilson, M. W.; Hill, A. R.; Coutinho, T. J.; Anderson, R.; Elliott, R. S.; Mohanraj, D.; Cleary, D. W.; Lucidarme, J.; Borrow, R.; Faust, S. N.; Gorringe, A. R.; Read, R. C.; Dale, A. P.; Laver, J. R.
data.author_corresponding_institution: Controlled Human Infection Group, School of Clinical & Experimental Sciences, Faculty of Medicine, University of Southampton, Southampton, UK
data.abstract: Introduction Previous work has shown that experimentally induced colonisation with Neisseria lactamica (Nlac) is safe and associated with reduced meningococcal colonisation. This pilot study aims to establish the safety, induction of colonisation and immunogenicity following intranasal inoculation with a mixture of four strains of genetically modified Nlac (GM-Nlac). Each of these strains express meningococcal vaccine antigens present in current vaccines: Neisseria adhesin A (NadA) and one of four different variants of Factor H-binding protein (FHbp), the latter of which is specifically mutated to abrogate its ability to bind the human complement protein, Factor H. Methods and analysis In this controlled human infection model experiment, 10 healthy participants aged 18-45 years will be inoculated with a mixture of 4 strains of GM-Nlac (collectively referred to as the challenge agent, 4xrNlac). They will be followed up over 28 days to assess colonisation, immunogenicity and efficacy of eradication with a single oral dose of ciprofloxacin (500 mg). Participant contacts will also be recruited to assess for onward transmission of GM-Nlac. Ethics and dissemination This study involves the deliberate release of four genetically modified organisms, which has been approved by the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (reference: 25/R50/01). The clinical study has also been approved by South-Central Oxford A Research Ethics Committee and the Health Research Authority (reference: 26/SC/0072). All participants will provide written informed consent prior to enrolment. Findings of the study will be submitted for publication in a peer-reviewed scientific journal and for presentation at scientific conferences. Registration This study is registered on the ISRCTN registry with study registration number ISRCTN10930766

Methods and analysis In this controlled human infection model experiment, 10 healthy participants aged 18-45 years will be inoculated with a mixture of 4 strains of GM-Nlac (collectively referred to as the challenge agent, 4xrNlac). They will be followed up over 28 days to assess colonisation, immunogenicity and efficacy of eradication with a single oral dose of ciprofloxacin (500 mg). Participant contacts will also be recruited to assess for onward transmission of GM-Nlac. Ethics and dissemination This study involves the deliberate release of four genetically modified organisms, which has been approved by the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (reference: 25/R50/01). The clinical study has also been approved by South-Central Oxford A Research Ethics Committee and the Health Research Authority (reference: 26/SC/0072). All participants will provide written informed consent prior to enrolment. Findings of the study will be submitted for publication in a peer-reviewed scientific journal and for presentation at scientific conferences. Registration This study is registered on the ISRCTN registry with study registration number ISRCTN10930766

data.title: Preprint: Implementing a Group Education Model for People with Type 2 Diabetes in a Socioeconomically Deprived Primary Care Population: A Quality Improvement Report
data.authors: Bond, E.; Sennett, J.; Veighey, K.
data.abstract: People with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) receiving injectable therapies require ongoing education and support to optimise self-management and glycaemic control. Group education may offer a cost-effective approach that combines professional guidance with peer support. Homewell Practice serves a socioeconomically deprived population in Hampshire with significant health inequalities. Many patients receiving insulin or GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy had poor glycaemic control, frailty, or increased risk of hospital admission. Traditional one-to-one consultations provided limited opportunities for peer learning and support. A 12-month quality improvement project was conducted between May 2022 and April 2023. Adults with T2DM receiving injectable therapy were invited to attend monthly community-based education sessions. Attendance data, HbA1c outcomes and patient feedback were collected and analysed descriptively. Patient-centred group sessions were delivered using adult-learning principles and peer discussion. Topics included insulin titration, hypoglycaemia management, nutrition, glycaemic targets and diabetes complications. Fifteen patients attended at least one session. Improvements in glycaemic control were associated with repeated attendance. Mean HbA1c reduction was 12.4% in patients attending four or more sessions, compared with 5.6% for those attending three sessions and 2.4% for those attending two sessions. Patients attending only one session demonstrated a 1.8% increase in HbA1c. All questionnaire respondents (9/9, 100%) reported improved understanding of diabetes and found the sessions useful; 8/9 would recommend the programme. Peer support was identified as the most valued aspect of participation. Attendance remained lower than anticipated, particularly among patients with multiple comorbidities and mental health needs. Group education for adults receiving injectable diabetes therapy was associated with high patient satisfaction and improved glycaemic outcomes among regular attendees. A hybrid model combining group education with individualised support may improve accessibility and engagement for higher-need patients.

data.title: Preprint: Development and 10-year validation of QRISK4-Lifetime for cardiovascular risk prediction in 13 million adults
data.authors: Hippisley-Cox, J.; Coupland, C.
data.abstract: Objective To develop QRISK4-Lifetime to estimate cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk to age 95, compare its 10-year performance with QRISK4 and examine differences in risk classification between the two time horizons. Methods We used the linked electronic health datasets and cohort framework of the original QRISK4 study. We fitted sex-specific cause-specific Cox models for incident CVD and death from other causes, using attained age at cohort entry. Predicted risks combined both cause-specific hazards. We assessed discrimination and calibration at 10 years overall, by age and ethnicity. We compared characteristics of patients with a 10-year QRISK4-Lifetime risk [≥] 10% with an equal-sized group selected using lifetime risk to age 95 Results There were 202,424 CVD events in the English derivation cohort of 9,976,306 people and 65,253 events in the validation cohort of 3,246,602 people. Overall C-indices were 0.860 (95% CI 0.858 to 0.862) in women and 0.845 (0.843 to 0.847) in men for both QRISK4-Lifetime and QRISK4. Observed risks were close to predicted risks. Each risk classification approach selected 310,648 patients (9.6%); 262,417 (8.1% of the cohort) met only the lifetime threshold. Of these, 72.8% were younger than 40 years and 79.5% were men. Conclusions QRISK4-Lifetime had similar performance to QRISK4 when evaluated at 10 years. Lifetime assessment identified a substantially younger population with increased lifetime risks but below the specified 10-year threshold of 10%, supporting its potential complementary role in prevention discussions. The validity of lifetime estimates and the clinical consequences of using both time horizons require further evaluation.

data.title: Preprint: Assessing anterior shoulder instability: Reliability of the humeral head centralization test
data.authors: Van Gastel, M. L.; Hekman, K. M. C.; Boden, B. J. H.; Scholten-Peeters, G. G. M.; Dijksman, L. M.; van den Bekerom, M. P. J.
data.abstract: Background: Motor control impairment of the rotator cuff muscles is reported to compromise the stability of the glenohumeral joint. However, an easily applicable, reliable parameter for quantifying anterior translation of the humeral head during active arm movements is lacking. Therefore, a novel (humeral head centralization) test was developed and evaluated. Study design: Case-control study with reliability analysis (Level III). Methods: This research project examined the shoulders of 25 patients with anterior shoulder instability and 25 asymptomatic controls. A physical therapist assessed humeral head translation in both groups during shoulder external rotation and elbow extension using ultrasound imaging. For test-retest and inter-rater reliability, the ultrasound assessment was repeated by the physical therapist and a radiologist after one week. Patients, the physical therapist, and the radiologist were blinded to the test results. In the evaluation of the difference in translation between the patients and controls, the Wilcoxon rank sum test was employed. The test-retest and inter-rater reliability were estimated using Intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC2,1). Results: In patients, in active elbow extension, a significantly greater anterior translation of the humeral head was observed compared to participants in the asymptomatic group (p < .001). The test-retest reliability of the physical therapist demonstrated poor agreement for the external rotation movement (ICC2,1 0.32 (95% CI -0.08-0.63)) and moderate agreement for the extension movement of the elbow (ICC2,1 0.66 (95% CI 0.36-0.84)). The inter-rater reliability of the physical therapist and radiologist was moderate for both the external rotation (ICC2,1 0.51 (95% CI 0.16-0.75)) and elbow extension movements (ICC2,1 0.62 (95% CI 0.30-0.82)). Conclusion: Although translation of the humeral head during active elbow extension movement was increased in patients compared to controls, this study found difficulties in reliably measuring anterior glenohumeral translation. Therefore, this novel test, in its current form, cannot be recommended for use in clinical practice or research.

data.title: Preprint: A Multicenter Retrospective Study on the Safety and Efficacy of the Surpass Evolve Flow Diverter System for the Treatment of Intracranial Aneurysms
data.authors: Zhu, D.; Zhang, M.; Ma, W.; Zhang, S.; Zhao, J.; Chen, G.; Fang, Y.
data.abstract: Objective: To evaluate the safety and efficacy of the Surpass Evolve flow diverter system for the treatment of intracranial aneurysms across three medical centers. Methods: A retrospective review was conducted on patients with intracranial aneurysms treated with the Surpass Evolve FDS between March 2023 and May 2024 at three participating centers. Primary outcome measures included the rate of complete aneurysm occlusion (Raymond-Roy class 1) and the incidence of periprocedural major stroke and mortality. Secondary outcomes encompassed follow-up modified Rankin Scale (mRS) scores, imaging assessment results, and complication rates. Results: A total of 132 patients (132 aneurysms) were included. The median age was 60.0 years (IQR 52.5?69.0), and 80 patients (66.6%) were female. The complete occlusion rate was 73.3% (88/120). The rate of major stroke was 2.3%, with no procedure-related mortality. At follow-up, 96.9% of patients had an mRS score of 0?2. Multivariate analysis identified non-use of an intraprocedural IIb/IIIa inhibitor and the absence of a branch arising from the aneurysm as independent predictors of complete occlusion. Conclusion: In this real-world, multicenter, retrospective study, the treatment of intracranial aneurysms with the Surpass Evolve FDS was associated with a high rate of complete occlusion and a favorable safety profile. Our findings indicate that complete occlusion was independently predicted by two key factors: periprocedural avoidance of IIb/IIIa inhibitors and a favorable aneurysm morphology without incorporated branches.
